Okay, elcome to one of my favorite sections

and these are very important steps
because we are going to automate all these steps
and this is super important.
So what is CIDD?
So first, CICD is about continuous integration,
and that means that the developers
are going to push the code
very often into a central code repository.

which is a third party service from AWS,
or CodeCommit, which is its AWS service,

and then there's going to be a test
or build server that will check if the code is correct

So the build server is going to fetch a code and test it,
and then as a developer, we're going to get feedback
as to whether or not the test
or checks will have passed or failed.
And so we get the build and test results,
but we've saved time.
So with this, we find bug early and we fix them early
because we are testing the code
as soon as it is pushed in a code repository.
So the developer doesn't need
to test the code on their machine,
they can just push the code and wait for the build server
to do it while they do some other tasks.
Therefore, the code is going to be delivered faster
because it's going to be tested.
Thanks to this, we're gonna be able to deploy often
because as soon as it's tested and ready, we can deploy it.
And then happier developers,
because developers have a healthier cycle for development.
So we saw CI and now there is CD,
so it could be continuous delivery, for example.
And so let's give you this example.
So here we have application servers of version 1,

Anytime we push the code onto the code repo,
it's going to be deployed if it's tested appropriately

So the developer pushes the code.
The code is going to be tested by the build server.

and then after the build is passed, so it is green,

then there's going to be a deployment server.
And this deployment server
is going to deploy our application
onto our application servers.
So version 1 at first.
But then if we push again, a new version

So with continuous delivery,
we ensure that deployments happen often

from a mentality of let's do one release every three months,
which is very long to do, you know, error prone
because it doesn't happen very often,

the code is going to be live

# 8. CodeCommit - Advanced
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858370
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So a few extra topics for CodeCommit.
The first one is that you can monitor any kind of events
happening in CodeCommit through EventBridge.
So anytime there is a pull request that is created
or that a pull request status changes,
or a new reference is created, or a new comment is created,
then you can react to that in EventBridge
which gives you some cool automation opportunities
because for example, say you wanted to react
to a new pull request, you could, through EventBridge,
invoke SNS, Lambda, or CodePipeline.
Also, how do you migrate a repository
from one place to CodeCommit?
Well, if your repository is hosted on another place
such as GitHub or GitLab,
then you can push it to CodeCommit very simply.
The way you do it is that first you need to create
your CodeCommit repository, but then you do a git clone.
Now, this git clone command is going to take
the entire content of your Git repository from the server
and put it on your local computer.
That means all project files, all commits, everything.
And then once the project is cloned
onto your local computer,
you can push it to a different URL.
So instead of pushing it back to the Git server,
you can push it to a new Git place
such as your CodeCommit repository.
And that's how you migrate a Git repo.
So how can we achieve
a cross-region replication in CodeCommit?
Well, we would want to do cross-region replication,
for example, to have lower latency
for pulls for global developers,
or to have a backup of a repo.
So say for example, we want to have a copy of us-east-1
into eu-west-2 with replication.
So how does that work?
Well, for example, whenever we push to an existing branch
or we create and delete a branch,
CodeCommit will actually emit an event in EventBridge
called referenceCreated or referenceUpdated.
So this is the type of event that will appear.
And from there, EventBridge can trigger,
for example, an ECS task.
The ECS task will do a git clone
of the CodeCommit repository,
and then we'll replicate it
to the target repository in eu-west-2.
So we could use an ECS task, but I'm pretty sure
we could also use a CodeBuild task if we wanted to.
And so this is how thanks to EventBridge
we can achieve cross-region replication
of a CodeCommit repo.
So what about branch security in CodeCommit?
Well, as soon as you grant a user push permission
into a CodeCommit repo,
they can contribute to any branch they want.
And so to restrict to which branch they can contribute to,
you need to restrict the users.
And for this, we use IAM policies.
So say we have a CodeCommit repo
with production, staging, and development branch
and we want to only allow the senior developers
to push the code to the production branch.
So here we allow it through IAM policies,
but the other IAM policies we apply to the junior developers
will prevent them from pushing into production.
So this is the kind of IAM policy that looks like it.
So here we have a deny effect
and if we look at the condition, we say,
hey, we deny if it looks like you're pushing
into the main or the prod branches.
And so this IAM policy must be attached
to your junior developer groups, for example,
and then they won't be able to push into prod.
So you may say, well, what about resource policies?
What about an IAM policy directly attached
into your CodeCommit repository?
Well, for now, it is not supported yet.
So the only way to do branch security is to deal with it
at the user level or the group level directly in IAM.
Now, if there is a pull request,
so that means a proposed change into a branch,
then you can set up approval rules.
So these approval rules ensure that the quality of your code
has been reviewed and approved by a certain amount of people
before the PR, the pull request is merged.
So with a pull request approval rule,
we specify a pool of users to approve
and then a number of users we need to approve for the PR.
So for example, we have a pull request
on our CodeCommit repo
and we've defined a pool of five users
that can approve this request,
but we need two of them to accept it.
So maybe user one will review it and accept it.
User three will review it and accept it.
Therefore, your pull request will be accepted.
And once accepted,
then it can be merged into the repository.
So to specify who and what can accept pull request,
we can specify IAM principles ARN
such as users, federated users,
IAM roles, IAM groups, and so on.
Also, if you wanted to automatically create
these kind of approval rules on any pull request,
then we can use a template and we say,
okay, you should apply these approval rules directly
for any pull request in the dev and the prod branches.
Okay, so that's it for CodeCommit.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 9. [DVA] CodePipeline - Overview
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858378
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk about CodePipeline,
which is a visual workflow tool that will allow you
to orchestrate your CI/CD within AWS.
So with CodePipeline, you can show sources such as hey,
my code is in CodeCommit
or we have a Docker image in ECR,
or my code is in Amazon S3.
Or even external tools such as Bitbucket or GitHub.
Then you can move on to the build phase, which is, hey,
now that we have this code, let's build it.
So CodeBuild, Jenkins, CloudBees, TeamCity are all options.
Then once you have the build phase,
you can have the test phase.
So again, testing your code.
So CodeBuild or Device Farm
if you have an app, for example, an iOS, an Android app,
or any third-party tools you want.
Then once the code is tested, you want to deploy it.
So CodeDeploy, Beanstalk, CloudFormation, ECS, S3,
all these options can be handled by CodePipeline.
And Invoke to invoke a Lambda function or a step function.
And then when you have all these building blocks,
you can build stages.
So each stage can have sequential actions
and/or parallel actions.
You can do a lot of things.
Here's a very simple example.
Build, test, deploy onto staging,
then load testing to make sure staging is doing fine.
And then once the load testing is done,
maybe deploy again to production.
Now, there's also a way for you to define manual approval
at any stage in your pipeline,
really allowing you, for example,
just before deploying to prod
to have someone review the results
of the load testing, for example, if it was there.
And make sure it says, yeah, looks good.
Green light, deploy to prod.
So CodePipeline really is here to orchestrate everything
and it gives you a lot
of flexibility thanks to all the building blocks
as we'll see in the next lectures.
Now, how does CodePipeline work inside?
So let's assume we have a source,
a build and a deploy phase.
So source is CodeCommit.
Build is CodeBuild,
even though we haven't seen CodeBuild yet,
and Deploy is CodeDeploy
even though we haven't seen CodeDeploy yet.
So each pipeline can create artifacts.
Artifacts is whatever is created out of the pipeline
and the artifacts are going to be stored
in S3 buckets to be passed onto the next stage.
And this is how the next stage is going to be able
to do what it needs to do.
So let's do a concrete example.
Developer is going to push some code
into CodeCommit, right?
And then CodeCommit is going to be orchestrated
by CodePipeline, which is going to extract all the code
and create an artifact out of it
and place that artifact into an S3 bucket.
Now, when CodeBuild is invoked, the same artifacts
that were extracted are going to be inputted directly
into CodeBuild, and that's why CodeBuild doesn't need
to have straight access into CodeCommit.
Actually, it's CodePipeline that will be pushing the code
to CodeBuild through Amazon S3.
Then when CodeBuild is building the code,
it's going to create some deployment artifacts.
So these artifacts are going to be stored yet again
in your S3 bucket by CodePipeline,
and CodePipeline will push these artifacts yet again
to CodeDeploy and CodeDeploy says hey,
I have these artifacts, I need to deploy them.
Let's go ahead and deploy them.
So as you can see, these stages interact with each other
through Amazon S3,
and this is why we have artifacts in CodePipeline.
Now, some troubleshooting for CodePipeline.
So if you need to have a look
at all these things, for example, you need to look
at like CodePipeline action
or stage execution state changes,
you can use CloudWatch Events,
EventBridge to have a look at them.
So for example, you can create events for failed pipelines,
events for cancelled stages
and then receive an email notification, for example.
And then if CodePipeline has a failure at a stage,
you will see it visually
and you can get information through the console.
And if there is no way
for CodePipeline to perform a specific action, for example,
to invoke some code in CodeBuild
or to pull the code from CodeCommit,
then check the IAM service role of CodePipeline
and make sure it has right IAM permissions.
Also, if you need to have a look
at maybe some denied API calls within your infrastructure,
you can use CloudTrail,
which is a service used to audit AWS API calls.
So let's say for CodePipeline,
it will make a lot more sense once we go to the hands on.
So I will see you in the next lecture.
I hope you liked it and let's get some practice.

# 12. [DVA] CodePipeline - Extras
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858390
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about some few additional
points about CodePipeline.
The first one is that you have the concept
to start a pipeline of events, webhooks and polling.
So let's have a look at all of them
and see which one is best in which situation.
So events is going to be the preferred way in CodePipeline,
and this says to start a pipeline whenever we have an event.
So for example, when we have CodeCommit, for example,
we know that on a new commit,
an event will happen in EventBridge,
and the event bridge rule associated with that event
can trigger and start a CodePipeline.
This is the preferred way, and it's not only CodeCommit,
but could be any kind of events within AWS.
With GitHub, which is not part of AWS,
how do you have event driven starting of CodePipeline?
Well, to do so, you're going to use
what's called a CodeStar Source Connection.
It's just a fancy name for a GitHub application
that is going to connect GitHub into AWS.
And then from this you're going to trigger CodePipeline.
So these things are event driven and they are very fast
because as soon as the event happens,
CodePipeline is going to be triggered.
An older way of triggering CodePipeline is using webhook.
So if you choose that option, then CodePipeline is going
to expose an HTTP endpoint
and that endpoint can be triggered
by a script, whatever you want.
If that script sends a payload to CodePipeline
on that webhook, then CodePipeline is going to start.
And finally, you can have CodePipeline poll the source,
in which case you have regular checks, for example,
from CodePipeline onto GitHub, but that is not recommended
because it's not as efficient as events.
So events are the default
and recommended way to start a CodePipeline.
Next, we have this table on CodePipeline
that you don't have to learn.
I'm going to just help you decrypt it
and help you understand what it means.
So we have owner, action type, provider,
and then a valid number
of input artifacts and output artifacts.
The last two columns we don't need to look at,
we're going to look at the first three.
So the owner can be either AWS
and that means that it's an action related
to an AWS service.
It could be a third party.
That's when action is related to a third party,
such as GitHub or Alexa Skills Kit.
Or custom, and this is once you have something like Jenkins.
So remember AWS for AWS and third party and custom.
Now the action type corresponds
to different stages of your pipeline.
For example, you have the source for S3, ECR,
GitHub, CodeCommit.
We have the build for CodeBuild and Jenkins.
We have the test for CodeBuild, Device Farm, and Jenkins.
We have approval and the action type is called manual.
We'll see this in the next slide as well. That's important.
Invoke for Lambda and Step Functions, and deploy for S3,
CloudFormation, CodeDeploy, Elastic Beanstalk,
ECS and Service Catalog.
Now don't worry if you don't know some of these services,
you will see them in the course.
And of course you will very easily understand
if they are of type source, build, test and so on.
So why do I show you this?
Well, because the approval type of manual
is part of an exam question that can come up.
So let's go over the details of how manual approval works.
So when you have a CodePipeline
and you have a manual approval, the important part
is that the owner is AWS
because it says related to within AWS,
it's a capability offered by an AWS service,
and the action is going to be manual
because it says a manual approval.
In which case when you have a manual approval,
what's going to happen is that you can trigger an SNS topic,
which is in turn you can send in emails to a user
and the user will have an IAM user on AWS.
And then you will have to approve this stage.
And to approve this stage, it needs permissions.
And the permissions the user must have are twofold.
Number one is GetPipeline
because while the user must be able to get to your pipeline
to actually view it and to find that manual approval step.
So we want the GetPipeline* type of action,
and then we want the PutApprovalResult action
on the approval action itself
because we want to be able to say yes or no,
we approve or we deny.
So that's all you need to know.
But it's important to understand the IAM user permissions
as well as the fact that the step owner is AWS
and the action of the step is manual.
Alright, that's it for this lecture.

# 13. CodePipeline - CloudFormation Integration
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858392
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about using CloudFormation
as a target for CodePipeline.
So CloudFormation is a deploy action
and it can be used to deploy any kind of AWS resources
and including Lambda functions,
either as pure CloudFormation
or using the CDK framework or using SAML.
So the idea is that from CodePipeline,
you have your code in CodeCommit.
The code could be directly the template itself.
You can create a change set from CloudFormation,
then a manual approval to make sure
that the change set is what we want it to be.
And then execute the change sets.
This is one option.
You can just go ahead also and deploy things right directly
without doing a manual approval.
So on top of supporting CloudFormation in one region,
you support CloudFormation's StackSets to deploy
across multiple AWS accounts and AWS regions.
On top of things, you can configure multiple settings,
such as the stack name, the change set name,
the template input,
the parameters if you want to override them,
the IAM role, the action mode, and so on.
So let's have a look at an architecture
and a use case for using CodePipeline with CloudFormation.
So we have CodePipeline and we build our app in CodeBuild
and we create a template.yaml file out of it.
Next, we use CloudFormation
to actually deploy the infrastructure in our app
and we use the CREATE_UPDATE mode to create
or update an existing stack.
So our entire stack will be deployed.
For example, this is an ALB
with an auto scaling group and EC2 instances.
And then we have a new stage
to test the application using CodeBuild.
So CodeBuild can run, for example, test
against the ALB by using the HTTP protocol
and make sure our application is functioning as expected.
It could be a functional test, it could be load testing,
it could be whatever you want.
If all of this is working,
that means that our application version is working
as expected and we can, for example,
delete the test infrastructure using the DELETE_ONLY action
for CloudFormation to delete the stack.
And then another CloudFormation action,
this time to deploy the prod infrastructure
in prod by using again the CREATE_UPDATE action,
which in this time is going
to actually update our prod infrastructure.
So hope that makes sense, but that makes it very easy
for you to create infrastructure and destroy them as part
of your CI/CD pipeline.
So let's summarize the different action modes.
So the first one is about change sets.
So we can create or replace a change set
or we can execute a change set.
This is usually when you want to have a manual approval
in this to verify the change sets before applying it.
Or if you don't want to have a manual approval,
then you just want to deal with stacks.
So you can create or update a stack, delete a stack
or replace a failed stack.
All of these are action modes
in CodePipeline for CloudFormation.
You can also override template parameters.
So in this case, you just specify a JSON object
to override these parameter values.
And this object can be part
of the input artifact that you give to CodePipeline.
And then you say, okay,
which parameter gets replaced by what?
So all the parameters must be present in a template
and you can have a static override.
So use a template configuration file or dynamic
to use parameters to pass them into your template.
Bottom line is just to make it as simple as possible,
you can override the parameters
if you wanted to at runtime using CodePipeline.
So that's it for CodePipeline in CloudFormation.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 14. CodePipeline - Advanced
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858394
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, let's have a few more slides
on CodePipeline.
So, the first one is around best practices of CodePipeline.
So, in this example, we have one CodePipeline,
one CodeDeploy, and from CodeDeploy,
we do parallel deployments
into multiple deployment groups.
So, you would wanna do this, for example,
if you wanted to deploy into multiple environments
at a time, or multiple deployment groups.
So, instead of creating two CodeDeploy deployments,
you would create one with multiple groups.
There is also a way for you to speed things up
in CodePipeline using Parallel Actions.
So, if you have, for example, CodeCommit,
and you wanna run two kinds of build,
or some build and some test, or whatever you want,
then instead of having one after the other,
if you specify the same RunOrder value,
then they will be run in parallel.
So, this is very helpful when building, for example,
this is very helpful when deploying into multiple regions,
and so on.
Also, you can deploy to pre-prod
before deploying to prod,
and have a manual approval before deploying to prod.
This is a very common pattern in CodePipeline.
Any kind of events happening in CodePipeline
are going to be detected in EventBridge.
So, this is for any state's execution changes,
or, for example, to intercept failures.
So, if we have this CodePipeline and CodeBuild fails,
we can, for example, intercept it in EventBridge,
and then invoke a Lambda function to, for example,
diagnose the code, or trigger an SNS notification
to notify some users by email, for example.
If you wanted to run an API call from CodePipeline,
the best way for you would be to invoke,
and to invoke, you would use Lambda functions,
and Lambda functions can be invoked,
and from there we can run whatever code we want,
such as calling a REST API.
There is no way to have CodePipeline directly do this,
so invoking a Lambda function does extend the capability
of CodePipeline by a lot.
Also, if you wanted to start step functions,
you can now do this thanks to the Invoke Action.
So, we can start a state machine within the pipeline.
So, step functions allow us to do whatever we want,
such as, for example,
inserting items into a DynamoDB table,
or starting a task in ECS,
and having a graph, a workflow to show all these things
happening one after the other.
And so, it's possible thanks to step functions.
Then we can, for example,
once the step functions as executed
to go and start a CodeBuild build,
and, for example, CodeBuild could have a script
to retrieve some value out of some DynamoDB table.
Again, I don't have the precise example in mind,
but it just gives you an idea of how we can combine
step functions into a CodePipeline.
And finally, well after CodeBuild,
you deploy into CodeDeploy.
There's also a way for you to do multi-region deployments
with CodePipeline.
So, it's actually the fact that any or many actions
in your pipeline can be in different regions.
So, for example, the use case for this would be to deploy
a Lambda function through CloudFormation
into multiple regions, all from one CodePipeline.
So, to make this work, is very important for you to remember
that S3 Artifact Stores must be defined
for your CodePipeline for each region
where you have actions.
So, Artifact Stores is where the artifacts of CodePipeline
are being stored.
And, of course, we know there's one
for your main CodePipeline wherever it is located.
But in case you have actions in multiple regions,
you must define these Artifact Stores.
So, if you are doing so,
then, of course, your CodePipeline service role
must have read and write access into every artifact buckets
to be able to read and write the artifacts.
And if you're using the console to define your CodePipeline,
by default you're going to be using
the default CodePipeline buckets.
So, they're the ones that are shown in the bottom graph.
But if you are using, for example,
the CLI, or the SDK, to create your CodePipeline,
then you must create these artifact buckets ahead of time,
and make sure CodePipeline has proper permissions.
Very important for you to understand this.
And then the magical thing is that
whenever we have a cross-region action,
we just reference the input artifacts we want,
and CodePipeline is going to automatically copy them
from one region to the next,
which makes it super easy to configure
the cross-region actions.
To make this a little bit more simple,
a little bit more clear, I have created a diagram.
So, let's assume we want to deploy a Lambda function
into two regions.
The way we're going to do this, that first of all,
we define our CodePipeline, we have multiple regions,
so we will have multiple Artifact Store.
The first one is eu-west-1,
this is where our pipeline is located.
So, the code is in CodeCommit, it gets sent to CodeBuild,
and CodeBuild is going to build our code,
and also create the output yaml file that will be used
by CloudFormation to deploy the Lambda function.
And so, because we are deploying into multiple regions,
we need to create multiple templates to make sure
we have one template per region we're deploying to.
So, once this template is done, then we can have
a CloudFormation action in the region of our pipeline,
which is going to reference as an input
the template we have created from before from CodeBuild,
and deploy a Lambda function.
So far so good.
This is just a normal pipeline
we've seen in one specific region.
But because we are deploying cross region,
we can also define a CloudFormation action
in another region.
So, this one is us-east-2.
And so, because we have multiple regions now
for CodePipeline, we must create an Artifact Store
in us-east-2 as well, an S3 bucket.
And this Artifact Store is going to get
the input artifacts copied automatically by CodePipeline
so that, for example, my template-us-east-2.yaml file,
is copied, and then what's going to happen
is that CloudFormation is going to take that file
as an input, and then use that file automatically
from the correct Artifact Store.
So, from a configuration perspective,
we just told CodePipeline to define a CloudFormation action
in another region, and that the input artifact
was this template-us-east-2.yaml,
the location of which is going to be automatically handled
and copied behind the scenes by CodePipeline.
And so, therefore, a Lambda function in another region
will be deployed.
And that's it.
So, now you know more advanced concepts for CodePipeline.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now let's talk about CodeBuild.

there will be some build instructions.

you need to know the name of that file.
So it's buildspec.yml, and that file needs to live
at the root of your code.
And I will show this, what it means, in the hands-on,
or you can also insert these instructions already
in the console, but the best practice is to use,
buildspec.yml.
And this is what the exam will test you on.
So once the application is built,
the output logs can be stored into Amazon S3 and
CloudWatch logs for later analysis,
you use CloudWatch Metrics to look at the
builds statistics,
EventBridge to detect failed builds
and trigger notifications,
CloudWatch alarms in case you have too many failures,
for example, and then the build projects themselves can be,
and this is a bit confusing, defined either within
CodeBuild of course, or also within CodePipeline,
but CodePipeline could also invoke an existing CodeBuild
build project.
So, if we look at CodeBuild, what can it test?
Well, if you have a Java, Ruby, Python, Go,
Node.js, Android, .NET Core, PHP application,
Then there is a prebuilt image for you to run

And if you want to have any other environments,
you can extend a Docker image, and by extending it,

But again, this is up to you,
to support your own environments.
So how does CodeBuild works?
Well, we have our code, and in this example,
is in CodeCommits.
So we have our source code, a bunch of files,
and then there's this very important file
that lives at the top of your repo,
which is buildspec.yaml.
Now CodeBuild is going to fetch this code and then,
CodeBuild itself, will have to have a container.
So, as I said, there's going to be a build environment.
So Java, Go and so on.
And this container is going to load
all the source codes and the buildspec.yml
and is going to run all the instructions that are inserted
into this buildspec.yml file.
Now to build this container CodeBuild will pull
a Docker image.
So either it's pre-packaged by AWS
for the environments I just told you before,
or you provide your own Docker image to run
whatever code you need.
Okay, so CodeBuild will run
all the instructions from buildspec.yml,
and sometimes they can be quite lengthy.
So there is a feature and CodeBuild to be able to
cache a bunch of files in S3 buckets.
If you want you to reuse some files from build to build,
okay, this is an optimization,
but there's a way for you to cache some files.
This is optional though.
Then all the logs are going to be
into CloudWatch logs and Amazon S3 if you enable it,
and then once CodeBuild is done, to build your code or even
test your code, it can produce some artifacts,
and these artifacts will be extracted out of the container,
put into an S3 bucket, and this is
where you can find your final outputs of CodeBuild.
So the buildspec.yml file is super important.
This is what it looks like, we'll have a look at it,
obviously in this course.
But some very important things are that
the buildspec.yml file must at the roots of your code.
So at the very, very top of your code directory.
Environment allows you to define
some environmental roles for the execution
of buildspec.yml.
So you have variables that can be plain text
or you can pull them directly from the SSM Parameter Store,
or you can pull secrets directly from Secrets Manager.
This would allow you, for example,
to get a password or for database,
and so on directly from some places, that
of course you wouldn't want to store these passwords in
plain text into a file like buildspec.yml.
Then phases, which is actually going to define
what CodeBuild is going to be doing,
so it's a bunch of installs, for example,
to say, "Hey, what commits you wanna do",
to install some pre necessary packages and so on.
Pre-build, which is the commands to execute.
just before the build.
Build, the actual build commands, very important.
Then we have post_build, which are the finishing touches.
For example, once it's built, maybe create
a good zip output and so on,
and then the artifacts.
So which files at the Docker container should be extracted
and sent into Amazon S3.
That should also going to be encrypted.
And finally,
there's this cache block, to say which files
your dependencies are going to be cached in
Amazon S3 for speeding up the future builds.
Okay, so this is, could be at a high level,
but from this file, just remember, to me,
the most important thing is the name of the file,
where it sits. And again, just understand
the general idea of how CodeBuild works
and you should be good to go.
Now CodeBuild is something that runs on the cloud,
but it is possible for you,
if you need to do some deep troubleshooting beyond the logs
to run CodeBuild locally on your desktop.
First you need to install Docker, obviously,
and then you leverage the CodeBuild Agent,
the instructions are here, and this allows you to reproduce
a CodeBuild build, on your machine
and really see what's going on when you have failures.
Also CodeBuild can be launched within the VPC.
So by default, you could build containers,
instances are launched outside your VPC.
That means that it's going to run fine,
but it cannot access some resources
that are within your VPC.
So you can specify a VPC configuration for CodeBuild
with a VPC ID, subnet IDs, Security Group IDs, and so on.
And then thanks to this then CodeBuild containers will
be able to access resources in your VPC, such as RDS,
ElastiCache, EC2 instances, ALBs and so on.
So in this example, I'll have
RDS database in a private subnet in my VPC,
and then I can directly launch
my CodeBuild container in here.
And then my CodeBuild container could access
my RDS database instance if we needed to.
So to use cases to have CodeBuild inside your VPC,
is to do integration testing, data query,
to talk to internal load balancers and so on.
So that's it for CodeBuild, I hope you liked it

# 18. CodeBuild - Advanced
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858416
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so a few more things
you need to know about CodeBuild.
The first one is around Environment Variables.
So we know that there are some variables
in our CodeBuild project at runtime, but what are they?
The first category is Default Environment Variables.
As you can see, they're defined and provided by AWS
for every of your build.
And they include, for example, the AWS default region,
the build ARN, the build ID, the build image,
and a lot of metadata around your build.
The second is Custom Environmental Variables.
So they have two kinds.
The first one are static
and static are defined at build time.
So you can say, for example, that this build is for
the environment production or whatever
and you can override them when you use
the start-build API call if you need it to.
The last kind is Dynamic Environment Variables.
Here, we are pulling the value of the environment variable
through the SSM Parameter Store or Secrets Manager.
So this is an integration, for example,
we have a secret value, we cannot pass it statically,
but we can, for example, have CodeBuild retrieve the value
of the secret directly from Secrets Manager at runtime.
So what about security of CodeBuild?
So CodeBuild has a service role,
and this service role is used to access AWS resources
on your behalf.
So we assign a role and, for example,
we can download code from CodeCommit.
We can fetch parameters from the SSM Parameter Store
or we can, for example, upload artifacts to S3 Buckets,
all the things this service role can help us do,
for example, is fetching secrets from Secrets Manager,
storing logs and CloudWatch logs and much more.
So on top of it, we have in-transit
and at-rest data encryption for your cache, for your logs,
et cetera, et cetera.
And any build output artifact is going to be encrypted
and that requires access to KMS.
Okay, so what about build badges?
So for example, we are in CodeCommit
and we want to have a look at whether or not
our pull request is passing or not.
So here is an example where there's a comment
on the CodeCommit pull request where the build is passing.
And here is an example where the build is failing.
So this passing and failing little image
is called a Build Badge.
So these badges are dynamically generated
and they display the status of the latest build
in CodeBuild.
And so that can be accessed through a public URL
for this build badge.
And it's supported for CodeCommit, GitHub and BitBuckets.
Now these badges are available at the branch level
and so that means that if you are doing a new pull request
on the specific branch,
then you can have a CodeBuild related to that branch
and then the build will display some information
about the status of the branch itself.
Now what about CodeBuild triggers?
So how do we trigger a CodeBuild?
So multiple ways, we can have CodeCommit push
an event into EventBridge
and that event may trigger directly CodeBuild.
So there is an integration
between EventBridge and CodeBuild.
We can have CodeCommit as well
push an event to EventBridge.
We can then trigger Lambda function,
do something a little bit more complicated
and then from Lambda, use the API call to invoke CodeBuild.
We can also, for example, use GitHub
because CodeBuild can work at GitHub.
In that case, GitHub will push an event
into a Web Hook for CodeBuild
and this web hook will trigger a CodeBuild build.
So all these things are possible
and the reason I'm telling you this is that
because we have a architecture we can use
to validate pull request in CodeCommits.
So how do we do this?
Well, for example, we say we have pull request
in CodeCommit, so there is new proposed code changes,
but we want to validate them.
We want to test them before they get merged
to make sure that the build is working.
This allows us to ensure a high-level of code quality
and avoid code conflicts and then as a result,
we could also display the badge on your PR.
So how does that work?
Well, we have a CodeCommit repository with several branches
and we want to merge development branch
into production branch.
So for this, we're going to create a pull request
and then whenever that pull request is created
or updated, then an event is going to be published
into EventBridge.
From there we can trigger a first Lambda function
whose role is going to update the pull request
with a comment saying that the test build has begun.
And EventBridge as a second destination,
which is going to be CodeBuild.
So CodeBuild is going to be invoked on that specific PR
and so it's going to check out the code, do a test,
and then either the test are,
and the build is successful or not.
So that is going to be published to EventBridge
which can then invoke Lambda function
which knows how to parse these events.
And then is going to update the pull request
with a comment with the build outcome.
And then we're good to go.
We can actually merge that pull request
if we're happy with it.
So visually, here's an example of this architecture.
So on the left hand side, we have a first comment
in the bottom that says that the build has been started
and then we have a second comment on the top
saying that the build has been failing.
And on top of it, we add the build batch
to say it was failed.
And on the other side, in case the pull request is passing,
we have a comment saying
that the CodeBuild is also passing, and so we're good to go.
We know we can safely merge that pull request
into our master branch.
So CodeBuild is running a lot of tests
and there's a way for you to get a visual test report
directly from the CodeBuild UI.
And so as such, this is called a report groups
and test reports.
And so as you can see in this UI,
we have a 75% pass rate for the test rerun within CodeBuild.
And so that gives us the idea of what is failing
or what is not failing.
We don't have to go through logs to determine this.
So how do we go to create these test reports?
Well, they contain details about the test
that are run during builds.
And so this could be any kind of test
such as unit test, configuration test, and functional test.
And you can create your test cases with any test framework
that will create a report file,
and then there is some format that CodeBuild can understand.
So we have the JUnit XML, the NUnit XML, the NUnit3 XML.
We have the Cucumber JSON, the TestNG XML,
and the Visual Studio TRX.
And so the idea is that whatever framework you use
as long as the report is one of these formats,
for example, the Cucumber JSON,
then automatically, you can create a test reports
directly in CodeBuild.
So the way to do it is that in your buildspec.yml,
which indicates how to function to your CodeBuild,
then there's just a report group and you define
where the files that represent your reports
are located on your build
and automatically they will surface back into CodeBuild,
which is quite nice.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 19. [DVA] CodeDeploy - Overview
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858436
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS CodeDeploy.
So as the name indicates, it is a deployment service
that will automate application deployment.
What does that mean?
Well, that means you have a version one
of an application running
and somehow, you want to upgrade it to version two.
Now where can we deploy version one and version two?
Well, these application versions can be deployed either
to EC2 instances, on-premises servers
or Lambda functions or ECS services
so three different kinds of targets
because EC2 instances and on-premises servers
have the same methodology.
On top of it, CodeDeploy can allow you
to update an application but also rollback.
So in case your deployment is not working as expected,
it is failing, or there's an alarm that gets triggered,
then we can automatically initiate a rollback.
That makes it a very safe automated deployment.
On top of it, we can control how fast we want
to deploy our application.
We will see this later on,
but we can say one instance at a time or all at a time
or HalfAtATime or blue/green.
Finally, to control how CodeDeploy works,
there's a file named appspec.yml
that can help define how the deployment will happen.
So now, let's talk about the EC2/on-premises platform.
So this allows you to deploy to EC2 instances
and on-premises servers, your application, and your code.
And you can perform two kind of deployments,
either in-place deployments or blue/green deployments.
We'll see them both to understand the difference.
And to work, we must first deploy the CodeDeploy agent
onto the target instances because the agent is the thing
that will be performing the updates on the instances.
We can define the deployment speed
so, as I said, we can have a gradual deployment.
For example, we can do AllAtOnce,
which will update all the instances at once,
but will give us the most amount of downtime
because we will be down.
HalfAtATime, for example, to reduce capacity by 50%
or OneAtATime, which is going to be the slowest
because we take down one instance at a time
and update it, but of course,
it's going to give us the lowest availability impact
because only one instance will be down at a time
or you can define your own custom deployment speed
if you wanted to.
So let's have a look at how, for example,
in-place deployment works for HalfAtATime setting.
So here we have the v1 running on four EC2 instances.
Because we're in a HalfAtATime setting
in in-place deployment,
two instances are going to be taken down for maintenance.
So the agent will stop the application on two instances
which then are going to be upgraded again
by the agent to version two.
And once it is done,
then the other half is going to be taken down for install
and then upgrade it to version two.
And so this is the process of in-place deployment
for HalfAtATime setting.
What about blue/green?
Well, blue/green is the idea that you have,
for example, an Application Load Balancer pointing
to version one
and all your instances are in Auto Scaling group.
What's going to happen
is that we're going to create a new Auto Scaling group
so this can be done either manually
or automatically by CodeDeploy.
And CodeDeploy is going to create as many EC2 instances
in this new Auto Scaling group.
So we have v1 and v2 now running in parallel
and the load balancer through some process
is going to be pointing now to the v2 Auto Scaling group
and the v1 will be taken down.
So this is a simplified version,
but at least you see the process, and it's called blue/green
because new instances are taken up
and the old ones are terminated.
So this CodeDeploy agent I've been telling you about,
it must be installed on the EC2 instances as a prerequisite.
So we have the EC2 instance,
and we install the CodeDeploy agent.
Now you can install it directly using some Linux commands
to install any software
or if you wanted to have some kind of automation.
If your EC2 instances are managed using Systems Manager,
then you can automate the install
of CodeDeploy agent using Systems Manager.
Now this EC2 instance with the CodeDeploy agent
will need sufficient IAM permissions to access Amazon S3.
Why?
Well, because in Amazon S3
will be stored the application revision.
So when we want to update from version one to version two,
then the CodeDeploy agent
with the proper IAM permissions attached to the EC2 instance
will download the application revision from the S3 bucket.
And now you know enough for CodeDeploy and EC2 instances.
Now let's see how CodeDeploy works with the Lambda platform.
So CodeDeploy can help you automate traffic shift
for Lambda aliases.
And the idea is that you can shift from v1 to v2
under an PROD alias.
I'll show you this in a second.
Now this feature is fully integrated
within the SAM framework that you will see soon.
And so that allows us to just use the SAM framework
and internally use CodeDeploy.
So how does that work for the traffic-shifting function?
Well, say we have a PROD alias, okay?
And we have v1 that we've deployed before
and v2 that we've deployed after,
and we wanna shift the traffic between the v1 version
and the v2 version under the PROD alias.
So the way it works is that CodeDeploy
is going to make this X vary until X equals 100%.
So at first, X will be zero.
So that means that all the PROD alias points
to the v1 function, and then X will gradually increase
until he reaches 100% so that all the traffic
on the PROD alias is redirecting to the v2 function.
Now we have several strategies to make X evolve.
So we have linear
where we grow the traffic every N minutes until 100%.
So in this example, LambdaLinear10PercentEvery3Minutes,
that means that every three minutes, 10% will be added.
So we'll have 10 and then 20 and then 30% after 9 minutes,
and so on until we reach 100%.
And so you have different strategies.
For example, 10PercentEvery10Minutes and so on.
So this is linear.
Then we have canary,
which is to have a small amount of traffic
on the v2 function and then ramp up to 100%.
So here we have LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes.
So that means that for five minutes,
the new v2 function is going to receive 10% of the traffic.
And then, if everything goes well,
then all of a sudden, we switch to 100% of the traffic.
That's why it's called canary.
So we have, for example, the 10Percent5Minutes
or the 10Percent30Minutes strategy.
And finally, AllAtOnce,
which immediately jumps from v1 to v2
but we don't have the time to test it if it's working.
Now, CodeDeploy for the ECS platform is actually similar.
So we can automate the deployment
of a new ECS task definition.
And this only works for blue/green deployments.
So let's take an example.
So we have an Application Load Balancer,
and it's related to a target group
where our ECS tasks are running under an ECS cluster.
And we'll use CodeDeploy to do a blue/green deployment.
So very similarly to EC2 instances,
there will be a new target group
with the v2 version of our application.
And this v2 version comes from the new ECS task definition
that will be run with the same capacity as before.
And that can deploy is going to affect the load balancer.
And so it's going to redirect the traffic
from the v1 target group, the blue target group
into the v2 target group, the green target group.
And what's going to happen here
is that we're going to shift traffic again
between the first one and the second one
with similar strategies as before.
So we have the linear strategy,
and this is just like before we gradually increase
until we reach 100%.
We have the cannery strategy
to test a small amount of traffic on the new target group,
and then all of a sudden,
we switch everything to the new target group
or we have the AllAtOnce to immediately switch
from the blue to the green target group.
So that's it for an overview of CodeDeploy.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 20. CodeDeploy - EC2 Deep Dive
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858450
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a deep dive
into the CodeDeploy deployments
for the EC2 on-premises platform.
So we've seen in-place deployments,
and the way to perform an in-place deployment
is either to use EC2 tags to identify instances.
So for example, you say, hey, I want all my instances
with the project name Finance App to be updated
and therefore the in-place deployment will happen
for these instances.
Or if the instances are part of an autoscaling group
we can just identify the autoscaling group,
and any instances part of these autoscaling groups
is going to be updated.
If you're using the autoscaling group technique,
then any new instance launched
as part of the autoscaling group
will have CodeDeploy automatically deploy
new application versions to the EC2 instances,
which is a very good added benefit.
If you're using a load balancer on top of it,
as in your application is, for example,
a web application and is fronted by a load balancer,
then the traffic to the EC2 instances is stopped
before the EC2 instance is updated,
and then it's started again after the instance is updated.
Now, when we update an EC2 instance
we are using deployment hooks,
and the hooks are scripts that can be run
during the EC2 instance update lifecycle.
So let's go and have a look at this lifecycle.
And it could be quite daunting at first
but actually it makes sense.
So, if you're using a load balancer
and we do an in-place deployment.
then of course the first thing we need to do is
to block the traffic to the EC2 instance.
And so you have these three steps right here.
We have BeforeBlockTraffic, BlockTraffic,
and AfterBlockTraffic.
So it turns out that anything in blue
allows you to run your own scripts on the EC2 instance
to perform some action.
So for example, say that before the traffic
was blocked by the load balancer,
you want it to run some analytics
and send that away to an analytics platform
to know how many requests you've served, who knows.
So then you have the option to run a script
in the BeforeBlockTraffic.
Then the BlockTraffic is gray
because it's reserved by CodeDeploy
and the traffic is actually stopped
from the load balancer to the EC2 instance
and you cannot do anything in this step.
And then AfterBlockTraffic is also a way
for you to run the script if you wanted to,
now that you know that the EC2 instance
doesn't receive any more traffic.
Then you have the ApplicationStop.
So ApplicationStop is for you to actually run a script
to stop the application.
So CodeDeploy kinda expects for you to run a script here.
Then CodeDeploy will go ahead and download a bundle.
So this is a step performed by the CodeDeploy agent,
and it will download the bundle, for example,
from Amazon S3.
Then you have the option to run script
before the installation of the bundle.
Maybe you want to change some file permissions, whatever.
Make sure that everything is ready
because then we have the install script,
and this will tell CodeDeploy, this is the agent,
how to move files around on your EC2 instance
to install the new bundle that has been downloaded.
Then you have the option to run a script after the install.
Maybe you want to check a few things.
Again, change some file permissions, I don't know.
Then there is the ApplicationStart.
So you need to indicate to CodeDeploy
how to start the application,
meaning what script to do to run the application.
And then you have the option,
once the application is started,
to run another script to validate the service
to make sure that, yes, the application is indeed running
and it's working as expected.
So you don't have to provide a script
for all these steps in blue,
but it's very common to have at least ApplicationStop
and ApplicationStart as provided scripts
because you need to tell CodeDeploy
how to stop and start the application.
Next we have the last steps.
So if you're using a load balancer, again,
the traffic is restarted.
And so we have a hook for BeforeAllowTraffic,
then AllowTraffic, so the load balancer starts
to send traffic to our application.
And finally we have an AfterAllowTraffic hook
where we can, for example,
verify that our application is still working
even after it receives actual traffic from the users.
And finally the flow is over.
So, hopefully everything makes sense in these steps
and we will see them a lot in this section.
And the idea is that,
well, you can run your scripts and hooks at specific moments
but then some moments are reserved by CodeDeploy,
for example, when the traffic is blocked
when using a load balancer,
then when the application bundle
is downloaded and installed,
and finally when the traffic is allowed
from the load balancer.
So now let's talk about how these deployment hooks
are actually run on the EC2 instance.
So the CodeDeploy agent is going to deploy some files
including, for example, some scripts that you have defined.
And the appendectomy file is going to define
the hooks section and saying,
hey, how should these scripts be run?
And so we have, for example here,
the BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart,
ValidateService scripts, hooks,
that define the location of the script to be run.
And so that means that the CodeDeploy agents
at specific amount of time during the deployment
will run these scripts.
And so, for example, if we are in the AfterInstall,
then, as you can see, the appendectomy file
says that we should run the script RunResourceTests.sh.
So the CodeDeploy agent is going to execute the script.
And then this is how we have the option, for example,
to test whether or not our application
was successfully installed.
On top of it, the CodeDeploy agent is going to inject
environment variables that we can pick up
as part of these scripts.
So for example, the deployment group name is provided
as an environment variable from CodeDeploy.
And so our scripts can, for example,
reference the deployment group name
if we need this during our execution.
So here are a few examples of deployment hooks.
So in the BeforeInstall phase, we can use it, for example,
for preinstall tasks such as decrypting files
or creating a backup of the current version.
AfterInstall can be used for tasks
such as configuring your application
or changing file permissions.
ApplicationStart is used to start services
that were stopped during ApplicationStop.
ValidateService is for you to make sure
that the deployment was completed successfully.
And BeforeAllowTraffic, for example,
for you to run tasks such as health checks
to make sure that the EC2 instances applications
are working correctly
before we start having real traffic from the load balancer.
Now let's talk about blue/green deployments.
So we have two modes to do a blue/green deployment.
We have the manual mode,
which we identify the blue instances by tags.
And then we also identify the green instances by tags.
But we must manually provision the blue
and the green instances ahead of time.
So we have a load balancer pointing to v1,
and then all of a sudden we will have
a gradual shift from v1 to v2
until the v1 version doesn't receive any traffic.
So in the manual mode we have to provision
v1 and v2 instances manually.
In the automatic mode we have an auto scanning group
and we just reference it.
And then automatically a new autoscanning group
is going to be created by CodeDeploy
with the same settings that are going to be copied.
So we have the same settings, the same capacity.
New instances will be created
as part of the new autoscaling group
and then the ALB is going to redirect traffic from v1 to v2.
Please note that when you have a blue/green deployment
you must have a load balancer as well.
Okay, so in this case we have seen
the manual and automatic deployment.
And you may ask me about,
well, what about instance termination?
So when we have a blue-green deployment
we have two options.
We have the option to actually terminate
the blue instances automatically
after a successful deployment.
And so we can specify after how long
we want these instances to be terminated
and the reason we need to wait how long is that,
for example, the default is one hour
and you have one hour to realize that if you did a mistake
you can roll back and the max takes two days.
But once the time is elapsed,
then we have the blue instances,
the v1 instances, being terminated.
The last option, which is the safest
but also the most expensive, is to keep alive the instances.
That means that the instances will not be terminated
and it's up to you to terminate them.
Now, for the hooks, well the hooks
are exactly the same as before.
Okay, so we have the same,
but they are run in a slightly different order.
Why?
Well because some hooks are run on the v2 instances
and some hooks are run only on the v1 instance.
So let's have a quick description.
So the v2 instances don't have any traffic on them,
and so therefore we go directly
into the ApplicationStop, BeforeInstall,
Install, AfterInstall steps,
because we just look to install the application
on the v2 instances,
and then we go into BeforeAllowTraffic,
AllowTraffic, and AfterAllowTraffic,
because the ELB start to send traffic
into our v2 instances.
So that makes sense.
And then once the traffic is gradually shifting
from v1 to v2, then the v1 instances
will have less and less traffic from the ALB
and therefore the hooks running on the v1 instances
is going to be only BeforeBlockTraffic, BlockTraffic,
and AfterBlockTraffic, which then,
because the instances may be terminated,
we don't need to go into ApplicationStop
and all these kind of things.
So, same hooks, just some of them are run on v2
and some of them are run on v1.
But this should make sense to you
based on what blue/green is and how it's functioning.
Now to control how fast deployments are being made
we have some control over the deployment configuration.
So we can specify, for example, AllAtOnce
to deploy to as many instances as possible at once,
which will give you some downtime,
HalfAtATime to deploy up to half
of the instances at a time,
or OneAtATime to deploy one by one.
You can also create your own custom deployment configuration
with your own percentage if you wanted to.
Finally, CodeDeploy sends updates into an SNS topics
for your deployments.
So, for example, we deploy to a group of EC2 instances,
but one deployment has failed.
Then the event InstanceFailure is going to be sent
into an SNS topic, and then from it we can send emails.
So the kind of events that are sent into your SNS topic
are for the deployment success, the deployment failure,
or an instance failure, and so on.
So that's it for CodeDeploy regarding the EC2 instances.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 21. CodeDeploy - ECS Deep Dive
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858454
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a deeper dive
into how CodeDeploy works with the ECS platform.
So with the ECS platform,
we can automatically handle the deployment
of a new ECS task definition into an ECS service.
So this only supports blue/green
and your service must be connected to a load balancer.
So for CodeDeploy to work, in this case,
the ECS task definition
and the new container images
that you associate with this new task definition
must be already created.
So you as a developer, have the responsibility, for example,
to push a new container image into ECR.
Then you will create a new ECS task definition revision.
And this revision must reference
the new image you have created in ECR.
So then you're good.
And then you create a appspec.yml file
that is going to reference this new ECS task definition
you have created from before.
And also specify some load balancer information if need be.
So this appspec.yml file that you've created
must be placed into an S3 bucket
and from there, we can invoke CodeDeploy.
We reference which appspec.yml file we want to run,
so CodeDeploy will know how to run it.
It will know which ECS task definition to deploy
and then it will deploy a new set of ECS tasks
onto your ECS cluster.
And when done, it will delete the old ECS tasks.
So in this instance, as you can see,
the CodeDeploy agent is not required
because everything is handled
by the ECS service and CodeDeploy.
So what you need to remember out of this
is that the appspec.yml is your responsibility to create
and it references a new ECS task definition revision
that you must also create yourself.
So if you wanted to automate everything
from the pushing code to deploying on the ECS cluster,
of course, we could use a deployment pipeline.
So we'll use CodePipeline,
will which have a code repository in CodeCommit.
Then we'll have a CodeBuild step
and CodeBuild will do three things.
Number one, it will build a Docker image
and this Docker image will be pushed into ECR.
Then it will create and register
a new ECS task definition revision on the ECS service.
And finally, it will create an appspec.yml file,
and this appspec.yml file is going to reference
the new ECS task definition.
So this is what a simple appspec.yml file looks like.
As you can see under properties, there is task definition
where we have the ARN of the new ECS task definition
has been created as well as load balancer info
such as the container name and the container port.
Then when all of this is done,
we can have the CodeDeploy step
in which we reference as an input artifact the appspec.yml,
and then CodeDeploy will know how to deploy
and shift the traffic from our ECS cluster
to register a new ECS tasks and delete the old ones.
So in this case, we have still the responsibility
to create all the task definitions and so on,
but all of this is automated thanks to CodePipeline.
Now let's see how fast we deploy from v1 to v2.
So the load balancer has the responsibility
to redirect traffic from the two target groups,
but we have different strategies.
We have canary, linear, or all at once.
So for the ECS Linear strategy, we have for example,
10% every one minute or 10% every three minutes.
That means that over time,
every one minute there will be 10 more percent added
onto the new target group
and removed from the old target group.
We have the canary strategy,
for example, ECS Canary, 10%, 5 or 15 minutes
in which we are going to send 10% of the traffic
for 15 minutes to the new target group.
And if everything goes well,
we shift all the remaining traffic after this
to the new target group.
And then we have ECS All At Once
to just shift all at once from the v1
to the v2 target group.
There is also for you the possibility to define
a second listener on your load balancer
called the Test Listener
that is going to just send some test traffic
to your new target group
before the main production listener
is redirecting all the traffic.
So we'll see this in a second with the deployment hooks.
So the hooks this time on ECS, they cannot be scripts,
they are Lambda function
and they're executed once per deployments.
So we have the before install hook,
then we have install and install is basically
the ECS service creating the new ECS task,
thanks to the new ECS task definition.
And then we have the after install.
So for example here, we can run a Lambda function
called ValidateAfterInstall.
So we're going to invoke a specific Lambda function
that is going to make sure, for example,
that our new task group is working as expected.
Then we have the test traffic.
So if we've defined a test listener,
then we can send some test traffic to this new target group.
And then we can verify with a new hook
with a new Lambda function that, for example,
everything is working on these ECS tasks.
For example, we can run a Lambda function
to make sure that the new instances did indeed
correctly handle the test traffic.
So this could be health checks.
Then we have the before allow traffic.
So this is before we allow traffic,
the whole production traffic to be shifted.
Then we have the allow traffic where
the production traffic is shifted.
And finally, once everything is shifted,
we can run another Lambda function called AfterAllowTraffic,
where we can observe if the new ECS task
is actually handling the traffic really well.
So that's it for ECS deployments, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 22. CodeDeploy - Lambda Deep Dive
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858456
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's do a deep dive
into the Lambda deployments for CodeDeploy.
So the idea is that you create a new Lambda version
and then you want to deploy it onto and alias.
So for this, right now,
the alias is pointing to version one,
but we wanted to point to version two.
So we're going to specify the new version information
in an appspec.yml file.
And then this file is going to be placed in an S3 bucket.
Then we going to invoke the CodeDeploy service
with this appspec.ylm file.
And then CodeDeploy
is automatically going to update the Lambda alias
to reference to the new version, version two.
And then automatically
traffic is going to be shifted from version one
to version two
and everything will be updated.
So as you can see in this example
the CodeDeploy agent is not required
we just need to create the new version ahead of time
and create this appspec.yml file.
Now, if you look at the content of it,
it is actually extremely simple.
We just specify the name
of the Lambda function to deploy,
which is required,
the name of the alias of the Lambda function,
as well as the current version
and the target version.
And then CodeDeploy will do its thing.
So when we deploy to Lambda in an automated fashion
we can use again, code pipeline.
So we push code into code commit.
CodeBuild is going to build the code,
deploy a new Lambda version
and then create this appspec.yml file we have just seen.
And then CodeDeploy is going to take
this appspec.yml file as an input artifact
and use it to shift traffic
onto the areas for your Lambda function
between the current version
and the target version.
So we have control
into how fast the traffic shifting happens for your alias.
So we have the Canary, Linear
or All At Once type of deployments.
So Linear we've seen.
So we can do, for example,
Lambda Linear 10% every three minutes.
So it goes from 10% to 20%
and so on every three minutes.
Or we can do Canary, for example,
10% for 10 minutes
and then shift all the traffic to V2,
or Lambda All At Once
to shift all traffic at once.
So we also have deployment hooks for Lambda
but they're very simple.
So the hooks are run as Lambda functions.
And we only have three hooks.
So we have three steps.
So we have before allowed traffic, allowed traffic,
and after allowed traffic.
And it turns out that before allowed traffic
and after allowed traffic
are the only place where you can run hooks
and they are Lambda function.
So for example, if we are using
before allow traffic,
we can invoke a Lambda function
named Validate Before Allow Traffic,
to make sure that we have
some health checks in place.
Or after allowed traffic,
to make sure that after deploying the new Lambda version
everything is working as expected.
And that's it.
So now you know a lot more about Lambda and CodeDeploy.
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 23. CodeDeploy - Rollbacks & Troubleshooting
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858594
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, let's talk about redeploys and rollbacks.
So, a rollback is when CodeDeploy actually redeploys
a previously deployed version of your application.
And a rollback can happen in the following cases.
Either it's automatic because, for example,
we have failed to deploy to a new EC2 instance
or ECS task or whatever.
Or we have linked a CloudWatch Alarm
and the CloudWatch Alarm got triggered.
Or you can have manual rollbacks if you wanted to.
Now, you can also disable rollbacks
and say that no matter what happens,
do not perform a rollback.
If a rollback happens, just remember that CodeDeploy
is going to go ahead and initially issue
a new deployment of the last known good version.
It's not a restored version.
Now, you need to know a little bit of things
about CodeDeploy troubleshooting.
So, in case you see this invalid signature exception,
that's because there is a time mismatch
between CodeDeploy and the EC2 instances
because we need accurate time references.
And so if the date and time on your EC2 instances
are not set correctly, you may see this kind of error.
So, the solution to this is just to synchronize the time
between your EC2 instance and for example,
the time provided by AWS.
So, sometimes the deployment or life cycle events
are going to be skipped and we're going to get
some of these errors such as the overall deployment failed
because too many individual instances failed deployment,
or too few healthy instances are available for deployments.
Or some instances in your deployment groups
are experiencing problems such as health constraints.
Then, you may have a few problems.
So, make sure that the CodeDeploy agent
is installed and running.
Then, make sure that the Service Role
or the IAM instance profile have the required permissions.
If you are using an HTTP Proxy,
make sure the CodeDeploy agent
is running with the proxy_uri parameter.
And make sure the date and time mismatch
is good between CodeDeploy and the agent.
So, just some normal troubleshooting.
On top of it, any kind of deployment failures
from CodeDeploy can also be intercepted using EventBridge.
If you have a deployment to an ASG,
and then the ASG has a scale out event,
meaning that new instances are added during the deployment.
Well, it turns out that the scale out event
will deploy the V1 version
because the new deployment has not finished being done.
And so, you may come into a case where the ASG
will have V1 and V2 versions of your application.
But don't worry, by default,
after a successful deployment onto an auto-scaling group,
CodeDeploy is going to automatically start
a follow on deployment
to update any outdated instance from V1 to v2.
Usually going to have some time
where you're running both versions at the same time.
Then, we have Blue-Green deployments and it turns out
that the allow traffic step is failing.
So, the app was correctly installed,
but the traffic cannot be allowed.
So, what happens because we don't see any errors
in the deployment logs?
Well, that may be because the ELB
has inconfigured or misconfigured health checks.
And so you need to review the health checks of the ELB,
make sure they are correct.
And of course, if the ELB health checks are not correct,
then traffic cannot be allowed to the EC2 instances.
But if the health checks are passing and correct,
then traffic can be allowed from the ELB
to the new EC2 instances.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 24. [DVA] CodeArtifact - Overview
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858624
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's discuss CodeArtifact.
So the idea is that when you build software,
you use other software that your own software depends on.
This is called code dependencies.
And every time you build software
it's very common to push the software into a repository,
and then other software can build onto it.
So there is this whole dependencies,
and this whole dependencies web
is called artifact management.
So traditionally, when you use artifacts
you set up your own artifact management system,
and the idea is that it could be quite complicated.
So using CodeArtifact, you get a secure, scalable,
cost-effective artifact management system
for software development.
And CodeArtifact has more than this.
I'll show you this in the diagram,
but it has integration
with common dependency measuring tools
such as Maven, Gradle, npm, yarn, twine, pip, and NuGet.
And the idea is that using CodeArtifact,
both developers and CodeBuild can retrieve the dependencies
straight from CodeArtifact within your AWS cloud.
So let's do a diagram is going to be much clearer.
So with CodeArtifact,
all your artifacts live within your VPC, within AWS.
Sometimes if you use other artifact management systems
they could be third parties outside of AWS,
or if you deploy your own artifact measurement system
they could live on these two instances, for example.
In which case, yes, of course it will be within your VPC.
So with CodeArtifact, you're going to define domains,
and each domain is just a set of repositories.
Now, as a developer, the cool thing is
that you can tell the developers, hey,
you need to, for example, for your JavaScript developers
run the npm command to fetch dependencies
for your JavaScript packages to CodeArtifact.
And CodeArtifact is going to be a proxy
for public artifact repositories.
So instead of having your JavaScript developers
actually directly reach into
the public artifact repo themselves,
they're going to reach to CodeArtifact,
which is going to be wired to public artifact repositories
and the request will be proxied.
Why will you do this, well for two reasons,
number one, network security.
So your JavaScript developers
only interact with CodeArtifact,
and CodeArtifact will proxy the request to the public repo.
But also as the dependencies are being fetched,
they're going to be cached into CodeArtifact itself.
Which means that even if the dependency disappears
from the public artifact repository,
you will still have your own copy within CodeArtifact.
Which is good to make sure that your code
can always be built in the future.
Now this works for not just JavaScript,
but also for Python with pip.
It works for .net with NuGet and Java with Maven.
Okay? So all these things can be proxied
from CodeArtifact into this own repositories.
But the second thing you can do is obviously
push your own artifacts.
And so your IT leader or your developers can publish
and approve packages to be pushed into other repositories
within CodeArtifact.
That means that all your artifacts will live
in one place in your VPC.
And everything will just depend on everything,
all the code that's already within your CodeArtifact,
artifact management system.
And if developers can get
all these artifacts out of CodeArtifact,
then of course CodeBuild can also too.
And it is that now CodeBuild
instead of fetching from public repositories,
can also fetch all this information
directly from CodeArtifact.
Next, how does CodeArtifact changes
trigger some stuff downstream in AWS?
So we will see this service in detail later on,
but CodeArtifact events such as when a package is created
or modified or deleted will emit events
into what's called EventBridge.
And EventBridge is like a repository of events within AWS.
And from EventBridge, you can pretty much integrate
and trigger many different AWS services,
such as Lambda functions, Step functions, SNS, SQS.
And if none of these terms mean anything to you by now,
that's okay.
We will see these later on in this course.
And also, for example, CodePipeline.
So it is possible for CodeArtifact
to trigger CodePipeline through EventBridge,
whenever a package version for example is updated.
And so why would we wanna do this?
Well, for example, CodePipeline could have CodeCommit
so that we know that the dependency has been updated.
Then triggering CodeBuild to rebuild your application
with the updated dependency maybe for security reasons.
And then finally deploy the new application
to your production environment using CodeDeploy.
So this could be a nice automated way
to build a full automated pipeline
that ensures that you always have the latest dependencies
in your code within your builds.
So any artifact repository within your accounts
can be easily accessed by your users of your accounts
or your roles with your accounts with an IAM policy.
But if you want to authorize another account,
and users and roles of that account to access CodeArtifact
then you need to use a resource policy.
So when you grant someone access
to a CodeArtifact repository,
what's going to happen is that you
either give them access to all packages or none of them.
You cannot say only access these packages.
So when you authorize another account to access your repo
you authorize, for example, Bob in Account B
to access all packages within that specific repo.
And to give access to Bob to your accounts,
what you can do is use a resource policy in which
you authorize, for example, Bob of the other
accounts to read the packages in your code artifact repo.
And this cannot be done without a resource policy
but it's just something you need to know
for one question at the exam.
But this is a recurring topic in AWS.
Whenever you need cross account access
sometimes, most of the times, resource policies
are going to be the way to go.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.
