# 25. [DVA] CodeArtifact - Upstream Repositories & Domains
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858630
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's do a deeper dive
into how the repository works
and the concept of upstream repositories.
So, when you have a Code Artifact Repo,
you can actually have multiple upstream repositories.
So let's have an example.
Here, the repository "my-repo"
can have an upstream of Repository A
and an upstream of Repository B.
So what does it mean to have upstreams
and why is it helpful?
Well, when you have an upstream,
any package manager that is trying to access your base repo,
can also try to find dependencies
in all the upstream repositories.
But, the benefits of this, is that's for your developer,
for whoever connects to your repo,
there's only a single repository endpoint,
and then you can have
up to ten upstream repositories per repository.
So that means we're going to be able to search
a tree of repositories for the right dependencies.
Now also, when you define a repository,
you can have what's called a external connection,
and it can only be one per repository.
So for example,
Repository A can be connected to an external repository,
and this is called an external connection,
and it could be the public NPM repo
and algorithms that we get.
We get the benefits that,
by connecting to just one single repo,
we have access to our private dependencies
but also any public dependencies that we've defined
through external connections.
So let's talk about these external connections
a little bit more.
So when you have an external connection,
it is by default a connection
between one of your repos and an external public repository.
For example, it could be Maven for the Java world
it could be NPM, for the JavaScript world,
PyPI for the Python world
and nuggets for the dot-net c-sharp world.
And so we have here a-
the opportunity to connect NPM to a repository
within CodeArtifacts, called an external connection.
And then what's going to happen is that,
if a package that is fetched from NPM is not available
in Repo A, then we're going to fetch it
and is going to be stored as a cash diversion in our Repo A.
And so this is why there's only a maximum of one
external connection per public repository to
have like a perfect cash mechanism.
But if you want to have multiple public repositories
then you can just have many repository
within CodeArtifacts.
So for example, here we want to connect to npmjs.com
and so we're going to configure one repo with one
external connection in your accounts, and then
all the other repositories of your account that needs to
also fetch from NPM can just
have defined the Repository A as an upstream.
And now that we have this, any package fetched
from NPM the "js" are going to be cashed
in the upstream Repo A, and then automatically
the Repo B, C, and D will have access to these packages.
So as a developer, when you pull a package
it's going to be cashed in repo A
and then sent right through to your build system.
So what about the retention
of these artifacts in CodeArtifacts?
So, if you have a requested package
and it's found in an upstream repo
then a reference to it is going to be retained
and always available to the downstream repository.
And then if you somehow change the package
in the upstream repository, it's not going to
affect your own copy in the downstream repository.
And any intermediate repository that allowed you to
fetch that package will not be able to keep the package
for efficiency purposes.
So let's have a look. If we take a package from npmjs.com,
but to get there we have two upstreams,
What's going to happen is
that the package manager is going to request this package.
Then it's not present in any of the three repos
so it's going to be fetched, then it's going to be fetched,
it's going to be retained in Repository A.
That's because it's the most downstream repository
and it's the one we connect
to from our developer machine.
Repository C, as well,
because that's the one that has the external connection
to the NPM public repository.
So we'll keep a copy cashed in it
and the Repository B will not have anything
because it is considered
in this chain an intermediate repository.
Finally, it looks like we're copying stuff all around
and so we are sort of duplicating packages
but this is a good time to introduce domains.
So when you have repository
you can also introduce the concept of a domain.
And a domain can span across multiple accounts
and multiple repositories within these accounts.
And when you have a domain, actually you define one storage
for all your repositories and so you de-duplicate storage
because, if the same dependency
must be in different repository,
then it's going to be stored once
in a domain in shared storage and then only references
to it will be stored in your repository.
So it makes it extremely efficient.
And then you can see, then you can create
as many upstream connections as you want.
You also have fast copying
because when you pull repository dependencies
then, instead of copying them,
you just create a new reference to the shared storage.
Also, it's very easy to share stuff
in the domain across teams
because you have the same metadata, the same assets,
and you encrypt everything with the same KMS key.
And on top of it, if you wanted to define an
access policy into your repositories,
you can just define what's called a domain
resource based policy, which is going to be applied
to all the accounts and all the repositories
within the the domain.
And you can define advanced rules,
such as who has the right to set up
and modify external connections.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 27. EC2 Image Builder
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858656
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the EC2 Image Builder service.
So it's a service used to create and automate the creation
of virtual machines or container images.
So basically you want to automate the creation,
maintain, and validate and test your EC2 AMIs.
So you can run the Image Builder on a schedule.
For example, build an AMI every week
or whenever packages are updated, et cetera, et cetera.
Or you can run it
with some automation as we'll see in the next slide.
It's a free service
so you only pay for the underlying resources created
and these are EC2 instances
as I will show you right now.
On top of it, once you create an AMI
from the EC2 Image Builder service,
you can publish that AMI to multiple regions
and multiple accounts.
Which is going to help with your distribution.
So the EC2 Image Builder service, once you set it up
and you set up, you build instructions,
is going to create a builder EC2 instance.
It's an instance that comes with almost nothing on it.
And then the Image Builder service is going to
run what's called the Build Components to
customize the software on your instance,
based on the instructions you gave it.
So it's going to build your AMI as it goes.
Then when the build instructions are done,
the AMI is going to be created from it,
and this AMI is going to be tested.
So a new EC2 instance,
from that AMI is going to be created.
All the tests are going to be run on the AMI,
for example to test if the AMI is working,
if it's secure and so on.
And then the image, the image itself,
so the AMI, is going to be distributed,
of course in the region it was created,
but also to other regions if you wanted to,
and to multiple accounts if you need to.
Which really gives you a central way
to build your AMIs on AWS.
So let's have a look at the CICD architecture
for the EC2 Image Builder service.
So first we have a CodePipeline to orchestrate everything,
and within the CodePipeline we start
from CodeCommit to get our code source.
So we're going to create our application there
and then it's going to be passed onto CodeBuild so that
the application is being built, the code is being compiled,
and then we have an executable.
Then once the application is ready to be shipped,
we need to build an AMI,
and therefore we're going to use CloudFormation.
Which is going to automate
and launch the EC2 Image Builder service,
which is going to take the code,
lastly built from CodeBuild
and then create an AMI out of it.
So this is the stage two, where we build this AMI
and the stage three is the rollout of this AMI.
So again, we're going to use a CloudFormation template,
this time to perform a rolling update
onto an auto scaling group,
where EC2 instances are using the previous AMI,
and therefore CloudFormation has some logic to
upgrade your images once at a time.
So your instances are going to be upgraded
over time from the old AMI to the new AMI,
and that gives you a fully automated way to push code
into CodeCommit to build an AMI from it,
and to roll out the AMI in production to your instances.
So that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it,

# 28. EC2 Image Builder - Extras
# Section: Domain 1: SDLC Automation
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858662
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So a few extra concepts
on the EC2 image builder service.
The first thing is that you can share the images,
the recipes, and the components that you create
within EC2 image builder using RAM.
So RAM is resource access manager
and this allows you to share a lot of things
throughout different accounts
or throughout your organization.
So say you have two accounts
and you are actually building images AMIs
with the EC2 image builder service.
So we can use RAM to automatically share them
and accept them, okay into other accounts.
But once done, this is done forever.
And so once the AMI is available for usage in accounts B
then EC2 instances can be launched from it.
So remember using RAM, you can share images, recipes
and components from the EC2 image builder service.
What about tracking the latest AMI?
So we have a will to always store the latest AMI ID
that has been built using the EC2 image builder
in the SSM parameter store.
The reason we do that is, for example
we have a weekly build that has the latest security fixes.
Then want to make sure that everyone in our organization
is aware of what is the latest AMI ID for that image.
So let's take an example, automatically, a new AMI
is created every week because we have a weekly build.
Then this will create a notification into SNS
from which we can invoke Lambda
and Lambda can be used to actually store the AMI ID
into the SSM parameter store.
From there, our users can just go into the parameter store
to find the latest AMI ID.
Or if you're using CloudFormation to actually
create EC2 instances
you can make sure to reference the AMI ID
as a dynamic reference from the SSM parameter store.
Therefore, anytime someone will use CloudFormation
you have the guarantee that the latest AMI ID
is going to be used.
Okay. So that's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 31. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858722
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's learn about AWS CloudFormation,
which is one of my personal favorite services in AWS.
So CloudFormation is a way for you to outline
your AWS infrastructure for any resources for this
using just code.
For example, in a CloudFormation template,
you're going to say, I want a security group.
I want two EC2 instances
that are going to be using the security group.
I want Elastic IPs for these EC2 instances.
I want an S3 bucket.
I want a load balancer in front of these EC2 instances.
And then by declaring what you want by just saying,
hey, all these things should exist
and they should be linked together, automatically,
CloudFormation will create them for you in the right order
with the exact configuration that you specify.
So this removes any need of doing manual configuration
and manual work, and all the things is provisioned
through CloudFormation.
So a CloudFormation template is going to be some code,
and the code will involve in a declarative way
what you want your infrastructure to be composed of.
And then we'll be able to visualize this infrastructure
using Infrastructure Composer
to see how the components relate to each other
in CloudFormation.
So why should you use AWS CloudFormation?
Well, first, it is your infrastructure as code.
That means that no resources are being manually created,
which is going to be excellent for control.
And all the code that makes up
these CloudFormation templates can be used
for version control, for example, using Git.
Also, any changes to your infrastructure
is going to be reviewed through code changes.
In terms of cost,
well, all the resources within your CloudFormation stack
is going to be tagged with an identifier
so you can easily see how much a CloudFormation stack
is going to cost you.
And we can also estimate the cost of resources
from your CloudFormation templates.
And finally, you can have saving strategy.
For example, in your development environment,
you could automate the deletion of the templates at 5:00 PM
and recreate them automatically at 8:00 AM in a safe matter
because everything is automated.
For productivity,
this is amazing because you have the ability to destroy
and recreate an infrastructure on the cloud on the fly.
And this is really leveraging the whole power of the cloud,
which is to just create and delete things
and only pay as you go.
You also have automated generation of diagrams
for your template, which is very good
for your architecture diagrams
and its declarative programming.
So you don't need to figure out the order of the creation
of the resources and the orchestration of things.
All these things are done by CloudFormation for you.
There's also a separation of concern.
You can create many CloudFormation stacks
for many applications and many layers.
For example, you may want to have stacks
for your network and your VPCs.
You may want to have stacks for your applications and so on.
Finally, you don't reinvent the wheel
because you can leverage existing templates on the web
and the documentation
to quickly write your CloudFormation templates.
Now, how does CloudFormation work?
Well, your templates must be uploaded in Amazon S3
and then referenced from CloudFormation.
So you upload it, and then from CloudFormation
you reference it and a stack will be created.
And what is a CloudFormation stack?
Well, it is made of AWS resources,
and it could be any kind of things you can create on AWS.
If you wanted to update a template,
you cannot edit the previous one.
What we have to do is to re-upload
a new version of the template to AWS
and then update your stack.
Now, your stacks are identified by a name within the region,
and if you delete a CloudFormation stack,
every single artifact and resource
that was created by CloudFormation will be deleted.
Now, how do we deploy CloudFormation templates?
Well, there is the manual way
in which we're going to use something
like Infrastructure Composer
or a code editor to directly create
our CloudFormation templates, and then we use the console
to input the parameters and so on.
And we'll do this method mostly in this course
for learning purposes, or you can go the automated way.
So you're going to edit your templates in a YAML file,
and then you use the CLI to deploy the templates,
or you use a continuous delivery tool
to this automatically on the cloud.
And it's recommended if you want to fully automate your flow
to deploying CloudFormation templates.
Now, the building blocks of CloudFormation.
So your template is made of different components,
and we'll have a look at them in detail,
so don't be overwhelmed by this,
but we have the AWSTemplateFormatVersion,
which defines the version of how to read the templates.
This is for internal purposes from AWS.
The description, which is the comments about the templates,
the resources, which is the actual only mandatory section
in CloudFormation, which is going to define
all the AWS resources that are declared in the templates,
the parameters,
which are the dynamic inputs for your templates,
the mappings, the static variables for your templates,
and we'll see the differences
between parameters and mappings,
the outputs to get references to what has been created
in your templates,
conditionals, which are a list of conditions
to perform resource creation,
and we'll have a few template helpers
such as references and functions.
But don't worry.
We'll have a look at all of this
and code examples in this section, so don't worry.
So that's it for an introduction to CloudFormation.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 36. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Parameters
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858810
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
CloudFormation parameters in detail.
So parameters are a way for you to provide inputs
into your CloudFormation templates.
So you have a CloudFormation template
and you want your user to provide parameter values,
and these parameters are defined
as part of the CloudFormation templates.
We actually used them before
when we were giving a security group a description.
So, they're super important to know about
if you want to reuse your templates across the company
so that many people can put many parameters
and because the inputs cannot be determined ahead of time.
So the parameters are extremely powerful,
they're controlled, and they also can prevent errors
from happening in your templates thanks to the types,
and we'll have a look at those in a second.
So when should you use a parameter?
So this is the SecurityGroupDescription parameter
we have used from before,
and the question you need to ask yourself
when defining if something should
or shouldn't be a parameter is this.
Is this CloudFormation resource configuration
likely to change in the future?
If so, make it a parameter,
because whenever you want to update that value,
you will not have to re-upload the template
to change its contents.
Also, if it cannot be determined ahead of time,
then again, you should make it a parameter.
So the parameters have multiple settings
and the first one is Type.
It could be a String, a Number, a CommaDelimitedList,
a List of numbers.
It could be an AWS-Specific Parameter,
for example, to help you catch invalid values
or a list of those.
It could be an SSM Parameter.
It could also have a Description.
It could have a DonstraintDescription
if you have a constraint.
It could have a Min and a MaxLength,
a Min and a Max Vlue, a Default value,
a list of AllowedValues,
regex of an AllowedPattern and NoEcho,
and it could have other things
maybe not represented in this slide.
So you don't have to remember all of those,
but what you need remember
is that the parameters are not just strings.
You can have constraints and validation,
allowing you to make sure they are safe to use.
So I want to give you two important examples
going into the exam.
The first one is AllowedValues.
So here is an example.
We have a parameter called InstanceType.
To choose an EC2 InstanceType of Type: String.
But we have defined AllowedValues being t2.micro,
t2.small, or t2.medium
with a Default being t2.micro.
And this parameter is reused in the EC2Instance.
So thanks to it, we'll have a dropdown
and the user can only select one of these three values,
hence giving them choice while giving you control.
Then we have NoEcho.
So for example, say we want as a parameter
to put in the database password,
but of course it is a password
so we have to keep it secret.
So we want to remove it from the logs and so on.
So we'll have NoEcho: true
so that the password is not displayed anywhere.
Now, how do we actually use these parameters?
So it is this little !Ref function you've seen before.
Maybe if you had to look at the CloudFormation templates.
So this function !Ref can be leveraged
to reference parameters,
and these parameters can be used then
anywhere in the templates.
So you've seen I wrote Fn::Ref,
but actually there's a shorthand version in YAML
called the !Ref.
So it's easier to use and easier to read.
And so this function allows you to reference parameters,
but also reference other elements within the template.
So let's have a look at the templates
we have to see how this was being used.
So here I am in my template,
and as you can see, one parameter was being defined.
We named it.
We had the description, Security Group Description,
and a Type: String.
So it was a very simple parameter.
We did not have any types of constraint on it.
Now, this SecurityGroupDescription
is representing the description of a security group
and therefore we're going to find its usage
by scrolling down.
And in here for our second EC2 SecurityGroup,
under properties GroupDescription, we have a !Ref.
So here the !Ref function,
pointing to SecurityGroupDescription,
which is the exact same name here
as the name of our parameter above.
So this is the usage of the !Ref function
and how to reference a parameter
within your CloudFormation templates.
But on top of it, this !Ref function
is used in other places.
For example, under the SecurityGroups property
of our EC2::Instance we had a !Ref for SSHSecurityGroup.
And this SSHSecurityGroup
is the exact name as the resource SSHSecurityGroup
defined in our template.
So here we have used the !Ref function
to reference a resource and not a parameter.
So they're used the same way.
And that's why you need to make sure
that your resources don't have the same name
as your parameters.
So here we have the !Ref to SSHSecurityGroup.
We have a !Ref to ServiceSecurityGroup.
And then for the elastic IP we have a reference
to MyInstance, which was defined right above.
Now that we've had a look at parameters in depth,
let's look at pseudo parameters.
So AWS is offering us pseudo parameters
in any CloudFormation templates.
And these are things that are already existing
even if you don't create them,
and they can be used at any time and are enabled by default.
So I'm giving you a list of important ones, not all of them,
but so you can understand.
So for example, if you use a !Ref
to the AWS AccountID reference value,
then the return value will be your actual account ID.
So from your CloudFormation template, it is possible
to figure out automatically your account ID.
Or the AWS region you are in, or the stack ID
or the stack name or notifications ARN
or just no value too.
You don't get any kind of value.
So these pseudo parameters are very handy
and I think one of the most used is, for example,
to figure out the region and the account ID.
So you don't need the user to actually tell
your CloudFormation templates that they are in us-east-1.
The template knows itself that it is in us-east-1
thanks to pseudo parameters.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 37. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Mappings
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858822
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
mappings in CloudFormation.
So mappings are fixed variables
within your CloudFormation templates,
and they're very handy if you want to differentiate
between different environments.
For example, dev versus prod,
and give different values for those,
or regions, such as AWS regions or AMI types and so on.
So all the values that are possible are hardcoded
within the template and here is the format of mappings.
But to make it a bit more concrete,
I'm going to show you a region map.
So here, based on the region you have, so us-east-1,
us-west-1, or eu-west-1, and based on the architecture
you're using, for example, HVM64 or HVMG2,
this is going to give you a different AMI ID every time.
Well, we know that the AMIs are specific
based on the region, so of course it makes sense
to have a different AMI per region.
So it's a great candidate for a mapping.
Now to access the mapping values, here is an example.
So we have an EC2 instance that is using an ImageId.
And this ImageId is using the FindInMap function.
And to use this FindInMap function,
we first need to use a map name.
So here we have the RegionMap.
Then we have the top level key.
So what we want to use in here,
we have a reference to the pseudo parameter AWS::Region.
So if you launch this template in us-east-1,
it's going to be us-east-1,
and if you launch it to us-west-1,
automatically this pseudo parameter
is going to resolve to us-west-1.
And then finally, the type of architecture you want,
for example, HVM64.
And this works great because, well,
AMIs are region specific,
and so you want to make sure you have the right AMI
for the right region and the right architecture.
So when do you use mappings versus parameters?
Well, the mappings are great when you know in advance
all the values that can be taken
and that they can be deduced from variables
such as the region, the availability zone, the AWS account,
the environment, dev versus prod, et cetera, et cetera.
They allow you safer control over the templates.
But if you have values that really depend
on what the user wants
and what they're thinking about at runtime,
then you want parameters
to give the user a maximum amount of freedom.
So that's it for mappings.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 38. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Outputs & Exports
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858832
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, now let's talk about outputs
and CloudFormation.
So, the output section is optional
and it declares optional output values,
but then if we declare them,
we can import these values into other stacks.
And so, the idea is that we can link, for example,
a network stack which has an exported output,
which is your VPC ID,
and we can reference that exported outputted value
from another application stack.
So this is very handy.
We can also view the values of the outputs in the console
or by using the CLA.
And so it's very helpful to have an output if you define,
for example, a network CloudFormation stack,
and then you output the VPC IDs and the Subnet IDs
and reuse them other ways.
It's the best way
to also perform some collaboration across stacks
and let experts handle their own stacks
and collaborate this way.
So, if you have a look at the output,
here is a sample output.
So, we are creating an SSH security group
as part of one template.
And then we create an output
that has a reference to the security group.
And this specific output also has an export block,
which is going to export the value
of this output as a name.
So the name is SSHSecurityGroup.
And this name has to be unique across all your exports
in one specific region.
And so now we can access through this SSH Security Group,
the security group ID
for our SSH Security Group in our company.
So, how do we reuse it?
Well, here is another CloudFormation template,
and this one will leverage the security group from before.
So it has an import value function,
as you can see right now, outlined in red.
And so that means that for this EC2 instance
that we're creating, the security group
has its value imported from another stack
in which we had exported the value, which was right here.
So this is how you link
two different CloudFormation templates.
And therefore, because they're linked,
it's impossible for you to delete the first stack
that has its value exported
until all the other ones don't reference it anymore.
So it's important to know.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
Now you know about outputs.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

And then you have your conditions being created this way.

but it could also be an output, et cetera, et cetera.

CreateProdResources.

# 41. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Rollbacks
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC

So let's talk about CloudFormation rollbacks.
And they're very important to understand at the exam.
So if you create a stack and the stack creation fails you have two options.
The first one is the default option, which is that everything rolls back and that means gets deleted.
And you can look at the log of your CloudFormation create to understand what happened and why it failed.
But you cannot look at your resources.
But if one of these resources has a problem and you want to keep it, you have the option to disable
the rollback to troubleshoot what happened during your stack creation.
If it is a problem with stack updates, then automatically by default, the stack is automatically going
to roll back to the last previous known working state, again, deleting anything that was newly created.
And again, you can look in the log to see what happened and the error messages.
Now in case of a rollback failure.
So that means that there is a stack update.
It rolls back and during the rollback there is a failure.
Then this is a problem with your stack.
And you probably had resources that were manually changed.
In that case you need to go and fix these resources manually.
And then through the console or through the API, you can issue what's called a continue update rollback
to tell CloudFormation to try rolling back again.
So either you do it from the console or an API call, or from the CLI using the continue update rollback
API call.
Okay.
So let's practice failures.
So let's create a stack and we'll upload a template file.
And the file I'm going to upload is called trigger failure dot Yaml to number two.
So why is this file problematic.
Well if you go into trigger values.yaml you look at the image ID of my EC2 instance, it is an image
ID that does not exist.
So therefore it's going to create a failure.
So let's click on next and I'll call this one Trigger Creation Failure.
Click on next.
And here under Stack Failure Options we have two options.
Number one is to rollback all stack resources.
That means that they're going to be rolled back to the previous known stable state.
Or we can preserve successfully provision resources.
And this will keep the successfully provisioned resources and rollback any failed resources to the last
known stable state.
So if we do this, which is the Non-default option, and then we click on next and then submit.
As you can see, we generate an SSH security group and we generate a server security group.
And so as you can see I need to first of all there's one problem that I didn't provide the group description.
So it's a good example of the failure of this.
So as you can see though, even though my uh server security group was not able to be created, my SSH
security group was able to be created.
And if I go into resources, well, one is still being kept.
Whereas if you had a creation and by default it would fail, it would delete everything.
So this could be the occasion to just troubleshoot if you needed to.
But of course, because this leaves some Remainers, uh, you need to absolutely delete the stack to
get rid of it.
So you cannot update the stack and fix things.
So we will delete it.
And now it's gone.
So this is showing you the option of what it is when there is a create failure and you can do the exact
same thing.
So you can create a stack.
Right now I'll create a stack based on a correct template called just EC two dot Yaml.
And I'll call it uh, failure on update.
So right now we're good.
We know that this is going to work because well, this is the template we've used from before.
So let's wait for things to be created.
And as we can see we're good.
So I'm going to update my stack.
And if you don't see this button just refresh your page.
So update my stack.
But this time I will replace the template with the template file named Trigger failure.
So this time we'll have a group description called hello next.
And here we have again the option to rollback all stack resources or to preserve successfully provision
the resources.
So we're now would say rollback everything and see what happens.
And then we'll do the second option right after.
So let's click on next and then click on submit.
So this is going to create a few security groups.
And then it's going to trigger a rollback.
So my security groups right now are being created.
Now they're done.
And as you can see, the instance gets created.
But then there was an update failed because, well, the invalid army was not found.
So therefore what's going to happen?
Well, because we have specified everything to roll back, then everything is going to roll back based
on the last known state.
And so that means that my server, SSH security server, security group and SSH security groups should
disappear.
So let's wait for these events to happen.
And as you can see right now, my SSH security group and server security group get deleted.
And similarly as an exercise if you update the stack.
But this time you choose again the trigger failure and.
We just enter description again?
And then the stack failure option.
We just say preserve successfully provision resources.
Then you know what happens.
You can try it out on your own.
This would create SSH and server security groups, but it would not roll them back in case there is

So this is up to you to choose what you want.
But both both the behaviors can be desirable based on what you're trying to do.

# 42. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Service Role
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314068
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is one thing you need
to know about CloudFormation and security.
So CloudFormation can use service roles.
What are they?
Well, they are iam roles that you create
and they're dedicated to CloudFormation
and they allow CloudFormation
to actually create update
and delete stack resources on your behalf.
So if you want to give the ability to users
to actually create, update
and delete stack resources,
but they don't have the permissions
to directly work with the resources,
what you would do is use a service role.
So for example, we define a template
and our own iam permissions as a user is
to do actions on the CloudFormation.
And we have iam PassRole.
We also create a service role that we're going
to be dedicating to CloudFormation.
And this service role has the S3 star buckets,
permissions, for example,
to create, update and delete a bucket.
So here CloudFormation will be able
to create this S3 bucket thanks
to its service role because the user was able
to pass that role to CloudFormation.
So the use cases for security is if you want
to achieve the least privileged principle
and you don't want to give the users
all the permissions
to create the stack resources,
only the permissions
to invoke a service role on CloudFormation.
For this to work, remember the user
must have the permission named iam PassRole,
which is a necessary permission
to give a role to a specific service in AWS.
So let me show you an example
of iam roles with CloudFormation.

# 43. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Capabilities
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314094
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Finally, you need to learn
about CloudFormation capabilities.
So we have CAPABILITY_NAMED_IAM and CAPABILITY_IAM.
So they are capabilities you need to give to CloudFormation
whenever your CloudFormation template
is going to create or update IAM resources,
such as when you create a IAM user,
a role, a group, a policy, and so on,
through your CloudFormation templates.
So you specify NAMED_IAM if the resources are named,
otherwise, just CAPABILITY_IAM.
And the reason we do so
is that we want to explicitly acknowledge the fact
that CloudFormation is going to create IAM resources.
We have CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND,
which is when your CloudFormation template
is including macro and nested stacks,
so stacks within stacks,
to perform dynamic transformations.
And in here, we're acknowledging that the template
may change before being deployed.
And finally,
if you obtain a InsufficientCapabilitiesException
while launching a template,
that means that the CloudFormation templates
was requiring capabilities,
but you haven't acknowledged them.
So, as a security measure, you need to redo the templates,
upload, and launch using, this time, these capabilities.
It's just an extra argument in your API call,
or a box to tick on your AWS console.
So here, under 3_capabilities.yaml,
I'm going to show you a CloudFormation template,
which actually has an IAM role being created.
And it's named, so there's a role name, MyCustomRoleName.
And it's using a managed policy,
which is the AmazonEC2FullAccess.
So we're dealing with IAM,
and so as such, we are creating some IAM roles.
And so therefore, if I create this stack
and upload the template file being the capabilities.yaml.
And I'll call this one DemoIAM.
Next.
And scroll all the way down.
Next.
And scroll all the way down.
As you can see, there is an acknowledgement
that says that you need to have this capability,
and it says, "Yes, I acknowledge the fact
that CloudFormation might create IAM resources
with custom names."
And so therefore, we are giving the capability
to CloudFormation to actually run this template
and to create this role.
If we don't do this,
then the submission is going to fail, as you can see.
But if we do do this, then now we're saying,
"Hey, I understand the risk of it.
I understand the fact that we are creating IAM resources
from within CloudFormation."
And that's it, that's all I want to show you.
All right, I will see you in the next lecture.

# 44. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Deletion Policy
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314112
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about
CloudFormation- DeletionPolicy.
DeletionPolicy is a setting you can apply
to resources on your CloudFormation templates,
which allows you to control what happens
to a resource when the resource is removed
from your CloudFormation templates
or when the CloudFormation stack is deleted.
It's a way for you to actually preserve
and backup up resources.
So by default, we've seen
that when we delete a CloudFormation template,
all the resources within are also deleted.
That means that the default DeletionPolicy is delete,
so you don't have to specify it because it is the default.
Sometimes you wanna specify to be really explicit
that things are being deleted, but so here's an example.
We have an EC2 instance,
and as you can see, DeletionPolicy is delete.
So that means that the EC2 instance will be deleted
whenever the CloudFormation stack is deleted.
Okay. Here is another example.
We have an S3 buckets
and we have DeletionPolicy=Delete.
So everything probably should be working fine,
but actually if you have an S3 bucket, this is an exception,
and you have DeletionPolicy=Delete on it.
It will work only if the S3 bucket is empty.
If it's not empty, then the delete will fail.
So the way to fix this if you wanted to would be
to either manually delete everything within the S3 bucket
and then continue with the deletion
of your CloudFormation templates.
Or it would be for you to implement a custom resource
to actually delete everything within the S3 bucket
before automatically having the S3 bucket go away.
Now let's talk about DeletionPolicy retain.
So for the retain DeletionPolicy,
it's actually specifying which resources you want
to preserve in your CloudFormation templates.
So example here, we have a DynamoDB table,
and we know that by default, it would be deleted
when I delete my CloudFormation template,
but maybe we actually wanna keep it, keep the data within
because we care about the data of this table.
And so we would specify at the bottom
DeletionPolicy retain.
And so even if I delete my CloudFormation templates,
this DynamoDB table would stay,
and this works with any resources.
Finally, the last DeletionPolicy you need
to know about is snapshots.
So this is to create one final snapshot
before deleting the resource.
And it's supported by EBS volumes,
ElastiCache Cluster, ElastiCache ReplicationGroup,
RDS DBInstance, DB cluster, Redshift, Neptune,
DocumentDB, and maybe more.
And the idea is that you would specify at the bottom,
of course, a DeletionPolicy snapshot.
And so that instance of database from RDS would be deleted,
but a last snapshot would be taken
before that instance is gone.
And so that's very helpful for backups and safety purposes.
So, let's have a look.
And in this file deletionpolicy.yaml,
there is a security group
and the DeletionPolicy is retained.
So that means that if I delete my transformation stack,
this security group should stay.
And there is an EBS volume,
and the DeletionPolicy is a snapshot.
So that means that upon deleting the stack,
the volume should go away,
but a snapshot should be created first.
So let's verify this behavior by creating a stack
and uploading the template file being DeletionPolicy.
Next, DeletionPolicyDemo is the name of my stack.
Scroll down next and submit.
So this goes ahead
and creates very quickly my CloudFormation stack,
which is going to be made again of two resources.
We have an EBS volume,
and then we have an EC2 security group.
So now they're both created
and my stack has been fully created.
Now let's go ahead and try to delete it.
So let's delete the stack and let's look at the events.
So we see here that the My Security group
has a delete skipped.
This is because we did specify
a DeletionPolicy of retain.
So if I wanted to get rid of this security group,
as you can see, it is still here.
If I wanted to get rid of it, I would need
to manually delete it
because I told CloudFormation not to delete it.
Now, regarding the EBS volume, it has been deleted.
But if I go into the events, it turns out that
a snapshot has been created and it was successful.
And here is the snapshot ID.
Therefore, if I go into
my snapshots on the left-hand side, I have a new snapshot
of one gigabytes that was just created right now
from my EBS volume,
but my EBS volume, as you can see, is gone.
So if you wanted to fully clean up, please make sure
to also delete this snapshot manually.
And please make sure to also delete
the security group if you wanted to.
But that's it.
We've seen the power of the DeletionPolicy.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 45. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Stack Policy
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37858864
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's do a quick lecture
on CloudFormation Stack policies.
So, when you have a CloudFormation Stack update, by default,
any action is going to be allowed on all resources
so you can change your stack as you wish,
but sometimes, you may want to protect your stack
against updates, or part of your stack against updates.
This is where Stack policies come in.
Stack policies are JSON documents,
and they define what update actions are allowed
on specific resources during Stack updates.
So here, we have an example where the first statement
is saying "Allow update*" on everything,
meaning that everything in your CloudFormation Stack
can be updated, and the second part is saying "Deny update*"
on Resource Production Database.
That means that whatever is named "Production Database"
in your CloudFormation Stack is going to be protected
against any kind of updates,
so by default, and your production database is fine.
So, the goal of Stack policies is really
to protect resources against unintentional updates
and when you set a Stack policy by default,
all the resources are protected,
and so what you need is to have an explicit "allow"
for the resources that you want to be allowed to be updated.
So, that's it.
You should know enough to answer maybe one question
on the exam on this.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 47. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Custom Resources
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314146
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now, let's talk about
CloudFormation custom resources.
So as we said, many, many resources
are supported by CloudFormation.
But you have custom resources to define resources
that are not yet supported by CloudFormation
or to define custom provisioning logic
for resources that can be outside of CloudFormation.
For example, your own on-premises resources
or your third-party resources,
or if you want to have custom scripts
being run during the create, update,
and delete phases of your CloudFormation stack
through Lambda functions.
And one example I will give you, again,
is to run a Lambda function to empty and S3 bucket
before being deleted.
And this is a common exam question.
So to define a custom resource,
you define it in the template, and the type of it
is Custom::MyCustomResourceTypeName.
It's backed by either a Lambda function,
which is the most common one, or an SNS topic.
So how do we define a custom resource?
I will only go over the Lambda custom resource
because it's the most common one.
So we have a custom resource of type custom,
MyLambdaResource.
And then, in the properties, we have a service token.
And the service token is either your Lambda function, ARN,
or your SNS ARN.
They must be in the same region.
And the idea is that this Lambda function
is going to have its own logic
to provision your customer resource
or to do whatever it needs.
On top of it, thanks to input data parameters,
you can provide input values to your Lambda function.
So the use case, for example, as I said,
is to delete content from an S3 bucket
because it turns out that you cannot delete
a non-empty S3 bucket from CloudFormation.
So first, you must delete all the objects in it,
and then you delete the buckets.
To do so, you use a custom resource.
And the idea is that when that custom resource is deleted,
it's going to run API calls
to actually delete your S3 buckets.
So here's an example.
Whenever we run delete stack on CloudFormation,
then your custom resource backed by Lambda function
is going to run API calls to empty your S3 bucket.
And then only then,
when your S3 bucket is emptied,
then CloudFormation is going to actually attempt
to delete your S3 bucket,
and everything will work.
So that's the most common use case
from an example perspective.
And that's the one I wanted to show you
by the way of diagram.
So I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

Okay, so let's actually deploy

But first, let's understand
how it works to use custom resources.
So, we are going to develop a template
that has a custom resource,
and we can choose either Lambda or Amazon SNS
to back up that custom resource.
Now, when we have a Lambda or Amazon SNS backed resource,
what's going to happen is that CloudFormation

to comes back from an Amazon S3 bucket.
So, Lambda or SNS don't talk back directly
to CloudFormation.
They actually perform whatever API calls you want.
And then when they're done,
they're going to upload the JSON response to Amazon S3
using that S3 pre-signed URL.
So, there's gonna be a request that will contain a lot
of information from CloudFormation,
such as the parameters and so on, and the S3 pre-signed URL.
And then using that pre-signed URL Lambda
or whatever script you have,
is able to upload that response into Amazon S3.
So, now we know we cannot delete a non-empty S3 bucket.
So first, we must delete all the objects inside it.
And so for this, we're going to create a custom resource

to empty an S3 bucket before deleting it.
So, we'll have a stack

we'll empty the bucket upon deleting it.

So, if the event is going to be delete,
then we delete the S3 content.
And these are API calls
to actually delete all the objects in the bucket.
When everything is okay,
we send a response back to CloudFormation.
The CFN response package actually
uploads the request back into the temporary S3 bucket
where CloudFormation expects a response from.
And if it's not a delete event, then we just ignore it.
So, this script will actually empty our S3 bucket

Now, we also have an execution role,

And if I tried to delete it

This is just a safety

But because we have a Lambda function,

The S3 bucket will be emptied,

# 49. [DVA/SOA] CloudFormation - Dynamic References
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314026
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about dynamic references
in CloudFormation.
So we can store values in Systems Manager Parameter Store
or we can store secrets in Secrets Manager.
And we can actually reference these values
into your CloudFormation templates.
The idea is that CloudFormation
is going to retrieve the value of the specified references
during any create, update or delete operations.
For example, you may want to retrieve the master password
of a RDS Database Instance from Secrets Manager.
So here's an example. We have CloudFormation.
We're going to get either a value from the Parameter Store
or Secrets Manager by using the key.
So this supports three kinds.
It supports ssm for plaintext values stored
into the Systems Manager Parameter Store,
it supports ssm-secure for secure strings stored
in the Systems Manager Parameter Store,
and finally, it supports secretsmanager
for the secret value stored in the Secrets Manager service.
The syntax to resolve one of these values
is to use {{resolve:service-name:reference-key}}
So for SSM, we have {{resolve:ssm:parameter-name:version}}.
And here's the example.
So we have an Amazon S3 bucket
and for the access control settings,
we want to resolve it directly
from the SSM Parameter Store.
We have SSM Secure, so this time,
it's to store actual secrets value,
but from within the Parameter Store.
And so it's the same syntax.
But instead of ssm, you have ssm-secure
because we know that the value is encrypted.
And here is IAM user
and it turns out the password of this IAM user
is resolved from within the Parameter Store
as a secure parameter.
And finally, for Secrets Manager,
here we have an RDS Database Instance,
and we resolve the master username and the master password
directly from the Secrets Manager service
by using, again, the dynamic references in the syntax
that I just wrote above,
which is pretty long but very explicit.
So dynamic references are super important.
Now there is two other things you need to know
for the integration of CloudFormation
and Secrets Manager and RDS.
So it turns out that if you create a stack like this
which has a RDS Database cluster,
which is, for example, aurora,
and we have ManageMasterUserPassword: true,
that means that the secrets behind that aurora database
is going to be created implicitly.
That means that the RDS service itself
is going to create a secret in Secrets Manager
to manage the Master User Password and its rotation.
And so, to get the value of the secret ARN,
what you need to do is, in the output,
you use the GetAtt intrinsic function
to get the secret ARN from the Master User secret.
So here in this example,
CloudFormation only manages an RDS Database
and the RDS Database manages the secret in Secrets Manager.
The other way is to use a dynamic reference,
just like we saw.
So this time, we actually create a secret
from within our CloudFormation template.
And as you can see,
there is the GenerateStringKey for password,
which means that it's going to automatically generate
a secret password for us from within CloudFormation.
Next, we have our database instance,
which is going to reference the secret
in the RDS Database Instance
using the resolve function
we just saw through dynamic reference.
And so that means that the database instance
is going to leverage the secret out of Secrets Manager.
And finally, to link these two things together
and make sure there is a password rotation,
you create a secret RDS attachment
to let the database know that it should be linked
to this secret in Secrets Manager
so that the secret can rotate over time
and the RDS Database automatically updated.
And that's it!
You know everything about dynamic references
and CloudFormation with Parameter Store
and Secrets Manager.
So I hope you liked it,
and I will see you next lecture.

to start and enable HTTPD.
And finally, we had this echo command
to actually create our index.html file.

and it took 34 seconds,
and we had this content as a result
being ready on our web server.
So this is great,
and it turns out that our EC2 instance was created

Even though if we had issues in this

CloudFormation would return a success.

# 52. [SOA] CloudFormation - cfn-signal & Wait Condition
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314248
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about a way
for CloudFormation to know whether or not
your EC2 instance got properly configured
after running a cfn-init.
So for this, we'll use the cfn-signal script.
So the common convention is to run the cfn-signal script
right after the cfn-init script.
And it will tell CloudFormation if the resource creation
was a success or a failure.
For this, we also need to define what's called
a WaitCondition in CloudFormation.
And the WaitCondition is going to make the template wait
as the name indicates, until it receives a signal
from cfn-signal.
For this, we attach a creation policy,
and this also works on EC2 and ASG,
but right now will show you on WaitCondition,
and this is a creation policy
that has a resource signal including a timeout and a count.
If we define a count greater than one,
that means that we're expecting more than one resources
to signal their success to CloudFormation.
Otherwise you can keep it as one.
So the process is as such,
CloudFormation will launch an EC2 instance
and then it will have a WaitCondition.
The EC2 instance is going to run cfn-init on it.
Therefore we will retrieve the init data just like before,
but now on the init data right after,
we're going to do a signal from cfn-signal
to send data back to CloudFormation to the WaitCondition.
So let's have a look at the script
for us to better understand.
Okay, so here I am in my
CloudFormation signal template number two.
And we create an EC2 instance just like before
and we have user data.
And as you can see now the script is a little bit different.
So we still get the CloudFormation script for Bootstrap,
then we still run the cfn-init just like before.
But now we store the result
of the last command into this verbal named init_status.
So if cfn-init was successful,
then init status will be equal to zero.
And if cfn-init was not successful,
it would be an error code that would be different than zero
and init status would be equal to that error code.
And then we send the result back
to CloudFormation using cfn-signal.
So we're saying, hey, using the cfn-signal script,
send back the value of this variable init status
to my stack being my stack name.
And the resource is sample WaitCondition.
So let's confirm this.
So let's scroll down and have a look at the fact
that yes indeed we created a sample WaitCondition resource
in our templates.
So this is of type CloudFormation WaitCondition.
It's nothing physical,
it's just something that's going to wait
until the creation policy receives a signal.
So one signal and we have a timeout of two minutes
to receive that signal.
So if we don't receive anything within two minutes,
it's failed and otherwise we have two minutes to receive
either a success or a failure.
The rest is the same.
So we still have a security group
and we still have the very same CloudFormation init data.
So let's run this and see what happens.
So we're going to create a stack
and I'm going to upload a template file
choose it to cfn-signal.yaml.
Next, and I'll call this one demo cfn-signal.
Next, next, and then submit.
And now the create is in progress.
So now we can see that the SSH security group was created,
the instance in create is in progress.
And then we have a sample WaitCondition
that's also in create in progress.
Now if a refresh, even though the instance
is in create complete, as you can see,
the sample WaitCondition,
it's still in create in progress.
So before this would've been done
and this would've been a success,
but now we're actually waiting
to get a signal back from the EC2 instance

# 53. [SOA] CloudFormation - cfn-signal Failures
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314268
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So a common exam question you may get
is the fact that the wait condition did not receive
the required number of signals
from an Amazon EC2 instance.
So it could be several reasons to this.
First of all, it could be that the AMI you're using
doesn't have the CloudFormation helper scripts installed.
So if it doesn't include them, you can install them
of course to your instance.
You must also verify the output of the cfn-init
and the cfn-signal commands.
So a couple of log files can give you a lot of information
into how these commands went.
But of course, to get access to your instance,
you must first disable
the rollback on failure of CloudFormation,
otherwise, automatically CloudFormation
is going to delete the failed EC2 instance
as soon as it goes into a failed state,
into a delete state.
So it's important to disable rollback
so you can debug and actually go into your instance
to figure out what happened.
Also, you need to make sure
that the EC2 instance does have access to the internet,
especially if you launch it in the private subnet,
because well, it needs to be able to communicate
with the CloudFormation service.
So for this, you can run, for example,
a quick connectivity test to the Amazon.com website.
So now I've opened the file cfn-signal-failure,
and you'll find that everything is the same as before.
The only difference is that now in my CloudFormation
in its block, under commands,
I echo boom and then I exit 1.
So this command is going to be generating an error
because we have an exit 1
and 1 is a non-zero status code,
which means that there is an error.
And so because this command is going to fail,
then my cfn in its script is going to fail,
and therefore my INIT STATUS will be 1
because the error returned was 1,
and therefore the CFN signal command
is going to pass this 1 error status to CloudFormation,
which should make CloudFormation fail.
So let's observe this behavior right now
by going back into CloudFormation creating a stack
in this I will choose 3-cfn-signal-failure.yaml,
and I'll call this one cfn-signal-failure-demo.
Next, next, and then submit.
And let's have a look at the process in details.
So as we can see now, we have an SH security group
that is being created, an EC2 instance being created
and we have a wait condition.
And so what needs to happen is for my EC2 instance
to bootstrap and so to be properly created then
to run the script and it should fail
and let our wait condition know that there was
an issue with CFN signal.
So as we can see now, my instance was in create complete
and then about 30 seconds later, the wait condition
returned a create fail because it received a failure signal
with this unique ID.
So a failure was communicated by the EC2 instance
and therefore now everything is being deleted,
the entire stack is being rolled back,
and then the instance is being deleted,
the wait condition is being deleted,
and then my security group will be deleted.
So we're very happy because, well,
a failure in the bootstrap
of my EC2 instance resulted in the failure
of the CloudFormation stack and for everything to roll back
and to be deleted.
But if I wanted to debug things,
this is not very convenient.
So to debug things, you need
to use a different rollback setting
that I will show you in a second.
So again, you upload a file, this one,
next, enter whatever name,
and then here, under stack failure options, you need
to make sure to, instead
of rolling back all stack resources, instead
to preserve successfully provision resources to know exactly
what has malfunction.
So you can, for example, use EC2 instance connect,
look at the logs and see what happens,
and then figure out the root cause of your problems,
especially helpful during your development cycles.
So I hope that was helpful. I hope you understand now the
power of CFN signal and the wait conditions.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 54. [SOA] CloudFormation - Nested Stacks
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314306
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
"CloudFormation - Nested Stacks."
So, nested stacks are stacks within other stacks,
and they allow you to isolate repeated patterns
and common components in a separate stack
and then call them from other stacks.
For example, if you have a load balancer configuration
that is reused, you can do it as a nested stack,
or a security group that is reused and so on.
And the nested stacks are considered best practice
because, well, you let the knowledge
of one component in one stack,
and this is very good for reusability.
So if you wanted to update a nested stack,
you always update the parent, the root stacks.
And the nested stacks can also
have nested stacks within themselves.
So you can go very, very deep.
So this is very helpful,
but we've seen also cross stacks.
So what is the difference
between cross stacks and nested stacks?
So cross stacks are very helpful
when stacks have a different lifecycle.
Remember we had the VPC stack
and it was exporting some variables as an output.
And then we have the application stacks
referencing the output at that VPC stack.
And then we use the Fn::ImportValue
to actually import the exported value
into our application stacks.
So this is very handy
when you need to pass values between stacks.
Nested stacks are a little bit different.
It's when you have components that must be reused,
for example, how to properly configure
an application load balancer.
And it's only important to the higher level stacks,
so it's not shared.
So, your app stack may have an RDS stack,
an ASG stack, an ELB stack with other things in it.
And if you spin up another instance
of your application stack,
you will have another RDS stack,
another ASG stack, another ELB stack.
And so that is the difference
between cross stack and nested stacks,
and obviously from the context,
you will know which one to use.
So let's have a look at nested stacks.
And for this, I've created this file, nestedstacks.yaml.
And so as you can see in it,
we create an EC2::KeyPair.
So it is just a resource within our stack,
so this is completely normal.
But in here we have myStack
and the type of it is AWS::CloudFormation::Stack.
And so this represents a nested stack.
And so being a nested stack,
the first thing we need to indicate is the template URL,
so where to find this nested stack.
So, if you have a look at it here
and we paste it, as you can see,
I'm going to use the raw data.
As you can see, all of this is the nested stack
we're going to invoke, and this is a very long one.
So let's have a look at it
and let's see if we can make it look a bit prettier.
Okay, so as you can see, this is in the JSON form,
but we will be still be able to read it easily.
So the first parameter is a key name
and it's the name of an existing EC2 KeyPair
to enable SSH access to the instance.
So we have this parameter that we must fill in.
There's also a DBName, there's also a DBUser,
and we're seeing parameters with constraints
such as Min and MaxLength, AllowedPatterns, and so on.
This is a user, so it's secret,
so there is a "NoEcho": "true",
and so lots of different variables
and parameters we need to input.
Here, we have an instance type
and we have AllowedValues with a default value,
so very handy, and so on.
Then we have a Mappings to map the different instances
to different architecture,
so this is great.
And then we have resources.
So we have a WebServer EC2::Instance,
and it has a CloudFormation::Init data
in which we're going to install "mysql",
"mysql-server", "httpd", "php", and so on.
We have files that we're creating.
So index.php is being created with all that content.
We have setup.mysql being created and so on,
more files being created.
Some services being initialized such as "mysql",
"httpd", and "cfn-hup", some comments to run,
and then the properties itself of the EC2 instance.
So as you can see, it's quite a lot of things.
And we have the CreationPolicy with a ResourceSignal
to wait for this timeout until we know
that the resource has been successfully created.
So, all of this is great, and so therefore,
because we want to use this stack into myStack,
then we're going to need to send parameters to it.
So we're sending the KeyName as a reference
to the KeyPair we have created above.
We are sending the database name,
the user, the password, the root password,
the InstanceType, and the SSHLocation.
And from the outputs, we get a reference to our stack
as well as the output of the stack itself.
So OutputFromNestedStack being the WebsiteURL.
So let's go ahead and actually launch this template.
So we're going to upload a sample template,
nestedstacks, DemoNestedStack,
Next, and then Next.
And one thing you're going to notice
is that we have capabilities.
So here we are creating IAM resources.
So we have to check this capability.
And then we have this one called CAPABILITY_AUTO_EXPAND.
That is because we are using a nested stack.
And so this template we had from before,
which looked very simple, will be expanded
by the content of this template.
And so we don't know,
of course we know what's inside,
but we may not know what's inside,
and so this is a specific capability.
And so we're saying, yes, we know that CloudFormation
will auto expand our template,
and so therefore, we are aware of the risk
and we trust what we're expanding.
So let's click on Submit.
And now the create is in progress.
And so this stack is going to be created,
and you'll see in a second
that the key pair was created very quickly.
And now we have myStack
and myStack is in CREATE_IN_PROGRESS.
And if I refresh on the left hand side,
as you can see now,
you see that myStack is nested, it says NESTED,
and there is a separate view in here.
So you can view nested or don't view nested,
but I like to view nested.
And so within the nested stack,
we have our own events.
So we have the WebServerSecurityGroup,
we have the WebServerInstance that is being created,
and let's wait a little bit.
So now we have a look.
So the web server was in progress and it was waiting,
and it received a SUCCESS signal.
So my CFN signal script was working correctly.
And then the create is complete.
So the nested stack had a CREATE_COMPLETE.
And so back into my main stack, as we can see,
the myStack went into the CREATE_COMPLETE phase,
and then therefore my overall parent stack
also was complete.
So now both of them are working.
If I look at the output of this one,
this is the nested stack,
it only has one website URL.
But if I look at the output of this nested stack,
it has the stack reference
as well as the output from the nested stack.
So if I click on it, I get the hello page of PHP,
which is saying that everything is connected,
I'm connected to my localhost database,
here is my server ID, and so on.
So this is quite basic,
but just showing that my LAMP server,
LAMP for the piece for PHP is working great.
And so this is the whole power of nested stack.
And so the thing is you should never update
the nested stack itself.
You should always update the parent stack
with a new template, and then automatically,
it will update the nested stack if necessary.
As well for deletion purposes,

and this is going to delete the nested stack as well.
So that's it for this lecture,

# 55. [SOA] CloudFormation - Depends On
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314330
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about DependsOn.
And DependsOn is a way for you to specify a specific order
for the creation of resources.
So here in this template, we have an EC2 instance
and we have an RDS database instance.
And if I did not have this DependsOn right here,
they would both be created at the same time.
But because I'm adding DependsOn DBInstance, it turns out
that my DBInstance is going to be created first,
and only if it gets successfully created,
then my EC2 instance will be created on its own.
And so DependsOn allow you to specify some hints
at the order of which resources should be created at.
Now we've seen that CloudFormation also makes judgment calls
about in which order to generate resources.
And it turns out that if,
from your EC2 instance you're using, for example,
a reference intrinsic function
to a security group, then CloudFormation knows
that your EC2 instance depends on your security group
and therefore will create it only after your security groups
are created.
But if you're not using a ref function
or a get attribute function to link two things together,
then you can link them together
with the DependsOn attributes,
and that works with any resource.
So let's have a look at it right now.
So here is the file, 5-dependson.yml,
and we have two resources in it,
we have an EC2 instance of Type EC2 Instance,
the properties is a specific ImageId,
and an InstanceType of t2.micro,
and MyBucket, in MyBucket is an S3 bucket,
but we made it depend on MyEC2Instance,
and I need to rename things correctly,
otherwise it's not going to work.
Here we go.
And so what it means is that,
well, the S3 bucket will not be created
up until the EC2 instance is created.
If I did not have this line, if this slide was not existing,
then they would both be created at the same time
because there is no link between my EC2 instance
and my S3 buckets.
So let's observe this real quick.
We're going to upload the file, being this one, next.
Then we'll, DependsOn,
and submit.
And so as we can see, let's look at the events
to really make sure this is working as expected.
So as you can see,
MyEC2Instance is the only thing being created
and even if I refresh,
well, there is no S3 bucket being created right now.
And only when the EC2 instance is going to switch
to create completed will my S3 bucket be created.
Again, this is due to the DependsOn attribute,
so now MyEC2Instance is in create complete,
and as soon as it was done, as you can see,
MyBucket is being created and we're good to go.
So now my S3 bucket is being created.
And this works the exact same way on the deletes,
so when you have a DependsOn attribute,
let's go through the delete now,
if I delete things,
it's first going to delete the S3 bucket
and then when the delete of the S3 bucket is completed,
will it actually terminate the EC2 instance.
And that shows you the power of DependsOn.
So I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 56. [SOA] CloudFormation - StackSets
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314440
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's do a deeper dive
into CloudFormation StackSets.
So StackSets, as we know,
is a way for you to deploy stacks
across multiple accounts
and regions all in a single operation.
So we have the stack instance being deployed
in different regions and different accounts.
Now the only way for you to do this
is to have the administrator accounts create StackSets,
and the target accounts are only used for the creation,
the adaptation, and the deletion of these instances
from the StackSets.
When you upload and update a StackSets
in the administrator account,
then all the target accounts are going
to receive this updates in all regions.
And you can also, to define what is a target account
and what is Administrative account,
apply this to accounts from within an AWS Organization.
So let's talk about the permission model.
So because there is the concept of administrator accounts
and then target accounts,
there must be permissions.
And so you have IAM roles
with trust relationships in both the administrator
and the target accounts.
And these IAM roles allow you
to deploy your CloudFormation templates
into the target accounts.
So in the administrator accounts,
there is a AWS CloudFormation StackSet administration role,
which has a trust relationship
with every AWS CloudFormation StackSet execution role
in every target accounts.
And it is for you to manually create these roles
if you are not using AWS Organization.
This is the self-managed permissions.
If you have service-managed permissions,
then you use AWS Organization,
and automatically, Organization is going to create
the IAM role on your behalf.
For this, we need to enable trusted access
within AWS Organization and all features,
and automatically, you can deploy
to any new accounts in the future,
including the new accounts in your organization.
So here, we have the management accounts
or a delegated administrator
that is deploying to the target accounts,
and we don't need to worry about IAM roles.
So on top of it,
if you have new accounts in your organization,
you can have a feature to enable deploying stack instances
automatically to these new accounts.
So this allows you to really make sure that, for example,
one stack is deployed across all accounts
in your organization as soon as they're created.
You can also decide
to delegate the StackSet administration,
to specific member accounts in your organization
for security and governance purposes.
Also, to make sure that this all works together,
you need to make sure that you have trusted access
within your organization to be enabled
so that the delegated administrator can deploy
to accounts managed by Organization.
So to summarize, StackSets with AWS Organization,
we have the organization itself.
We have maybe a delegated administrator account
that is going to deploy a StackSet
and manage stack instances
into all the target member accounts in different OU.
For example, the Prod OU and the Dev OU.
And if you have enabled it,
and you have a new account in one of the OUs,
then automatically, a stack instance
will be deployed to that new account.
And that is the whole power of using StackSets
with AWS Organization.
So that's it for it.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.
