# 60. [SOA] CloudFormation - Troubleshooting
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314506
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's go over a little bit
of troubleshooting on CloudFormation.
So if you have a DELETE_FAILED status,
that means that you're trying to delete a stack,
but somehow the delete did not work.
So it could be a reason
such as some resources
must be emptied before being deleted,
such as your S3 buckets.
So this is a very common exam question.
If your S3 buckets cannot be deleted,
it's because they're not empty.
So either you empty them manually
or you use Custom Resources with Lambda functions
to automate the emptying action of your S3 buckets.
Also, for example,
you cannot delete a security group
if other EC2 instances are using the group.
And so therefore, if you're using, for example,
different stacks that use the same security group,
or you've done a manual attachment
of that security group to other instances,
then, of course, the delete
will be failing because it cannot be deleted
even if you try through the console.
Also, if you have too much trouble
with the deletion of a resource,
you can use DeletionPolicy=Retain
and it's going to skip the deletion
of that specific resource.
If you get UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED,
that means that you didn't update, it failed,
and then it tried to rollback
and even the rollback has failed.
So this could mean several things.
This can be caused by resources
changed outside of CloudFormation.
This could be insufficient IAM permissions.
This could be an Auto Scaling Group
that doesn't receive enough signals, and so on.
So the advice here
is to manually fix the error to make sure
that you've troubleshooted it and it works,
and usually the event log is going to give you some hints.
And then once you know the errors have been fixed,
you need to issue an API call
called ContinueUpdateRollback.
The rollback will continue
and hopefully, because you fixed the error,
the rollback will be successful at the end.
Now, for StackSets troubleshooting,
so for example, you'll have a stack operation,
it has failed, and then the stack instance status
is going to be an OUTDATED.
So it could be an issue with insufficient permissions
in the target accounts for creating the resources
that are specified in your templates.
Or the template could be trying to create global resources,
but they must be unique.
For example, if you have an S3 bucket,
the name should be unique and if you specified a name
in your template, then in one of the stack instances,
it's going to work,
but in another account or another region,
it's not going to work because the name
will have already been taken, by you, of course.
And so it could also be an issue with trust relationship.
For example, the admin account
does not have the required trust relationship
with the target accounts.
Or for example, you're creating EC2 instances
and somehow in one of the target accounts,
you've created one too many EC2 instances
and therefore, you'll have reached a limit or a quota
and you will have an issue
with that specific stack instance.
So StackSets are a bit more difficult
to troubleshoot because you're deploying
the same stack to many accounts and for some reason,
for some accounts, it may not work again
based on permissions, quotas, resource names, and so on.
So it's something to have a look at and something
to be able to troubleshoot.
Other things you need to troubleshoot is that, for example,
you cannot set an EC2 instance PrivateDnsName
in the CloudFormation templates.
There is no PrivateDnsName attributes.
And as a matter of fact,
you can't set anything that you wouldn't be able
to set through the AWS Console.
So the exam may test you on this.
It's less of a CloudFormation question
and more about, can you set this property on this resource?
So think about, can you set it
through the console, yes or no?
If you can, then yes, you can set it for CloudFormation.
If you cannot, then you cannot through CloudFormation.
This is something that can come with the exam.
Also, if your CloudFormation template works
in one region but doesn't work when deployed
in another region, several reasons.
It could be that the services
you're using in the one region
are not available in the other region.
It could be that you're using AMI IDs
that have been hardcoded in the templates.
And so therefore, because AMI IDs are regional,
if you don't transport them to a new region,
they will not work.
And also check for any hardcoded region-specific values.
For example, ARNs.
Finally, check unique names for resources that are required.
For example, if you set an S3 bucket name
to something because it's a global name,
then if you move the CloudFormation
to another region without first deleting the S3 bucket,
then it will not work as well.
All right, so that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

the configuration init,
in which specify the stack that we have.

and the interval I wish to check.

StackName, for the resource MyInstance

# 63. CloudFormation - Drift
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/42314544
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about CloudFormation Drift.
So we know that CloudFormation
allows you to create infrastructure,
but it doesn't protect you against
performing manual configuration changes
to whatever you create.
And so how do we know
if your resource configuration has changed?
How do we know if they have drifted?
So drifted is the same as changed.
For this we can use, of course, CloudFormation Drift.
So the idea is that we upload a template
into CloudFormation, for example,
this one creates a security group.
But we're going to modify this using the EC2 console
to change it to that.
Then using the Drift feature,
CloudFormation is going to compare the configuration
of your security group to what is expected,
and is going to tell you that it has drifted.
And this is very handy.
So you can detect the drift on an entire stack
or even individual resources within a stack.
So you can also use the CloudFormation Drift
detection on StackSets.
And the idea is that when you apply this,
it's going to apply drift on every stack instance
within the StackSets.
So in case there are problems
and resources have drifted,
then the stack will be considered drifted.
Every the stack instance as well will be considered drifted
and the StackSet as well.
So again, all these warnings will be displayed
at the resource stack, stack instance, and StackSet level.
So drift detection is going to allow you
to really identify any unmanaged changes
outside of CloudFormation.
And then if it's made through CloudFormation though,
but not at the StackSet level,
then it's not considered drifted,
although it's not best practice to update a stack instance
outside of a StackSets.
And you can also stop this drift detection
on the StackSet if you wanted to.
Alright, so now let's have a look at this drifting feature.
So let's go ahead and practice drift by creating a stack.
The template is ready.
I'm going to upload it,
and we'll choose 3-drift-security-group.yaml.
We can view this template in the designer,
just to have a look.
And if you look at the template itself,
which is not very handy here,
we have two security groups, one and two.
And if we look at them, there is an SSHSecurityGroup
and an HTTPSecurityGroup as well as a VPC parameter
to link it to the security groups.
And so we want to do is to ensure that the configuration
of the security groups has not changed over time.
So let's go ahead and first create the template.
So I'm clicked on the Cloud upload button,
which is going to make me click on Next,
and then I'll call it DemoDriftSG.
We need to specify a VPC ID.
So I will use drop down and specify my default one.
Click on Next, scroll down and click on Create Stack.
So the effect of this is that this is going to create
two security groups for me.
And as you can expect, I'm going to change manually
the security group configuration.
So this should be very quick.
The security groups are in create in progress,
and they're now both completed.
So if I go to Resources,
I have a link to my both security groups.
So if I go to my HTTP security group
under Inbound Rule, I can edit it.
And for example, I can change this rule to say
that I want a different CIDR, and I can add a description.
So Foobar and then this one maybe I want to add HTTPS
as well in this security group from anywhere.
Okay, click on Save Rule.
And in terms of the other security group,
which is right here, this one I can go into Inbound Rule
and I can edit them and just delete this rule overall.
And click on Save.
So obviously the configuration
of our security groups have changed,
and so therefore I'm going to have to detect the drift.
But right now CloudFormation is not
aware that anything has changed.
So to make it aware, we can click on Stack Actions
and then click on Detect Drift.
And this is going to start a drift detection mechanism.
And then under Stack Action view Drift results,
you can look at the results.
And as you can see, it's already finished.
The drift status is drifted.
And so there are two modified security groups,
and we can click on one for example
and click on View drift detail.
So it is saying that the CIDR IP is not equal,
and there's been one rule added.
So there are two differences,
and it shows us what the expected configuration is
and what the actual configuration is.
So as we can see here, well they're not equal.
And so we can go ahead and either update our templates
to match the actual configuration,
because maybe this is something we want
to include in our templates,
or we want to revert our stack
by making sure this is applied instead.
And we could go, for example, into CloudTrail to understand
who has changed our security group,
and when to really understand the root cause of this.
And so for the SSH security group, again,
I can click on View drift details and it's modified.
And we can see here there's a change.
This rule has been removed, and so the expected is this
and the actual is that.
So it's really, really cool to see really the drift,
because they're really helpful to know
if your CloudFormation templates
have drifted once in a while.
So I would recommend for you to run the drift quite often.
If you can.
You can also access the Drift menu
from the left hand side on the Drifts,
and this will take you to the Drift menu.
But that's it.
And when you're done, just delete this template
and you're good to go.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 64. Service Catalog - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37859030
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay so, next let's talk about AWS Service Catalog.
This is for the users that are going to be new to AWS.
They will have too many options to create stacks
and they may create stacks that are not compliant
or in line with the rest of the organization.
So we want to provide these users with
a self-service portal and then where we launching
only authorized products and these authorized products
will be predefined by administrators.
So it includes for example, virtual machines,
databases, storage options such as EFS, et cetera.
The idea is that with the Service Catalog,
we are giving users a controlled environment
to deploy stuff onto AWS.
So how does it work?
Well, it relies on the CloudFormation.
So first, you have two parts in Service Catalog.
You have the admins, and then you have the users.
So the admins are going to define products.
And what is the product in Service Catalog?
Well, it is a CloudFormation template
that the admins have to write.
And because the admins are power users,
they're going to write these CloudFormation templates
very, very well.
And they will put all these products together
and create a portfolio.
So a portfolio is going to be a collection of products.
And then each portfolio will be assigned
some IAM roles to give control.
So we're going to say,
who can access these portfolios and when.
So then the users are going to be presented
with a product list through the Service Catalog.
And the products they see,
are only going to be the products
that are authorized by IAM.
And then these users, for example,
they need a stack with an EC2 Instance,
then they will launch these products
and the products because they correspond to
CloudFormation templates, will be launching
whatever the CloudFormation templates is configured to do
and that will give you provisioned products.
Now they're ready to use, they're properly configured
and they're properly tagged.
So think of Service Catalog
as a set of CloudFormation templates
that your users can use based on their IAM permissions.
So in this example, we don't give the users,
to launch CloudFormation templates themselves,
we give them the ability to launch
the CloudFormation templates that only the admins
have been given the rights to do.
And so the idea here is that
we are giving a lot less control to our users
and we're giving making sure that our users
only can do the things that they are authorized to do
with Service Catalog.
So now, let's go back to the theory of Service Catalog.
We're creating and managing a catalog of IT services
that are going to be approved by our administrators on AWS.
Each product is a CloudFormation templates
and so you can do whatever you want
with CloudFormation templates,
but you can have a virtual machine image, servers,
software, databases, regions, IP address ranges,
whatever you want.
The idea is that by using CloudFormation,
we help ensure consistency,
and we have standardization by the admins.
So we don't give the users the right
to use CloudFormation directly.
We give them only the right to use Service Catalog,
which in turns is using CloudFormation as its backbone.
So then, the products will be assigned
to portfolios or teams, and the teams will be presented
with a self-service portal
when they can launch the products.
And all the deployed products are centrally managed
through Service Catalog.
Why do we do this?
Well, to help with governance, compliance, and consistency.
And so, this is what you're going to have to look like
for the exam, okay?
Whenever a user needs to be launching products,
but doesn't require deep AWS knowledge,
or doesn't need to know all the options of AWS,
the idea is that,
you should use something like Service Catalog,
and you should define these templates in advance
for your users to make sure that they can only do
exactly what you intended them to do.
So you can have standardization in tagging,
you can have standardization in the way things
are being configured, et cetera.
Finally, Service Catalog does integrate with
self-service portals, such as ServiceNow.
So it is possible for you to completely hide
the facts is Service Catalog and have your users
use your internal ServiceNow portal to request for example,
a EMR cluster to perform some big data.
And that's it.
So that's it for this lecture.
Remember, Service Catalog is only when
you're in just consistency, standardization
and give less control to the users
and more controls your admin.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 65. Service Catalog - Extras
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37859032
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's have a look at a few more
service catalog concepts for the exam.
So the first one is to use stack set constraints
to configure how you want your product
to be deployed using CloudFormation stack sets.
So you can actually restrict by accounts,
you can restrict by region
and you can define which IAM role should be used
to deploy this stack set into the target accounts.
So let's say we have a product
and we apply some stack set constraints around the regions.
For example, we say only eu-west-1
and us-west-2 are authorized.
Then we cannot deploy, for example, to us-east-1.
And that's very important because CloudFormation stack set
itself doesn't give you any kind of control about
where you can or cannot deploy.
But if you put a product as part of service catalog,
you have this kind of guardrails that you can create
for accounts, regions, and permissions.
So it's very important going into the exam
to know the differences between them two.
Next we have launch constraints.
So this is how you want a product to be launched
and which IAM role is going to be used
to launch that product.
So the idea is that if you have a user that doesn't have
the required permission to launch a product
because they don't have, for example,
permissions to use the EC-2 service or the RDS service
but the product itself uses EC-2 and RDS,
then you use a launch constraint,
and this launch constraint is just an IAM role
that has full CloudFormation permission,
that has all the services that you are defining
in the CloudFormation template to be able to create them.
And then the S3 bucket to be able to
read the CloudFormation templates.
And from that, this IAM role is assigned
to the service catalog product
and therefore any user who has the right
to launch the product will be able to launch the product
because the product will be launched thanks to that role.
So how can we have version control on service catalog?
For example, we want to synchronize everything
from a CodeCommit code repository into service catalog.
Well, for example, when we push a new product
into CodeCommit and we can maintain a file called
mapping.yml which says which products corresponds
to which templates, then we have some kind of
version control over these templates.
All we need to do now is to apply them into service catalog.
So for this, we can invoke a Lambda function
and this Lambda function will be invoked
on every Commit or every push into CodeCommits.
And this Lambda function will be able to
read all this information from the templates
such as the data itself,
so the yml templates and the mapping.yml.
And then the Lambda function will have some logic
to update or create the products in service catalog,
and you have effectively created a synchronization
between CodeCommit and service catalog.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 66. [SAA/DVA/SOA] Elastic Beanstalk - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869100
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's talk
about Elastic Beanstalk.
So so far in this course
when we've been deploying an application,
we've had the same architecture.
So we have a load balancer
that is taking all the requests from our users
and then we have an auto scaling group
with multiple available zones and in each AZ
there will be some EC2 instances being deployed there
and then in the backend,
we have maybe some data subnets,
so we have an RDS database to take the reads and writes,
maybe we have replicas and so on.
And if you're in the caching layer,
in the caching layer, we need to look at ElastiCache, okay?
So if there are so many applications for us to deploy
and they follow the same architecture,
it may be a pain to recreate it every single time.
So as a developer, it's complicated
to manage infrastructure, to deploy code,
we don't want to be configuring all the databases,
the load balancers, et cetera, et cetera.
And of course we want everything to be scaling.
So as we can see, most of the web applications
will have the same architecture
with a load balancer and an auto scaling group
and as a developer, all I want to do
is for my code run, okay?
I don't want to worry about everything else.
So also, if I develop in different programming languages
and have different applications and environments,
I possibly want a single way of deploying my application
and this is where Beanstalk comes into play.
So Beanstalk gives a developer centric view
of deploying an application on AWS.
The idea is that from one single interface,
it's going to reuse all the components we've seen before,
such as EC2, ASG, ELB, RDS,
but it's going to be a managed service
that will deploy all these things for you.
So it will handle the capacity provisioning,
it will handle all the configuration of the load balancer,
the scaling, the application health monitoring,
the instance configuration and so on.
And the only responsibility for you as a developer
is going to be the code itself, okay?
You still have full control over the configuration
of each component, but at least they come bundled
as one single interface in Beanstalk
and the idea is that Beanstalk also has a really cool way
of updating applications.
So the Beanstalk service is free on its own,
but you're going to pay for the underlying instances
that are going to be leveraged by Beanstalk
or your ASG or your ELB, those kinds of things.
So components of Beanstalk consist of an application,
which is a collection of Beanstalk components,
such as environments, versions and configurations.
A version of the application itself
is an iteration of your application code.
So you can have version one, version two,
version three, et cetera, et cetera.
Then an environment, it's just a collection
of your resources running the specific application version.
So you can only have one application version at a time
in an environment, where we can see
we can actually update an application version
within an environment from version one to version two.
We have tiers, so we can have two different tiers.
In Beanstalk, we have the web server environment tier
and the worker environment tier.
We'll see those very quickly.
And we can also create multiple environments in Beanstalk,
such as dev, test and prod
and whatever environment you have in mind really.
So the process is to create an application,
then we upload a version.
Then we are going to launch an environment
and then we're going to manage an environment lifecycle
and if we wanted to iterate on that,
we could update the version by uploading a new version
and then deploy that new version again in our environment
to update our application stack.
So Beanstalk supports many programming languages,
such as Go, Java SE, Java with Tomcat,
.NET Core on Linux, .NET on Windows Server,
Node.js, PHP, Python, Ruby,
Packer Builder, Single Docker Container,
Multi Docker Container, Pre-configured Docker.
So the idea is that on Beanstalk
you should be able to deploy pretty much anything.
Now to finish, what do I mean
by server tier and worker tier?
Well, the web tier is looking like this.
This is the traditional architecture that we know,
where we have a load balancer
and then it's sending traffic to an auto scaling group
that has multiple EC2 instances
that are going to be your web server.
This is the architecture number one with Beanstalk
and the architecture number two with Beanstalk
is going to be around a worker environment.
So this time there is no clients accessing directly
your EC2 instances.
We're going to use an SQS queue, which is a message queue
and the message will be sent into the SQS queue
and the EC2 instances are going to be workers,
because they're going to pull messages
from the SQS queue to process them.
And in this case, the worker environment
is going to scale based on the number of SQS messages.
So the more messages, the more EC2 instances.
And then the cool is that you can put the web environment
and the work environment together
by having the web environment push some messages
into the SQS queue of the worker environment.
Finally, there are two deployment modes
you need to know for Beanstalk.
The first one is a single instance,
which is great for development purposes.
In this case, you'll have one EC2 instance
which will have an Elastic IP,
potentially it can also launch an RDS database and so on,
but it's all based on one instance with an Elastic IP.
It's great for development purposes,
but then if you wanted to scale
a real Elastic Beanstalk mode,
then you would go for high available with a load balancer,
which is great for production environments,
in which case, you can have a load balancer distributing
the loads across multiple EC2 instances
that are managed for an auto scaling group
and multiple available zones.
And finally, you may have an RDS database
that's also multi AZ with a master and a standby.
All right, that's it.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 69. [DVA] Elastic Beanstalk - Deployment Modes
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869124
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the Beanstalk
deployment options whenever you're doing
an update to your application.
So you have several ones, and each of them
is going to be described with diagrams
in the next few slides, so don't worry about it.
But I just wanna give you an overview
of what they are before we dive into them.
So the first one is all at once,
where you deploy all in one go.
It's the fastest, but then your instances
are going to be down because they will be updating,
and so you'll have some downtime.
You have rolling, where you update
a few instances at a time, and then you move on
to the next set of instances, called a bucket,
once the first bucket is healthy.
You can also do rolling with additional batch.
This is just like rolling, but you spin up new instances
to update instances over time so that you'll still have
the old application available with the same capacity.
You have immutable.
This is when you have instances in Auto Scaling group.
You deploy new instances altogether.
You deploy the version to these instances,
and then you swipe out all the instances
when everything is healthy.
You have blue/green, where you create
a whole new environment altogether,
and then you switch over when ready.
And finally, we have traffic splitting.
This is for canary testing.
Canary testing is when you send a small percentage
of the application traffic to a brand new deployment.
So all these things, obviously,
you're going to learn in the next few slides,
so don't worry, this is just an overview,
and you'll learn about the diagrams for all of these.
So let's talk about all at once.
Here is our four EC2 instances,
and they all run the version one,
which is blue, of our application.
Then we are going to do an all at once deployment.
So we want deploy v2.
And what happens, that first Elastic Beanstalk
will just stop the applications on all our EC2 instances.
So then I put it as gray, as in they don't run anything.
And then we will be running the new V2,
because Elastic Beanstalk will deploy V2 to these instances.
So what do we notice?
Well, it's very quick.
It's the fastest deployment.
The application, though, has downtime,
because you can see in the middle they're all gray,
and so they can't serve any traffic.
I think it's great for when you have quick iterations
and development environments when you wanna deploy your code
fast and quickly, and you don't really care about downtime.
And finally with this setup, there's no additional cost.
Now let's talk about rolling.
The application will basically be running below capacity,
and we can set how much below we want to set,
like running the capacity.
So that's called the bucket size.
And so let's have a look.
We have four instances running v1,
and the bucket size will be two for the example.
So what happens is that the first two instances
will be stopped...
Not the instances, sorry, the application on the instances
will be stopped, and so they're gray.
But we still have the other two instances running v1.
So you can see we have maybe half capacity here.
Then these first two instances will be updated,
so they'll be running v2, and then we will roll on
to the next bucket, or to the next batch.
And so that's why it's called rolling.
As you can see now, the bottom two instances
will have their application v1 taken down to some gray,
and then updated to v2.
And so at the end, we have all the EC2 instances
that have been updated to run the v2 application code.
So as you can see now, the application,
at some point during the deployment,
is running both versions simultaneously.
And there is no additional cost, okay?
You still have the same number of EC2 instances
running in your infrastructure.
And so if you set a very small bucket size
and you have hundreds and hundreds of instances,
it may be a very long deployment, okay?
Right now, in this example,
we have a bucket size of two and four instances,
but we can have a bucket size of 2 and 100 instances.
It will just take a very long time to upgrade everything.
Now, there's an additional mode
called rolling with additional batches.
And so in this case, the application is not running
under capacity, just like before.
Before, at some point, we were only running
two instances out of four.
So that was below capacity.
In this mode, we run at capacity,
and we can also set the bucket size.
And basically our application will still be
running both versions simultaneously,
but at a small additional cost.
That additional batch, that we'll see in a second,
will be removed at the end of the deployment.
And again, the deployment is going to be long.
It's honestly a good way to deal with prod.
So let's have a look.
We have our four v1 EC2 instances,
and the first thing we're going to do
is deploy new EC2 instances,
and they will have the v2 version on it.
So now, from four instances, Elastic Beanstalk
automatically created six instances for us,
so an additional two.
and you can see that the additional two
are running, already, the newer version.
Now we take the first batch to the first bucket of two
and they get stopped, the application gets stopped,
and the application gets updated to v2, excellent.
Then the process repeats again, just like in rolling.
So the application running v1 gets stopped,
and then the application is updated to v2.
And so at the end, you can see,
we have six EC2 instances running v2.
And so at the end of it, the additional batch
gets terminated and taken away.
So why would you do this?
Well, now we can see that we are running always at capacity.
The lowest number of EC2 instances running the application
we have at any time is four.
So sometimes we are running at over capacity, obviously,
and this is why you have a small additional cost.
It's very small, but there is an additional cost.
And sometimes the exam asks you,
is there an additional cost to this kind of stuff?
Then we have immutable type of deployments.
And these deployments are also zero downtime,
but this time the new code is going to be deployed
to new instances.
So before, it was on previous instances,
now it's deployed on new instances.
And where do these instances come from?
Well, they come from a temporary ASG.
So there's a high cost, you double the capacity
because you get a full new ASG,
and it's the the longest kind of deployment.
As a bonus though, you get a very quick rollback
in case of failures, because to just mitigate failure,
you just have to terminate.
Not you, but Elastic Beanstalk
will just terminate the new ASG.
So it's a great choice for prod,
if you're willing to take a little bit more cost.
So here's the idea.
We have a current ASG with three applications v1
running on three instances.
And then we're going to have a new
temporary ASG being created.
At first, Beanstalk will launch one instance on it,
just to make sure that one works.
And if it works and it passes the health checks,
it's going to launch all the remaining ones.
So right now, three instances.
When it's happy, it's going to sort of merge
the ASG with a temporary ASG.
So it's going to move all the temporary ASG instances
to the current ASG.
So now, in the current ASG, we have six instances, okay?
And when all of this is done and the temporary ASG is empty,
then we have the current ASG
that will terminate all the v1 applications,
while the v2 applications are still there.
And then, finally, the temporary ASG will just be removed.
Finally, there's something you may hear in the exam
or in the white papers, it's called blue/green,
and it's not a direct feature of Elastic Beanstalk,
but I'll try to give you my best version of it.
It's basically a zero downtime,
and it helps with the release facility,
allows for more testing, et cetera, et cetera.
And so the idea is that you wanna deploy
a new stage environment.
So it's just another Elastic Beanstalk environment,
and you'll deploy your new v2 there.
So before, all the deployment strategies
were within the same environment,
here, we create a new environment.
And so the new environment stage, or green,
can be validated independently in our own time
and then roll back if issues.
And then we can use something like Route 53, for example,
to prevent the traffic from going into the two directions.
So we can set up weighted policies
and redirect a little bit of traffic
to the stage environment so we can test everything.
And then when we're happy using
the Elastic Beanstalk console,
you can swap URLs, when done, with a test environment.
So this is not a very direct feature,
and it's actually very manual to do.
It's not embedded into Elastic Beanstalk,
so some documentation will say there is blue/green,
some will say it's not there, but overall it's very manual.
So just one graph, I try to make it simple.
But in the blue environment, running into one
Elastic Beanstalk environment, we have all the v1,
and then we'll deploy a green environment
with all the v2, okay?
And they're both running at the same time, just very fine.
And then in Route 53 we're going to set up a weighted
type of policy to send 90% of the traffic to blue.
So just keep most of the traffic going
to the instances we know work,
and maybe only 10% of the traffic to the green environment,
just to test it out and make sure it's working
and the users aren't having any problems.
And so the web traffic basically gets split 90/10,
but it's whatever you want, as far as the weight goes.
And so when you're happy where you're testing,
when you measured everything you want
with your v2 environment and you think you got it,
then you basically shut down the blue environment
and swipe the URL to make the green be the main environment.
So that's it for blue/green, right?
And it's pretty complicated,
and I think pretty manual, Elastic Beanstalk,
but that's the way it is.
Another kind of deployment you can do with Elastic Beanstalk
is called traffic splitting.
And this will be used for canary testing.
So if you see canary testing on the exam,
think traffic splitting.
So what is canary testing?
Well, a new application version is going to be deployed
to a temporary Auto Scaling group with the same capacity.
So we have the main Auto Scaling group
and a temporary Auto Scaling group with the same capacity.
So three instances in the main one,
and three instances in the temp.
So it doubles the capacity.
And what's going to happen is that a small percentage
of the traffic is going to be sent to the temporary ASG
for a configurable amount of time.
So we have an ALB, and we're going to say,
"Okay, 90% of the traffic goes to my main ASG,"
"while 10% of the traffic goes to my temporary ASG."
And all of this is automated.
The deployment health of the new temporary ASG
is going to be monitored.
And in case there is a deployment failure,
or there is a metric that goes wrong,
this will trigger an automated rollback,
which will be very, very quick
because the main ASG is already here,
and all we have to do to roll back
is to stop sending 10% of the traffic to this temporary ASG.
So there is no application downtime.
And then once everything is stable and correct,
then the new instances are going to be migrated
from the temporary ASG to the main original ASG.
And then the old application version
is going to be terminated.
So I really like that, because all of this is automated,
and this could be a big improvement
on top of the blue/green technique that I just described
in the previous lecture.
So if you wanted to compare all of those,
there is this link on the Beanstalk documentation,
which shows you the difference

because it gives you the method name,
the impact of a failed deployment,
the deploy time, if it's zero down time,
if there's a DNS change, what is the rollback process,
and where the code is deployed to.
So if you understood this lecture,

# Caption: en_US (manual)

So a few extra concepts on Beanstalk.
So the first one is the difference
between a web server type of deployment
and a worker environment type of deployment.
So web server makes sense
when you are trying to serve webpages,
but say your application performs tasks
that are long to complete
and they may not fit into the web server thing,
so you may want to move them
into a dedicated worker environment,
and that's called decoupling.
We decouple your application into two tiers.
One tier is for serving webpages,
and the other tier is to do long tasks,
such as processing a video,
or generating a zip file, et cetera, et cetera.
You can also define periodic tasks in a cron.yaml file
that allows your worker environment
to perform these tasks once in a while.
So here is an example.
In the Web Tier,
we're going to have a load balancer
as well as an auto scaling group of EC2 instances.
And if there's a request, for example,
to process a video, that request is going to be offloaded
into an SQS Queue so that the queue has the request itself.
And then the worker tier that we have deployed
into Beanstalk is just an autoscaling group
that is continuously pulling that SQS Queue for work.
And whenever there is a video to process
or a zip file to generate, then we can do that
in the worker tier and not affect the speed of our web tier.
So this is the whole idea.
And both these tiers,
the web tier and the worker tier
can be managed from within Elastic Beanstalk.
The other thing is around Beanstalk notifications.
So Beanstalk does emit quite a few notifications
in EventBridge, so you can react to the following events.
You can react to environment operation status,
such as create, update, and terminate.
We can have other resources status,
such as whenever ASG, ELB and EC2 instances
are created and deleted.
You can have a managed update status,
such as whenever the Elastic Beanstalk
updates its own platform.
Has it started?
Has it failed? And so on.
And environment health status.
So this is the one I want to show you an architecture.
So for example, we can have a look
at whenever the environment status degrades
into either a warning or a severe status, which is bad.
In that case, we can use EventBridge
to trigger an SNS notification
and send emails to administrators,
or invoke a Lambda function that
will send a message into Slack
or whatever discussion channels
you have in your company.
All right, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 72. [DVA] Serverless Application Model (SAM) - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869144
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS SAM.
So SAM is this little squirrel,
but it's also the Serverless Application Model.
It's an actual framework to develop
and deploy serverless applications.
So that means that you write your code
and then you're going to use a configuration
in the YAML format, which is going
to be compliant with the SAM framework.
And automatically, SAM is going to generate
very complex CloudFormation files
from simple SAM YAML files.
It supports anything from CloudFormation.
So you can still use outputs, mappings, parameter,
resources, et cetera in your SAM YAML code.
Now, SAM behind the scene can also use CodeDeploy
to deploy Lambda functions,
and SAM can help you run Lambda, API Gateway,
and DynamoDB locally.
So SAM really is intended
to be focused on serverless applications
and allow you to debug them locally
and to deploy them very quickly using CloudFormation
into the AWS cloud.
So SAM is made of recipes,
and at the very top of your template,
you're going to add a transform header
to indicate it's a SAM template.
And this is a transform header
which is going to tell CloudFormation to transform it
into a CloudFormation template.
Then you write your code,
but instead of using the CloudFormation constructs,
you're going to use the SAM constructs,
such as a serverless function, which is a Lambda function,
a serverless API, which is going to be the API gateway,
and the serverless SimpleTable,
which is going to be DynamoDB.
But you have these constructs to make it simpler
and easier for you to write your serverless applications.
And then to package and deploy this application onto AWS,
you're going to use the sam deploy command.
And it used to be two commands.
It used to be sam package and then sam deploy.
But now you can just do sam deploy on its own,
and it is going to package it for you as well.
There's also a way to synchronize your changes into
AWS Lambda very quickly using SAM Accelerate,
and the command is sam sync and then minus minus watch.
I'll give you a bit more
information on this in this lecture.
So let's have a look into SAM deployment.
So you have your application code
as well as your SAM template in the YAML format,
and then you're going to build the application
locally using sam build.
It's going to transform into a CloudFormation template
and your application code,
and then you can deploy it using sam deploy.
So you'll zip and upload everything into an S3 bucket,
and then automatically execute
or ChangeSet against CloudFormation.
Then your CloudFormation stack can be made
of different serverless components such as Lambda,
API Gateway, and DynamoDB.
So let's talk about SAM Accelerate.
So SAM Accelerate is its set of features that is used
to reduce the latency while deploying resources to AWS.
So you want to deploy as fast as possible.
And the command is going to be sam sync
to declare your project,
declare it with a SAM template into AWS.
And it's actually going to bypass CloudFormation
if you just do code changes
without updating your infrastructure
by using the service API.
So it's going to be a very, very quick deployment.
So you have SAM template and your application code,
and your Lambda function already deployed
and you're going to run sam sync.
And automatically, as you change the application code,
automatically SAM is going to synchronize its code
with your Lambda function.
Therefore, if you wanted to test your Lambda function
in the cloud, it's going to be very easy and very quick.
So different options, you can just run sam sync
to synchronize the code and the infrastructure,
or sam sync and just the code option
to synchronize only the code and not the infrastructure.
So you're not going to use CloudFormation,
it's going to be like the updates will be done in seconds.
Then you can specify a specific resource to say, hey,
I only want to update my Lambda functions
and their dependencies,
or I want to update this specific Lambda function
using the resource ID.
Or you can use the watch option,
which is going to monitor for file changes.
So it's going to run in the background
and automatically synchronize anything
when changes are detected.
So if you include configuration, use sam sync,
or if it's just a code,
then it's going to be using sam sync
and then the code option.
So I hope that makes sense.
I hope this is a good overview of SAM.
We'll do some hands-on to practice as well
so it becomes clear for you how it works.
So I hope you like this lecture
and I will see you in the next lecture.

Now let's talk about
the AWS Cloud Development Kit, or CDK,
which allows you to define your cloud infrastructure
in a familiar programming language,
such as JavaScript or TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.
So you may be saying,
"Hey, it looks like this is overlapping with CloudFormation,
because CloudFormation we can define
the cloud infrastructure using YAML.
But now we can do it using a programming language.
So what is this?"
Well, this is something that supersedes CloudFormation,
as we'll see in a second.
So let's say we want
to define our infrastructure using TypeScript,
and so we have this code right here
in which we are defining three different things.
We are defining constructs,
and so there are high level components
that we can use thanks to the CDK.
So the first construct we're using is a VPC.
So we create a new VPC, we give it a name,
and we give it three AZs.
And this creates a VPC for us
which is going to contain some pre-made configuration.
Then we define an ECS cluster.
And the ECS cluster is named MyCluster
and has a link to the VPC we just defined.
And then we define
an application load-balanced Fargate service,
so this is a Fargate service with an ALB
which is linked to the cluster we just defined.
We define how much CPU,
how many tasks we want, so six,
the task image options, the memory limits,
and that we want a public ALB.
So all of this is defined using a programming language,
which means that if we don't have functioning code
if the code doesn't compile,
then it's going to give us an error,
and that means that our template cannot be generated.
But if the code can be compiled
because it is sound and typesafe,
then it is going to be compiled
into a CloudFormation template.
It could be either JSON and YAML.
And so therefore, we are using the CDK
to define CloudFormation templates in the backend.
But this is allowing us to be a lot more flexible about it
and use a programming language.
So that also means that we can deploy infrastructure
and application runtime code together.
So this is great for Lambda functions,
great for Docker containers in ECS or EKS.
So this is a revolution
because CloudFormation template is YAML,
it's not typesafe, you can make errors,
and you only know at the very end if it worked or not.
But with the CDK, you can define those
using constructs and a programming language.
So if you want a diagram,
then we have our application constructs.
It could be Lambda functions, DynamoDB, Amazon S3,
ECS, some step functions, and so on.
And we can use programming languages,
such as Python, TypeScript, Java, .NET.
We write our CDK file, I guess,
and then we synthesize this using the CDK CLI
into a CloudFormation template
that we will apply into CloudFormation
to define our infrastructure.
So it is a step above CloudFormation
and makes it way easier to work with CloudFormation.
So you may ask me,
what is the difference between CDK and SAM?
Well, SAM is going to be serverless focused,
and we are going to write our templates declaratively

and this is great for quickly getting started with Lambda.
It also leverages CloudFormation in the backend, okay?
But the focus of SAM is Lambda function
and serverless applications.
For the CDK, well, it is a super set of CloudFormation,

for example, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET

# 76. [DVA] Step Functions - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869434
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's discuss AWS step functions.
So step functions allow you
to model a workflow as state machines
and you have one state machine per workflow.
So this could be used if you want
to have an order fulfillment or data processing,
a web application or any workflow you want.
The idea is that you will define
what happens and what happens next,
and then what happens based on some condition
and so on to define a workflow.
So as you can see on the right hand side,
there's a visual workflow.
We start and we have an example,
is it yes or no?
If it's no, then you go to the end.
If it's yes, then you wait three seconds.
Then you say, "Hello" and "World,"
you compile the result into "Hello World"
and you go into end.
So we'll be going through hands-on to make it specific
but the idea is that you define a workflow in JSON
and this JSON allows you to get
a visualization of the workflow
and then it gets executed visually,
and then we can see the history of the execution itself.
So the idea is that every little step
in the workflow is going to be, for example,
a Lambda function or inserting data into DynamoDB
or a specific ECS task,
and the step function is going to be
the thing that orchestrates this workflow for you.
To start a workflow, you can use an SDK API call,
you can use API gateway, you can use CloudWatch Events
or Amazon EventBridge, they're the same thing,
or you can launch, obviously,
a step function manually from the console,
as we will be doing it in the hands-on.
So step functions have a bunch of boxes
as you see on the right hand side
and these boxes are called tasks.
And so the task state is used to do some work
in your state machine.
So the task state could be invoking a Lambda function
or it could be invoking a Batch job
or running an ECS task and wait for it to complete
or to insert an item directly
from step functions into the DynamoDB
or to publish a message into SNS or SQS
or even to launch another step function workflow.
All these things can be defined in a task state,
or a task could also be running one activity
and that activity could be an EC2 machine
or an Amazon ECS task or on-premises server
that is going to be pulling for some work
from step functions to do the work
and then send back the results to the step function.
The idea is that here, we are more free in terms of that,
the app server is not invoked by the step function,
the step function at the app server
is actually pulling for step functions
to find activities and work to do.
Which is more similar to how
a service called SWF worked in AWS.
So I wanna make this super concrete.
So let's say we want to define a task state
to invoke a Lambda function.
So we're going to define a JSON
and as you can see, the name is "Invoke Lambda function,"
the type is task and the resource is Lambda function invoke.
Then the parameters is the function name,
so we specify the function name,
and we pass it on input payload to our Lambda function.
Then we say next, to go to the next state, and the time out,
to see if our Lambda function is timing out.
So what can be states in step functions?
We could have this Choice State,
to test for a condition to send it to a branch
or the default branch.
It could be a Fail or Succeed State,
to stop executing the step function workflow
with a success or a failure.
It could be a Pass State,
simply to pass the input to the output
or to inject some fixed data without performing some work.
It could be a Wait State, to provide a delay
for a certain amount of time
or until a specified date and time.
It could be a Map State, to dynamically iterate steps,
or a Parallel State to begin parallel branches of execution.
What you need to remember from the exam perspective
is most likely going to be the parallel states.
So, and the task state
that I showed you from before, obviously.
So I wanna show you what happens visually.
So we have a execution workflow and this is a workflow.
So we submit a job.
We wait for X seconds.
We get the job status.
Is the job complete?
Yes or no, if not wait again, and so there's a loop.
And when the job is complete,
either you get the final job status
because you completed successfully
or if the job failed,
then you maybe go and deal with that failure,
and all of this go to the end.
So as the execution is started,
we're going to start, submit a job.
We're gonna wait for X seconds
and the blue is whatever is in progress.
Then it goes into several loops
and then the job status is done,
and then we get the final job status and we go to the end,
and this gives us a visual aspect of our step functions.
So the step function is really is here
to orchestrate whatever work you need to do,
to define how your state machine is going to look like.
What your workflow is going to look like,
and I know that right now, this may be,
what the hell is this talking about?
This is very confusing.
I can do all of that in just one Lambda function to program,
but I will show you in the next lecture,
a hands-on on step functions.
It should make a lot more sense,
and then I will show you the whole power of state functions
in the further lecture by talking about error handling.
So I will see you in the next lecture for the hands-on.

# 79. [DVA] AppConfig - Overview
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869464
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS AppConfig.
So the idea is that when you configure your applications,
it is very common for you to actually ship the configuration
alongside your app,
and sometimes you can modularize the configuration
by using environmental variables.
But what if instead you want it to be
having the configuration outside of your app?
For this, you could use AppConfig,
which allows you to configure, validate
and deploy dynamic configurations into your applications.
So you can change this configuration
and your application will change independently
of you deploying any new code to your application.
So you don't need to restart your application,
everything works dynamically.
So the beautiful thing about it is that, for example,
you could use feature flags.
What is a feature flag?
Well say your application comes with a new feature
but for now you want to disable it,
so you just deploy your application,
and in AppConfig you say the feature is off or false.
And then when your application's been deployed
and you're ready to test it out,
you can just change the feature flag in your AppConfig.
Your application will pick it up
and automatically this new feature will be enabled.
On top of it, you can pretty much dynamically change
any kind of configuration,
so you can fine tune your application performance and so on.
You can, even for example,
if you had IP block list or allow list,
you can modify them in real time in AppConfig again,
without changing your application code.
So it's very useful for apps that you run
on EC2 instances, Lambda, ECS, EKS, and so on.
On top of it, if you have a configuration change
for example, let's go back to our feature flag,
you don't want to release the feature
to all of your instances at once.
You may want to gradually deploy this change
to see if you have any issues, and if so, get a rollback.
So that's possible with AppConfig as well.
So AppConfig has a few config sources.
It could be the parameter store,
it could be the SSM documents,
it could be your SRO buckets or somewhere else.
And then your EC2 instances are,
and, of course, the application running on them
are going to regularly pull for configuration changes
and then pull them.
And for example, when we switch change the configuration,
automatically we're going to be monitoring
with CloudWatch if there is anything going wrong.
If so, let's trigger an alarm,
and this alarm will trigger a rollback
of your configuration.
On top of it to make sure that you're not actually
distributing a configuration that is wrong.
You can validate it either using a JSON Schema,
which is going to check whether or not the config adheres
to some specific types and so on, or a Lambda function.
This is when you want to have code
and this code is going to check the parameters
in a more complex way.
And that's it, that's AppConfig.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

Now let's talk about SSM Automations.

creating an AMI or doing an EBS snapshot.

They're from outside your EC2 Instances,

# 85. [SAA/DVA/SOA] SSM Parameter Store
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869520
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about
the SSM Parameter Store.
It's a secure storage for your configuration
and your secrets.
And optionally,
you can choose to encrypt these configurations
and therefore make it secrets
by using the KMS service.
SSM Parameter Store is serverless,
it's scalable, it's durable,
and the SDK is very easy to use.
On top of it, if you update your parameters
then you have version tracking of them.
The security is provided through IAM
and you get notifications with Amazon EventBridge,
in certain amount of cases.
You have full integration with CloudFormation.
That means that CloudFormation can leverage the parameters
from parameter store as input parameters for your stacks.
So let's take an example.
We have an application
and then we have the SSM parameter store.
So we can store plain text configuration in this way.
Then the IAM permissions of your applications
are going to be checked.
For example, your EC2 instance role
or you can have encrypted configuration.
In that case
the SSM parameter store is going to encrypt it with KMS.
And so the KMS service is going to be used
for encryption and decryption.
And of course, you need to make sure
that your applications do have access
to the underlying KMS key to perform that encryption
and that decryption.
So you can store parameters in the parameter store
with a hierarchy.
So for example, you can define my department
as a path and underneath the My-app and then the Dev
and then we have the Dev DB-URL
and then the DB-password within that folder.
So that means that your parameters goes all the way down
into the hierarchy.
We can go one level up and store a parameter
for the Prod DB-URL, as well as a Prod DB password
and go up to another app or another department.
That really allows you to organize your parameters
the way you want in a structured fashion.
And then this is going to simplify your IAM policies to
allow applications to have access to an entire department,
or to an entire app,
or just to an app department environment specific path.
You also have the opportunity

# 87. [SOA] SSM Patch Manager and Maintenance Windows
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869530
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's see an overview
of the SSM Patch Manager.
So we use the Patch Manager to automate the process
of patching our managed instances.
This includes OS updates, applications updates
and security updates.
Of course, it supports both EC2 instances
and on-premises server
and Linux, MacOS and Windows.
You're going to patch on demand
so you can run the patch manager as you want
or on the schedule if you want to use a maintenance window.
What's going to happen
is that the patch manager will scan the instances
and will generate a patch compliance report
which is a list of all the machine patches.
And then this report can be sent to S3
and then we can act upon this report.
So patch manager has two components
we need to know about,
which is the number one is the patch baseline
and the number two is patch groups.
So patch baseline defines which patches should
and shouldn't be installed on your EC2 instances
and the ability to create custom patch baseline
is up to you if you want to specify approved
or rejected patches on your instance.
The patches can also be auto approved
within days of their release
in case someone is not there to approve them.
By default, the patch baseline is to install
only critical patches
and patches related to security
onto your SSM managed instances.
Now for patch group,
this is to associate a set of instances
with a specific patch baseline.
So if you define custom patch baselines,
then you can create patch groups
to associate them together.
And for example,
you can have a patch group for dev,
test and prod.
Now, instances when using patch groups
should be defined with a tech key patch group
and an instance at any time,
therefore can only be part of one patch group.
And the patch group can only be registered
with one patch baseline.
So we have two kind of patch baselines
in Patch Manager.
We have the predefined patch baselines
and they're managed by AWS
and they're defined for operating systems
that are different
and you cannot modify them.
Now to run one of these predefined patch baseline,
you can use the SSM document
named AWS Run Patch Baseline,
to apply both operating system
and application patches for Linux,
MacOS and Windows server.
You can also define your custom patch baseline.
So you define your own patch baseline
and you choose which patches are auto-approved,
which are allowed,
which are rejected,
and the operating system.
And you can also specify custom
or alternative patch repository.
So you can really, for example,
have an internal corporate patch repository for this.
Now I want to make this clear with a diagram.
So we have three types of easy two instances
all running the SSM agents.
The number ones are going to be tagged
with OS Windows patch group dev,
number two is OS Windows,
number three is OS Windows Patch Group prod.
And in Patch Manager
we're going to define patch baselines.
So the first patch baseline
is attached to the default patch group
which is when a patch group is not defined by default.
And this is default yes.
So any instance that doesn't have
a specific patch group
is going to get the first patch baseline ID.
And the second one
is running the patch group dev,
which is not a default patch baseline.
And we have a specific patch baseline ID.
So thanks to this tagging
the first instance which is under patch group dev
is going to have the PB98, whatever, patch baseline ID.
And the other two are going to have the PB0123
patch baseline ID
because they are not tagged with a patch group dev.
So here we're going to run a command
and this command is going to be running a document
called AWS Run Patch Baseline.
And this can be initiated from the console,
the SDK or the maintenance window.
And then the run command itself
will be applied to all these EC2 instances,
from within obviously,
to install the patches.
Now, the SSM agent on these instances
will query to the patch manager service
to get an idea of which patches to include
and to run thanks to the patch baseline.
So this may seem complicated
but hopefully this is something you understand.
And then obviously you can have rate control,
just like anything in SSM,
using a maintenance window.
So talking about maintenance windows,
this is when you want to define a schedule
for when to perform actions on your instances.
For example, OS patching,
updating drivers and installing software.
For example, this could be done
at night between 3:00 and 5:00 AM.
And a maintenance window contains a schedule,
a duration and a set of registered instances,
as well as a set of tasks
that can be run during that maintenance window.
So hopefully that makes sense.
From a exam perspective,
what you need to know is that
patch manager is used to patch your instances
but that comes, I guess, naturally.
And these patches can be run
within a specific maintenance window
with a specific rate control if you need to.
Okay, that's it.
I will see you in the next lecture.

# 89. [SOA] SSM Session Manager
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869538
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about SSM session manager,
which is a way for you to start a secure shell environment
on your EC2 instances and on-premises servers,
but you access it through the console,
the CLI or the session manager SDK,
and the real power of session manager is that you do not
need to get direct SSH access into your instances. Okay.
Neither using a bastion host or SSH key.
So this is different from the SSH traditional SSH,
or even the EC2 instance connect
that is in the backend using SSH. Okay.
So how does that work?
Where are EC2 instance is running the SSM agents
and is having the right permissions to be registered
with this SSM service.
And so our user is going to connect to the session manager
service with a correct IAM permission, of course.
And then the session manager will be able to execute
commands on our EC2 instance.
So it's using the same mechanism if you want,
as the run commands, the service feature. Okay.
But this time,
the session manager is used to just have a common shell
against our EC2 instance.
The cool thing is that it supports Linux, macOS and windows.
Okay. And all the connections, your instances,
and the executed commands are going to be logged.
So you can have them being sent to Amazon S3 or
CloudWatch Logs.
And the idea is that you have more control
and more security.
When someone does an SSH command into an EC2 instance,
you do not have the history of all the commands
that will run, and so less security, less compliance.
And CloudTrail can also be used to intercept
the StartSession events,
which is when session and measure is being used to start a
session onto your EC2 instance. For example, again,
for some automation, compliance and alerting.
So session manager requires IAM permissions,
and this is allowing you to control which users or groups
can access session manager and which instances,
and you can use tags to restrict access
to only specific EC2 instances.
So in this example,
this is an IAM policy that allows you
to connect to any instance,
as long as the resource type of environment is named dev.
So you also need access to SSM and write to S3 and
write to CloudWatch to allow you to send the Log there.
And optionally,
you can restrict even restrict commands that the user
can run in a session.
if you wanted to go deep down the security route.
So just for you to understand, using SSH,
well we have to open up our security group and our user with
specific IP address as a session to our instance and do
whatever he wants there, but using session manager,
we don't need any inbound rules. Okay.
You just need the instance with the SSM agents
and the right IAM role,
and then a user with a correct IAM permission
can use session manager to run commands against
our EC2 instance.
All the data of the session is going to be logged
or could be logged into Amazon S3 or CloudWatch logs.
So it's quite a cool service. I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture to do some hands-on.

# 92. SSM Default Host Management Configuration (DHMC)
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869558
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk
about the Default Host Management Configuration feature
for Systems Manager or DHMC.
The idea is that we know
that to enable access to Systems Manager,
our EC2 instances must have an IAM role with SSM access.
But it turns out that you can also do without.
So if you configure DHMC, then your EC2 instances
can be automatically managed instances without the use
of an EC2 instance profile.
So how does this work?
Well, we have an instance identity role,
which is a type of IAM role that has no permissions.
And this is for every EC2 instance that you create
but you don't control it.
And the role of this identity role
is to just identify the EC2 instance
to some AWS services, such as Systems Manager.
So this instance identity role is different
from your EC2 instance profile, okay?
It's just something that is on every EC2 instance
but you don't have control over it.
But what's going to happen is that thanks
to this instance identity role,
the EC2 instance identifies with Systems Manager,
which in return is going to pass an IAM role
to the EC2 instance, which will allow the EC2 instance
to be managed by Systems Manager.
And again, all of this is done outside
of the EC2 instance profile.
So for this to work,
you need to have the metadata version two enabled
and the SSM agent enabled that is updated enough
so it doesn't support IMDSv1.
Once the instance is managed by Systems Manager,
it will automatically enable all the features
of Systems Manager,
such as Session Manager, Patch Manager, and Inventory.
And on top of it,
the SSM agent will be automatically kept up to date.
This must be enabled on a per region basis.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 96. SSM with IoT Greengrass
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869572
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we've seen
how to activate EC2 instances,
how we can activate on-premises servers.
But now, we can also activate IoT Greengrass Core devices.
So these core devices are IoT things,
and they can be managed using Systems Manager.
For this, very simply, we must first install these SSM Agent
onto the Greengrass Core devices
and they will register themselves
as a managed node in SSM with the MI prefix.
Now, to install the SSM Agent, we can either do it manually,
or we can deploy it as a Greengrass component,
which is a pre-built software module
that you directly deploy on your IoT devices.
So once the SSM Agent is installed
on your Greengrass Core device,
you must define a Token Exchange Role.
Now, Token Exchange Role is a fancy name
for an IAM role for your IoT core device.
So you attach a token exchange role
and you make sure you add the permissions to communicate
with Systems Manager, the same way you would do it
for an EC2 instance, for example.
This supports all SSM capabilities
such as Patch Manager, Session Manager,
Run Command, and so on.
And then, thanks to the activation
of your IoT devices with Systems Manager,
you can easily update and maintain the operating system
and the software updates across all your devices.
So to summarize, your Greengrass Core device
is an IoT thing.
You're going to install the SSM Agent,
maybe through a component
and then you're going to define a token exchange role
which is an IAM role for your core device.
Then with the proper permissions,
it's going to get registered with Systems Manager
who must have also a service role
to manage your core devices, and you're good to go.
Okay, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 97. SSM Automations - Use Cases
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869578
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about a few use cases
for automations in Systems Manager.
The first one is to reduce cost by automatically starting
and stopping EC2 instances in RDS database instances.
So say you have an environment
that is just used for quality assurance
then we can use EventBridge to automatically schedule
an SSM automation that will start an EC2 instance
and start an RDS instance.
And SSM automation has the power to do these things.
At 5:00 p.m. we can also run an event bridge schedule
so that we stop the EC2 instance
and we stop the RDS instance
that are clear from an SSM automation.
If you want it not to start and stop,
but to just resize by downsizing at night
and increasing the size during the day
then you would run a AWS resize instance
type of SSM automation from the morning and at night.
And as you can see in the morning, we have a 2X large
and at night we have an M5 large.
So we still allow people to work,
but the instance is less powerful.
We can also build a golden AMI
using systems manager automations.
Obviously EC2 image builder is a better use case,
but it's still possible.
So EventBridge can invoke an SSM automation every week
to run the automation named AWS create creates image
which will go ahead and create an AMI.
And when an AMI is available,
we can invoke a Lambda function pass in the AMI ID
and then store this AMI ID in the parameter store.
So this is very similar to EC2 image builder,
but here we are using SSM automations.
Also, we know that automations are tightly integrated
with AWS Config.
So say you have a config rule to detect
whether the bucket versioning is enabled or not,
if the bucket versioning is disabled
it's going to be flagged at non-compliance.
And if we have a config remediation automatically set up
to run an automation,
then an SSM automation named configure S3 bucket versioning
can re-enable the versioning of your S3 buckets.
So that's it.
Hopefully it gives you a few good ideas
into how SSM automations are used.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 99. SSM OpsCenter
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869586
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about OpsCenter
in Systems Manager.
So OpsCenter allows you to view,
investigate and remediate issues in one place.
So all the issues will be centralized into systems manager.
So you can have your security issues
from Security Hub,
your performance issues, for example,
when your dynamicDB table is being throttled
or your failures,
for example, when a instance has failed
to be launched from an auto-scaling group.
So the goal of your having Opscenter is
to reduce the meantime to resolve issues.
So you have OpsItems in the OpsCenter
and they represent operational issues
or interruption that need investigation and remediation.
So it could be an event, a resource, a conflict change
a CloudTrail logs, EventBridge and so on.
And then out of this there are recommendations
as to which Runbooks
and which automations can help you resolve the issue.
So this supports both your EC2 instances
and your on-premises manage notes.
So all this data from, for example,
CloudWatch and Application Insights, EventBridge, Config
Security Hub, DevOps Guru,
and the SSM Incident Manager
is going to be aggregated into OpsCenter.
We can get notifications and build automations.
So here is an example where we are scanning
for EBS volumes that are orphan,
so not used for a long time,
and then we're going to flag them
in OpsCenter as an OpsItem and then delete them.
So if Rich, for example,
can everyday invoke a Lambda function,
which is going to scan the EC2 service
and look for EBS volumes that are over, for example,
45 days old.
And then if they are over 45 days old,
then we create OpsItems directly in OpsCenters.
And then from OpsCenter we can have recommendations
such as running a document to either create a snapshot
or delete the snapshots or delete a volume
and these will be run as SSM automations.
Okay, so that's it,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 100. SSM Session Manager with VPC Endpoints
# Section: Domain 2: Configuration Management & IaC
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37869602
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So here is a quick lecture
to show you how you can access your EC2 instances
that are in private subnets
within the systems manager service.
So for example, say you wanted to connect
to your EC2 instances using Session Manager,
but they don't have internet access.
So the way to do it is to use VPC endpoints.
So the first VPC endpoint that's required
is for the SSM service itself
and we allow inbound 443 port from the security group.
The second interface endpoint that is necessary
is for the SSM session manager service.
So this is a different one
and this will allow the EC2 instance
to privately connect to the session manager service.
Again, we allow inbound 443,
and then on our EC2 instance
we must at least allow outbound 443 to these services.
In case we're using KMS encryption,
we must also create a VPC interface endpoint for KMS.
And if we're using CloudWatch logs
to put all the logs into CloudWatch
from the session on Session manager,
we must also create a VPC endpoint for that service.
Finally, if the logs are sent into Amazon S3,
then we can use a VPC Gateway endpoint for Amazon S3.
And if you're using a VPC endpoint gateway
you must update your route tables
in your VPC to make this work.
So, okay, as bottom line,
what I want you to remember is that
if you wanted to privately use the SSM service,
you must create the appropriate VPC endpoints
to allow your EC2 instance
to access your service privately.
Okay, that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 101. [DVA] Lambda - Versions and Aliases
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37903772
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the concepts
of Lambda Version and Aliases.
So far when we've been working on the Lambda functions,
we used this &amp;LATEST version.
So this version was immutable
because we were able to edit our code and so on.
But one thing we haven't done is
that when we're happy with our code states,
we can publish the Lambda function
and create a new version.
So as soon as we hit publish,
it will become V1
and V1 is immutable.
What does immutable mean?
That means that you cannot change the code
or the environment variables,
or anything else afterwards.
So it is fixed as a version.
And so as you keep on publishing,
the versions will have an increasing version numbers.
So you go from V1 to V2,
et cetera.
Each version is independence
and will get its own ARN,
so Amazon Resource Name.
And so if we do know whatever it is now,
it is your code and your configuration.
Nothing can be changed.
It's immutable.
So each Lambda function version,
can be accessed as well as your latest.
So this is great to iterate
and mark your advance
until it releases you Lambda function.
But what if he wants to give
your end user a standard endpoint?
So for this, we can use Lambda Aliases.
Aliases are going to be pointers,
that points to your Lambda function versions.
And we can define a DEV test
and PROD Aliases.
For example and have them point
to different Lambda versions.
Aliases this time are mutable
and this is why we want to use them.
And so we have the latest,
which is a version in Alias,
This is fine.
Then with V1 and V2.
And so we're going to create a DEV Alias.
That's going to be mutable
pointing to the latest version of Lambda function.
This way we can edit code
and quickly see how it's going on.
In our users will interact with a DEV Alias
which will in turn call
the latest version of our function.
But we can create a TEST Alias
to test the V2 version of our function.
Again, that's mutable.
And we can create a PROD Alias
two test and not two test
actually two points to the V1 function
that we know is stable and working.
So why do we do Aliases
Well they enable canary deployments
Because we can assign weights
to the Lambda function versions we point to.
So for PROD for example,
say we want to switch
from the V1 function
all the way to the V2 function.
Instead of switching the pointer,
we can say 95% of the traffic
is going to go to V1.
And only 5% of the traffic is going to go to V2.
And the purpose of this
is that now we're testing V2 in PROD,
making sure it works
before we switch the full power
onto V2 and 100% of the traffic there.
So Aliases, enable stable configuration
for our triggers or user destinations.
They can be invoked stably,
but they can point in the backend
to whatever Lambda version we want.
So these Aliases will get their own ARNs.
And the great thing to note,
Aliases cannot reference
other Aliases.
They can only reference version
and it's something the exam may
try to trick you on.
Okay.
So let's go into the hands-on to see how they work.

create, test
