and Multi AZ and understand exactly the use cases for those.
So this lecture is really dedicated
to understanding Read Replicas and Multi AZ.
So let's get started with the Read Replicas.
Read Replicas as the name indicates
help you to scale your reads.
So let's have an example.
Here, we have our application
and we have an RDS database instance
and our application performs reads and writes
to our database instance,
but say we want to scale the reads
because that's, main database instance can not scale enough.
It receives too many requests.
Well, we can create up to 15 Read Replicas
and they can be within the same availability zone,
cross availability zone, or cross region.
So three different options
and they're very important to remember.
So say we have another RDS instance Read Replica
and another one and what will happen
is that they will be an asynchronous replication
between the main RDS database instance
and the two Read Replicas.
Asynchronous, that means that the reads
are eventually consistent.
What that means is that,
for example, if your application reads from the Read Replica
before they had the chance to replicate the data
then you may get all data.
And this is why it's called
eventually consistent asynchronous replication.
And these replicas, they can be awesome
for reading for scaling reads
but they can also be promoted to their own database.
So you can take one of these replicas
and say, okay I want it to be its own database now
and take rights.
And so you promote it to its own database.
It's completely out of the replication mechanism after that
but it's lives and has its own life cycle afterwards.
So in case you wanna use Read Replicas,
the main application in orange in the top of the screen
must update the connection string
to leverage the list of all the Read Replicas
you have in your RDS cluster.
Okay, very nice.
So let's talk about a classic use case
for you to Read Replica.
So in this example, we have a production database
and it is taking on normal load.
So here we go.
Our production database is having read and writes
to our main RDS database instance.
And the new team comes in and say,
we want to run some reporting
and some analytics on top of your data.
And so if you plug in that reporting application
onto the main RDS database instance
then it's going to overload it
and possibly slow down the production application
and you don't want that.
So instead what you do as a solutions architect
is you create a Read Replica to run the new workload there.
So you create a Read Replica.
There is some asynchronous, a replication
that happens between your main RDS DB database instance
and your Read Replica
and then your reporting application can just do reads
from your Read Replica and run the analytics there.
The production application is completely unaffected
in this case and that's perfect.
So remember, if you have a Read Replica
you need to ensure
that it is only for SELECT type of statements
and SELECT is a SQL keyword.
SELECT means read.
And so you can not use keywords
such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE,
which change database itself.
Okay, Read Replicas is only for reads.
So, let's talk about the networking cost
associated with RDS Read Replica.
So in AWS, you should know that's normally there is a cost
when the data goes from one availability zone to another
but there are exceptions
and these exceptions are usually for managed services.
So for RDS Read Replica, this is a managed service.
If your Read Replica is within the same region, okay?
Different AZ, but same region, you're not paying that fee.
So what this means that if you have a RDS DB instance
in us-east-1a and then a Read Replica in us-east-1b,
and there is asynchronous replication
because this is a Read Replica,
even though the traffic goes from one AZ to a different AZ
that replication traffic is going to be free
because RDS is a managed service
and they give you that traffic for free.
But if you are using a cross region replica,
so you are in one region, us-east-1
and you go to another region, eu-west-1, for example
then your RDS DB instance and your Read Replica
will have replication that will go across regions
and this will incur a replication fee for your network.
Finally, let's talk about RDS Multi AZ
and Multi AZ is mainly used for Disaster Recovery.
So we have our application
and it performs the reads and writes
to our Master database instance
which is in availability zone A
and what we thinks you have is a synchronous replication
to a standby instance in AZ B,
and they will replicate every single change
in the Master synchronously.
So that means that when your application writes
to the Master, that change needs to also be replicated
to the standby to be accepted.
And so what we get out of it is one DNS name.
So your application talks to one DNS name
and in case there is a problem with the Master,
there will be an automatic failover to the standby database.
Thanks to that one DNS name.
So thanks to this, we increase the availability.
This is why it's called Multi AZ and they will be failover
in case we lose an entire AZ or we lose the network
or there is an instance or storage failure
for the Master database.
In which case, obviously the standby database
will become the new Master.
He don't need to do any manual intervention in your apps
as long as it tries to keep on connecting
to your database automatically at some point,
it will fail over to the standby
that will be promoted as the Master, and you'll be good
and it's not used for scaling.
So as you can see here,
the standby database is just for standby.
No one can read to it.
No one can write to it, it's just here as a failover
in case anything goes on with your Master database.
So, quick question is, is there a possibility
to have the Read Replicas being set up as Multi AZ
for Disaster Recovery?
And the answer is yes, you can set up your Read Replica
as a Multi AZ if you want it to.

So that's it for the difference between Read Replicates
and Multi AZ, but you need to absolutely understand this

because a lot of questions will go and be about it.
So a question that can come up in the exam
is around how do we make an RDS database

So what you should know
is that it is a zero downtime operation.
That means you do not need to stop the database
to go from Single AZ to Multi AZ.
The only thing you need to do
is to click on modify for the database
and enable Multi AZ.
That means that your RDS database instance
is going to go to have a Master,
to have a standby DB with synchronous replication
without you doing anything except modifying that setting
and the database will not stop.
Now, this is what the exam will ask you
but I wanna show you what will happen behind the scenes
for it to work.
So, the following will happen internally.
There will be a snapshot taken by RDS automatically
of your main database
and that this snapshot will be restored
into a new standby database, okay?
And then once the standby database is restored,
there will be synchronization established
between the two database
and so therefore the standby database
will catch up to the main RDS database and there you go,

using the writer endpoint.

As for the reader endpoint, again it is updated based

and extended to ta1ke into account these two new replicas.

what we need to remember is that the clients must connect
to the writer endpoint to find the writer replica,
and must connect to the reader endpoint
to find the reader replicas.
Aurora also has the concept of global databases.
So you have two ways of doing it.

and very simple to put in place,
or you just use the feature named Aurora Global Database.
That's recommended because one of the region will be defined
as the primary region,
which will take all the read and the write loads.

and the replication lag will be less than one second.

which is very helpful for decreasing latency.
On top of it, in case of a disaster, you have an RTO
of less than one minute by promoting another region,
and on top of it, typical cross-region replication will take
less than one second.
So how does that work?
Well, we have a primary region
where the applications can do read and writes,
and then we'll have a secondary regions
where the replication will happen, and the applications

# 139. [SAA/DVA/SOA] ElastiCache - Overview
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904172
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Let's talk about Amazon ElastiCache.
So the same way you get RDS
to have managed relational databases,
ElastiCache is going to help you get managed Redis
or Memcached, which are cache technologies.
So what are caches?
Well, they are in-memory databases
with really high performance and low latency.
And what the cache will help you with is to help
reduce the load off of databases
for read-intensive workloads.
The idea is that the common queries are going to be cached,
and therefore, your database will not be queried every time.
Just your cache can be used
to retrieve the results of these queries.
What this also helps you do is
make your application stateless
by putting the state of your application
into Amazon ElastiCache.
And because we have the same benefits for RDS,
AWS will take the same maintenance of the operating system,
the patching, the optimization,
the setup, configuration, monitoring,
failure recovery, and backups.
Now, if you use Amazon ElastiCache,
just so you know that it will require you
to do some heavy application code changes
for your application.
This is not something you just enable,
and off you go, you have a cache.
You need to change your application to query the cache
before or after querying the database
and we'll see the strategies in a minute.
So now let's talk about the architecture
for using ElastiCache.
And there can be many, but I'm just giving you an example.
So, let's say we have Amazon ElastiCache and RDS database
and your application.
The application will query ElastiCache
to see if the query are already being made.
And if this has already been made
and it is stored in ElastiCache,
then it's called a cache hit,
and then it just gets the answer
straight from Amazon ElastiCache
and we're saving a trip to the database to do the query.
Now, in case of a cache miss,
then we need to fetch the data from the database.
We're going to read it from the database.
And then for other application or other instances
where the same query will be made,
we can write the data back into the cache
so that such as the same query next time will result
in a cache hit.
The idea is that it will help to relieve load
from your RDS database.
And because you're storing data in the cache,
there must be a cache invalidation strategy to make sure
that only the most current data is used in there.
And this is the whole difficulty
around using caching technologies.
Another architecture is around storing the user session
to make your application stateless.
So the idea is that your user will do login
into any kind of your applications,
and then the application will write the session data
into Amazon ElastiCache.
Now, if your user is redirected
to another instance of your application,
then your application can retrieve the session case,
the session directly from the Amazon ElastiCache,
and therefore your user is still logged in
and it doesn't need to log in one more time.
And so the idea is that
now you made your application stateless
by writing the session data of your user
into Amazon ElastiCache.
So if we compare Redis and Memcached,
so for Redis we have multi-availability zone
with auto-failover as a feature,
and you can create read replicas to scale the reads
and have high availability.
You also get data durability using AOF persistence,
and you have a backup and restore features
on the open source version of Redis.
It also supports sets and sorted sets,
which are a very nice way to create leaderboards
and provide you with some very nice features in a cache.
So the way I like to think of Redis is
a Redis node being replicated into another one
to give you an idea of how it works.
Of course, Redis is evolving fast
and this may not be general, but this is a simplification.
And for memcached, the idea is that
you have a multiple nodes set up
and they're partitioning your data.
That means it's called charting
so you have multiple nodes together.
And there's no high availability, there's no replication.
Again, not everything may be true, for example,
for the serverless version of of memcached,
but I'm just trying to draw a simple image here.
It's not personal data.
So if you have an issue with memcached,
you may lose your entire cache and you have backup
and restore features only for the serverless version
of memcached, not the self-managed version
of memcached on ElastiCache.
You also have a multi-thread architecture,
which may be good for performance.
So the way I like to think of memcached is they're sharding
so you have multiple nodes next to each other,
which are partitioning, which are sharing the data, okay?
So the exam may not ask you many questions
or any question about choosing Redis versus Memcached
but it's good for you to know as a reference point

So there are two types

So the first one is called Cluster Mode Disabled.

so all your data is in this shard,
we'll have one primary cache node
and then we can option optionally set up
up to five cache replicas.
So from zero to five replica nodes.
The idea is that when you have a primary node
and some replicas,
in case of the failure of the primary node,
then the replicas can take over.
So the replication is a synchronous between the caches
and the primary node will be used for read and writes
while the other nodes are going to be read-only.
So on top of disaster recovery,
you can also scale your read capability
in ElastiCache for Redis by enabling read replicas.
So you have one shard,
that means that all the nodes will have all the data
in your Redis cluster.
The idea here is that you are guarding
against data loss if there is a node failure
and you can also enable Multi-AZ,
it is enabled by default by the way,
in case you won't have Multi-AZ failover.
So again, this is helpful for Multi-AZ
and also for scaling the read performance
of your ElastiCache cluster.
So now when you've disable the Cluster Mode,
you have two kind of scaling.
You have horizontal scaling
and you do this by adding or removing read replicas.
Remember you have a maximum of five read replicas.
And then you have vertical scaling.
And so you can scale up or down
to either larger or smaller node type.
In that case, behind the scenes,
there will be a old node group that is going to be upgraded.
So a new node group is going to be created.
Replication will happen automatically.
Again, this is behind the scenes.
And then once the new node group is up to date,
the DNS will update and our applications
will be using the new node group.
Now there is a second mode
and this says with Cluster Mode Enabled.
And in this mode, the data is going to be partitioned
across many shards,
which is helpful if you want to scale your writes.
So let's have a look at a second.
So we have Shard 1 and Shard 2 or 3 or Shard N.
And the idea is that the data is going
to be partially on Shard 1, partially on Shard 2,
all the way up to Shard N.
So it's going to be divided across all your shards.
Now each shard will work just as what we saw before
when Cluster Mode was disabled.
Now mean we can have one primary node
and up to five replica nodes.
So the data is replicated
and you set up the number of replicas equally
across all the shards, okay?
There is also Multi-AZ capability, it's on by default.

That means that if you don't set up any replicas,

and that the data is going to be partitioned,
that means that data will live across many different shards.
Okay, so this is the main difference
when you have Cluster Mode Enabled or Cluster Mode Disabled
for ElastiCache.
So therefore, when you are in Cluster Mode Enabled,
you can actually set up Auto Scaling for Redis.
So you can actually automatically increase
or decrease the number of shards or replicas
in your cluster.
So this supports both Target Tracking
and Scheduled Scaling Policies.
And again, you must be in Cluster Mode Enabled
for this to work.
So there is a metric we're going to track.
For example, the CPU utilization.
And then we can have a Target Tracking Policy
so that we want that the target CPU utilization
remains at around 60%.
If so, we can trigger a CloudWatch Alarm
and this CloudWatch Alarm can then increase the number
of shards in our cluster and, therefore,
new shards will come up.
Of course, our applications need to be able
to leverage these shards.
And so to connect to the cluster,
we must use what's called
the Cluster's Configuration Endpoint,
which is a way to connect entirely to the cluster.
So let's talk about these Connection Endpoints actually.
For a standalone node, you can just connect for read
and write operations using the one endpoint of your node.
If you're using Cluster Mode Disabled,
you will have one primary endpoint,
this is for all the write operations.
And then you will have a reader endpoint,
this is for the read operations
across all the read replicas.
Finally, you have also node endpoints
if you wanted to access individual nodes
for read operations.
If you have the Cluster Mode Enabled, it's very simple.
Again, remember, it's called the Configuration Endpoint
and it's for all read and write operations
that are compatible with Cluster Mode.
So you just need to have a recent enough client
and you're good to go.
So use the Configuration Endpoint
and you're good for read and writes,
which is the benefits of the Cluster Mode clusters.
Finally, you can also access individual nodes
if you wanted to by using the node endpoints,
but only for read operations.
And that's it for this lecture,
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 142. [SAA] DynamoDB - Overview
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904266
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about a database
that will appear quite a lot at the exam
from an architectural point of view,
which is Amazon DynamoDB.
So it's a fully managed database, it's highly available,
and it has replication of data across multiple AZs.
DynamoDB is special because it is Cloud native,
it's made by AWS's proprietary and it's a NoSQL database.
So it's not a relational database like RDS and Aurora
although it has still transaction supports.
So with DynamoDB, the use case is that
you can scale to massive workloads
because the database is internally distributed.
That means you can scale
to millions of requests per seconds,
trillions of rows and hundreds of terabytes of storage.
The idea is that, and you need to remember this,
you have single digit millisecond performance
which is going to be fast, of course, and consistent.
Also for all your security needs,
everything is integrated with IAM.
So for security, authorization, and administration,
it's low cost, has auto-scaling capabilities
that we'll see in a second,
and there is no maintenance or patching,
it's always available.
So you don't need to provision a database,
it's already there.
You just need to go ahead and create a table
and say how much capacity you want to put in this table.
You have two kind of table class,
you have the standard class for frequently accessed data
and you have the infrequent access,
the IA table class for infrequently accessed data.
So the basics of DynamoDB is that
DynamoDB is made of tables
but you don't need to create a database, okay?
It's not like Aurora and RDS,
the database is already there,
that is the service named DynamoDB.
So you go ahead and you create tables
and each table will have a primary key
and you decide on this at the creation time,
and then you add data.
So each table can have an infinite number of items
and there are rows and each item will have attributes.
And they're pretty much columns, but you can add
the attributes over time and they can be null.
So this is a big difference in an RDS or Aurora database,
you can add columns over time, but it's complicated process
and it can be difficult to evolve your schemas.
But then in DynamoDB, you can add attributes just like that
over time without any pre-requirements.
So the item size, the maximum item size in DynamoDB
is 400 kilobytes,
so DynamoDB is not there to store very large objects.
You have different data types supported,
you have the Scalar types such as String, Number, Binary,
Boolean, and Null, you have list, and maps, and sets.
So DynamoDB is at the exam,
gonna be a great choice if you need to see from
the exam that the schema,
so that means how your data looks, how it's shaped,
if the schema needs to rapidly evolve.
In that case, DynamoDB is a much better choice
than Aurora or RDS,
so look for this at the exam.
So here is an example of a table in DynamoDB.
We have a partition key,
optionally a sort key, which composes your primary key,
and then we have attributes
and then it looks just like a database, okay?
But it's possible, for example,
for your attributes to be null or to add attributes
over time, which makes the strength of DynamoDB.
Another thing you need to choose,
if you need to choose DynamoDB
is the capacity mode for reads and writes.
So you can control how to manage your table's capacity
and there are two modes you need to know about.
There is the provision mode, which is the default
in which you are going to provision the capacity in advance,
so you're going to say how many reads
and writes you expect per second
and that's going to be your capacity of your table,
so you need to plan the capacity beforehand
and then you're going to pay for every provision RCU or WCU
which stands for Read Capacity Units
or Write Capacity Units.
Although if you want a planned capacity,
you can still automatically adjust it
thanks to autoscaling,
which will increase or decrease your RCU and WCU
over time based on the load of your table.
So this is the provision mode and it works great
if your load is predictable, it evolves smoothly,
and you wanna do some cost saving
but there is also the On-Demand Mode.
And here, the read and writes capacity
will scale automatically with your workload.
There's no capacity planning needed,
there is actually no concept of RCU and WCU,
so instead in the On-Demand Mode
you're going to pay exactly for what you use,
so for every single writes
and every single reads you're going to pay for it.
So it's a lot more expensive as a solution
but it's going to be amazing for unpredictable workloads
or workloads that have steep, sudden spikes.
So again, these are some keywords you need to look
at for the exam,
if you have an application that will scale
from a thousand transactions
to 1 million transactions in less than a minute,
Provision Mode is not going to be good for you
because it doesn't scale fast enough.
So in that case, you need to use On-Demand Mode
or if you have a workload that has no transactions at all,
maybe four or five times a day maximum then
On-Demand Mode is great because you're only going to pay
for these four or five transactions.
So look out for the differences and these keywords
and you will be able to select
between Provision Mode and On-Demand Mode.
So that's it for the DynamoDB basics,
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 144. [SAA] DynamoDB - Advanced Features
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904284
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the advanced features
that can come up at the exam for DynamoDB.
And the first one is DynamoDB Accelerator or DAX.
So this is a fully-managed, highly available,
and seamless in-memory cache for DynamoDB.
The idea is that if you have a lot of reads
on your DynamoDB table,
then you can create a DAX cluster
to solve read congestion by caching the data.
And with DynamoDB DAX,
you get microseconds latency for cached data.
So this is something you have to look out for
in terms of keywords at the exam.
It doesn't require for you
to change any of your application logic
because the DAX cluster is compatible
with the existing DynamoDB APIs.
So you have your DynamoDB tables and your application,
and you will just create a DAX cluster
made of few cache nodes, connect to this DAX cluster.
And then behind the scenes,
the DAX cluster is connected to your Amazon DynamoDB table.
The cache has a default TTL of five minutes,
but you can change this.
So you may ask me,
why should I use DAX and not elastic cache?
Well, DAX is in front of DynamoDB
and it's going to be very helpful
for individual objects cache or queries,
and scanned queries' cache.
But if you want to store, say, aggregation results,
then Amazon ElastiCache is a great way to do it.
So if you want to store a very big computation
that you've done on top of Amazon DynamoDB.
So they're not drop-in replacements for one another,
they're actually complementary.
But most of the time,
for caching solution on top of Amazon DynamoDB,
it's just going to be using DynamoDB Accelerator DAX.
You can also do stream processing on top of DynamoDB.
The idea is that you want to have a stream
of all the modifications that happen on your table.
Would it be create, update, and delete.
And the use cases for that will be, for example,
to react to changes on your DynamoDB table in real time.
For example, to send a welcome email
whenever you have a new user in your user's table.
Or if so, you may wanna do real-time usage analytics,
or maybe you want to insert data into a derivative table,
or you want to implement cross region replication,
or you want to invoke Lambda on any changes made
on your DynamoDB table.
So two kind of stream processing on DynamoDB.
You have DynamoDB Streams, with 24 hours retention,
a limited number of consumers,
and is going to be greatly used with Lambda triggers.
Or if you wanted to read it yourself,
there is something
called the DynamoDB Stream Kinesis Adapter.
Or you can also choose to send all your changes
directly into a Kinesis Data Streams.
And here you can have up to one year of retention,
you can have a much higher number of consumers,
and you have a much higher number
of ways to process the data,
whether we blend the functions, Kinesis Data Analytics,
Kinesis Data Firehose, Glue Streaming ETLs, and so on.
So let's have a look at an architectural diagram
to understand DynamoDB Streams better.
So your application does create updates
and delete operations on top of your DynamoDB table,
which is going to be either a DynamoDB Streams
or a Kinesis Data Streams.
If you choose to use Kinesis Data Streams,
then you can use Kinesis Data Firehose.
And from this, you can send your data into Amazon Redshift
for analytics purposes,
or Amazon S3 if you want to archive some of the data,
or Amazon OpenSearch to do some indexing
and some searches on top of it.
Or if you are using DynamoDB Streams,
you can have a processing layer
and you can use either the DynamoDB KCL Adapter
to run your applications
on top of EC2 instances or Lambda functions.
And from there, do some notifications on top of SNS
or do some filtering and transformations
into another DynamoDB table.
Or use the processing layer to do whatever you want,
such as, again, send the data to Amazon OpenSearch.
So I didn't represent all the possibilities
or our architectures.
Of course, you can have EC22 instances
reading from Kinesis Data Streams.
You can have Kinesis Data Analytics and so on
on top of Kinesis Data Streams, many, many transformations.
But again, you know enough now
to figure out what is going to be the right architecture
at the right time.
DynamoDB also has a concept of global table.
So a global table is a table, of course,
that is going to be replicated across multiple regions.
So you can have a table in US-East-1
and a table in AP-Southeast-2.
And there is a two-way replication between the tables.
That means that you can write to a table
either in US-East-1 and AP-Southeast-2.
So here, the idea with global tables
is to make DynamoDB accessible
with low latency in multiple regions.
And it is an Active-Active replication.
That means that your applications can read and write
to the table in any specific region.
And to enable global tables,
you must first enable DynamoDB Streams
because this is the underlying infrastructure
to replicate the table across regions.
DynamoDB also has a feature named Time To Live, or TTL.
The idea is that you want to automatically delete items
after an expiry timestamp.
So you have your table, SessionData,
and then you will have one last attribute
called ExpTime, which is your TTL,
and it has a timestamp in it.
And the idea is that you're going to define a TTL.
And as soon as the current time in the Epoch timestamp
is going to be over your ExpTime column,
then automatically it's going to expire items
and then eventually delete them through a deletion process.
So the idea is that the items in your data table
are going to be deleted after a while.
So the use cases for this will be to only store data
by keeping only the most current items
or to adhere to regulatory obligations by,
for example, deleting data after two years.
Or another use case that is very common at the exam
is the web session handling.
So a user would log into your website,
and then would've a session.
And you would keep the session in a central place,
such as DynamoDB for two hours.
And you would set the session data there
and any kind of applications can access it.
And at some point, after two hours,
if it hasn't been renewed,
then it will expire and move away from this table.
You can also use DynamoDB for disaster recovery.
So what are your backups options?
Well, you can have continuous backups
with point-in-time recovery, PITR.
So it's optionally enabled,
but you can have it for the last 35 days.
And then if you enable it,
you can do a point-in-time recovery
to any time within the backup window.
And if you do happen to do a recovery,
then it will create a new table.
If you wanted to have longer term backups,
then you can use on-demand backups,
and they will be retained until you delete them explicitly.
And doing these kind of backups
do not affect the performance
or the latency of your DynamoDB table.
And if you wanted to have
a better management of your backups,
you can use the AWS Backup Service,
and this will enable you to have lifecycle policies
for your backups and so on.
And also copy your backups across regions
for disaster recovery purposes.
And again, if you were to do a recovery
of one of these backups, it will create a new table.
Now, let's talk about the integrations
between DynamoDB and Amazon S3.
So you can export a table into S3, just like this.
And to do so, you must enable point-in-time recovery
and you would export DynamoDB table into S3.
For example, if you wanted to do some queries,
for example, using the Amazon Athena engine.
So you can export at any point in time
during the last 35 days
because you've enabled continuous backups.
And when you do an export,
this does not affect the read capacity of your table
or your performance.
So with this, you can perform,
for example, data analysis on top of DynamoDB
through exporting through Amazon S3 first.
You can also use this to retain snapshots for auditing,
or to do any kind of big transformation,
maybe any ETL of the data before importing it back
into a new DynamoDB table, for example.
The format of the export can be in DynamoDB JSON
or the ION format.
And similarly, you can import to Amazon S3.
So you can export from S3 into the CSV, JSON, or ION format
back into a new DynamoDB table.
And this does not consume any write capacity
and it will create a new table.
If there are any import errors,
they will be logged in CloudWatch Logs.
So that's it for DynamoDB. I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

スキーマ変換ツールということで､ AWS SCTをインストールしたサーバーを用意し､ オンプレミスで設定できるようにしました｡
これはベストプラクティスであり､ その後､ MySQLを実行しているAmazon RDSデータベースへのスキーマ変換を行うことになります｡
そして､ 全負荷と変更データキャプチャまたはCDCを行うDMSレプリケーションインスタンスを設定することで､ 継続的なレプリケーションを行うことができます｡
そして､ オンプレミスのデータベース､ ソースのOracleデータベースを読み込んで､ お客様のプライベートサブネットにデータを挿入することで､
データ移行を実行するわけです｡
それでいいじゃないですか｡
以上で､ DMSについては､ データベースマイグレーションサービスになります｡
移行元となるデータベースが2種類ある場合は､ 必ずSCTを使用する必要があることを覚えておいてください｡
そして､ DMSについては､ マルチアズ展開があります｡
つまり､ あるAZにDMSのレプリケーションインスタンスがあり､ そのインスタンスを別のAZに同期レプリケーションし､
スタンバイレプリカとするわけです｡
だから､ これを使うメリットは､ もちろんある｡
特定の1つの故障に強いけど､ データもくれる｡
冗長化することでIOフリーズをなくし､ レイテンシの急増を最小限に抑えることができます｡
というわけで､ 今回の講義はここまでです｡
お気に召していただけたなら､ 次回の講義でお会いしましょう｡

# 147. AWS DMS - Monitoring
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904394
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about monitoring for DMS.
So you can actually monitor
the replication tasks themselves.
So you have the task status,
if it's creating, running or stopped.
And the task status bar gives you
an estimation of the task's progress.
You also have the table states, so you know, by table,
if we are in before load or table completed and so on.
And you get some statistics around the number
of inserts, deletions, and updates for each table.
Now, there are some CloudWatch metrics
we can get out of DMS, so here are some examples.
You can get replication task metrics
such as the bandwidth and so on,
as well as host metrics such as the CPU utilization
or the freeable memory.
So the host metrics represent the performance
and utilization statistics for the replication host.
So we're talking about the CPU, the RAM,
the storage space, the IOPS, and so on.
And then the replication task metrics are statistics
for the number of incoming and committed changes,
the latency between the replication host
and both the source and target databases.
So you'll have these kind of metrics
such as the FullLoadThroughputRowsSource, RowsTarget,
as well as the CDCThroughputRowsSource
and the CDCThroughputRowsTarget,
based on if you're doing a full load
or a continuous replication.
Finally, table metrics, as I said, give you some information
about the number of inserts, updates, deletes,
and DDL statements completed for your table.
So that's it. I hope you liked it,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 148. [SAA/DVA/SOA] Amazon S3 - Replication
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904436
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about Amazon S3 Replication,
and there are two flavors of it.
So CRR is for cross-region replication
and SRR is for same-region replication.
The idea is that we have an S3 Bucket in one region
and a target S3 Bucket in another region,
and we want to set up asynchronous replication
between these two buckets.
So, to do so, we first must enable Versioning
in the source and the destination buckets.
And if we do CRR, so cross-region replication,
the two regions must be different.
If we do SRR, the two regions are the same.
Now, it's possible for you to have these buckets
in different AWS accounts
and copying happens asynchronously.
So the replication mechanism happens behind the scenes,
in the background.
And to make replication work,
you must give proper IAM permissions
to the S3 service so that it has the permission
to read and write from specified buckets.
So the use cases for replication are manyfold.
The first one is that if you use cross-region replication,
this can be helpful for compliance
or for providing lower latency access to your data
because it's in another region,
or to replicate data across accounts.
For SRR, or same-region replication,
this can be very helpful to aggregate logs
across multiple S3 Buckets
or to perform a live replication
between a production and test accounts,
so, you have your own test environment.
Okay, so that's it about replication.
I will see you in the next lecture for some practice.

# 150. AWS Storage Gateway - Overview
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904458
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we've seen Amazon S3
as a standalone service, but it is possible for you
to use it in a hybrid cloud type of setting.
So AWS wants you to bridge
between your on-premises environment to AWS
and that's called a hybrid cloud.
So part of your infrastructure is going to be on-premises
and the rest is going to be on the cloud.
Why?
Well, maybe because sometimes you have created,
for example, your on-premises infrastructure first
and you're doing a migration but it could be long
so you can do a long cloud migration
or for security requirements or compliance requirements,
maybe it's your strategy to have part of it on the cloud
and part of it on-premises.
You have really different use cases
for trying to have two different ways of doing IT.
Some of it on-premises and some of it on the cloud.
And Amazon S3, it's a proprietary storage technology,
so this is not something like the EFS service
or NFS protocol we saw from before
that we can use directly on two servers on-premises.
For exposing S3 data on-premises,
you have to use something called a Storage Gateway.
So if you wanted to summarize the storage options on AWS,
the block storage would be EBS
or an EC2 instance store.
The file storage would be a network file system
so Amazon EFS,
and object storage would be Amazon S3 or Glacier.
And where does the Storage Gateway fit in all this?
Well, the Storage Gateway is going to be bridging
your on-premises data and cloud data in AWS.
So your hybrid storage will allow your on-premises systems
to seamlessly use the cloud
to extend the storage capability.
So this can be used for disaster recovery,
backup and restore or tiered storage.
There are different types of Storage Gateway.
There is a File Gateway, there is a Volume Gateway
and a Tape Gateway.
Now you don't need to know all these types
going into the exam, okay?
What you need to know is that the Storage Gateway
allows you to bridge whatever happens on-premises
directly into the AWS Cloud.
So under the scene,
the Storage Gateway will be using Amazon EBS,
Amazon S3, and Glacier behind the scenes, okay?
So from a certified cloud petitioner perspective,
the Storage Gateway is a way for you
to bridge your file systems and your storage on-premises
into the cloud to leverage best of both worlds, okay?
For if you were to do
the AWS Certified Solutions Architect Associate course,
you would need to understand Storage Gateway
a little bit better, but I will save you this right now
for the Certified Cloud Practitioner.
Okay, that's it.
I hope you liked it
and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 151. AWS Storage Gateway - File Gateway Cache Refresh
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904468
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's do a deep dive
onto the File Gateway.
So the File Gateway, because it's backed by Amazon S3,
has a list of files that it can expose to the users.
And if your users write a file
directly into the File Gateway,
that file will be synced with your S3 bucket
and your File Gateway knows about this file.
But if a user uploads a file directly into an S3 bucket,
then the File Gateway
does not necessarily know about it right away.
And so you may have stale data on your File Gateway.
And so therefore, there is an API
called the RefreshCache API
which is going to refresh the list of file
that your File Gateway knows about.
So we can either do this on demand,
such as using the RefreshCache API,
or doing it periodically thanks to a Lambda function,
or even trigger it automatically from the S3 bucket
through a Lambda function, but that may be costly
if you have many files written to your S3 bucket.
The second method
is to use the Automated Cache Refresh feature
which has the File Gateway automatically stay up to date
with the S3 buckets.
So this will be automatic
and this will be done periodically.
And so this ensure that the users do not have stale data
on their file shares
and so you don't need to automatically or manually
invoke the RefreshCache API.
You still may want to use that API
if you want the cache refresh to happen right away
so that you know that a file
you've just uploaded into your Amazon S3 bucket
is available on your File Gateway.
So hopefully that makes sense.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 152. [SAA/DVA/SOA] Auto Scaling Groups - Scaling Policies
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904490
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So we have several scaling policies
for auto scaling group.
The first one is dynamic scaling and within this category,
we have the target tracking scaling,
which is very simple to set up.
The idea is that you define a metric for your ASG,
for example, the CPU utilization
and you define a target value, for example, 40%.
And automatically, the ASG is going to scale out or in
to allow you to keep this metric to around 40%.
We also have the simple or step scaling
and the idea is that you define CloudWatch alarms
that are being triggered when you want to add units
of capacity to your auto scaling group
or when you want to remove units of capacity
to your auto scaling group.
Then we have scheduled scaling.
So this is when you anticipate a scaling
based on a known usage pattern.
For example, you say that you know that every time
at 5:00 PM on Fridays, you're going to get new users
and therefore, you want to increase
the minimum capacity to 10.
Then we have predictive scaling.
So this is when you continuously forecast load
and then you start scheduling ahead of time.
So this is very good when you have patterns
that repeat themselves.
So automatically, the ASG is going to analyze
historical load then generate a forecast
and then schedule scaling actions based on the forecast,
which can be very handy if you have cyclical data.
So some good metrics to scale on is a big question.
So it depends really on what your application is doing
and how it's working.
But usually, here are a few.
So number one is CPU utilization,
because every time your instance receive a request,
usually, they will do some sort of computation
and so it will use some CPU.
And so if you look at the average CPU utilization
across all your instances and it goes higher,
that means that your instances are being more utilized.
And so it would be a good metric to scale on.
Another metric to scale on, it's more application-specific,
but it is a RequestCountPerTarget,
which is based on your testing,
you know that your EC2 instances operate
at an optimal request of 1,000 requests
per target at a time and so maybe this is the target
you want to have for your scaling.
So here as an example.
You have an auto scaling group with three EC2 instances
and your ALB is currently spreading the request
across all of them.
So right now the value of the request counts
per target metric is three,
because each EC2 instance, on average,
has three requests outstanding.
Next if your application is network-bound,
so for example there's a lot of uploads and downloads
and you know that network is going to be a bottleneck
for your EC2 instances,
then you may want to scale on the average network in or out
to make sure that if you reach some certain threshold,
then you're going to scale based on that.
Or any custom metric that you push to CloudWatch,
so you can set up your own metrics
that are going to be application-specific
and based on that, you can set up your scaling policies.
Now one last thing you need to know about scaling policies
is what's called a scaling cooldown.
So the idea is that after there is a scaling activity,
so whenever you add or you remove instances,
you are entering the cooldown period,
which is, by default, five minutes or 300 seconds.
And during that cooldown period,
the ASG will not launch or terminate additional instances.
And the reason behind this reasoning
is that you allow for metrics to stabilize,
for your new instance to enter into effect
and to see what the new metric will become.
So the idea is that when there is a scaling action
that occurs, the question is,
is there a default cooldown in effect?
If yes, then ignore the action.
If no, then proceed with the scaling action,
which is to launch or terminate instances.
And so an advice to you is to use a ready-to-use AMI
to reduce the configuration time for your EC2 instances
in order for them to be serving the request faster.
So if you don't spend time configuring your EC2 instance,
then they can be in effect right away.
And then because they can be active way faster,
then the cooldown period can be decreased
and you can have a more dynamic scaling up and down
of your ASG.
And of course, you need to make sure to enable
something like detailed monitoring for your ASG
to get access to metrics every one minute
and to make sure that you have
these metrics being updated fast enough.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 153. [SAA/DVA/SOA] Auto Scaling Groups - Scaling Policies Hands On
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904498

Okay, so now let's have a look
at automatic scaling for your ASG.
As you can see we have three categories,
dynamic scaling policies, predictive scaling policies,
and scheduled actions.
So let's start with the simplest.
So schedule actions
is when you want to schedule a scaling action in the future,
so you can create one
and then you say what you want the desired capacity
or the min or the max to be,
and then is it once every week, every hour,
is it's based on a specific schedule and so on?
And then a start time and an end time
if you wanted it to be done.
So this is pretty cool and this is allowing you to schedule
based on events that you can predict
and that you know in advance.
Because you know, for example
that you're going to run a big promotion next Saturday.
Next, predictive scaling policies
is where it's going to be machine learning driven.
So you need to scale it based on a forecast.
So you need to have a look at the actual policy
and the actual scaling based on the past
and then it will have a look at a metric to look at.
For example, CPU utilization or network in, network out,
the application load balancer request counts
or a custom metric that you want.
And then you want to, for example,
to have a target of 50% of CPU utilization for instance,
and then you can set up some additional settings,
but based on this,
and based on the actual scheduled utilization
for the past week, for example,
then a forecast is going to be created
and your ASG is going to be scaling based on that forecast.
So it's not something I can demonstrate with you
because I would need to enable this
for a very long time a week
and then make sure I have some usage on my application.
But at least you see that predictive scaling policy
is quite simple to set up,
you just specify the metric you want
and the target utilization,
and then some machine learning will be applied
for the scaling to happen.
So the one policy I can demonstrate to you
is the dynamic scaling policy.
So let's go ahead and create a dynamic scaling policy.
So here we have three options.
We have target tracking, step scaling and simple scaling.
So let's have a look at simple scaling first.
So here we have to specify a name than a CloudWatch alarm,
which is an alarm that can scale capacity
whenever it is being triggered.
So we need to create an alarm beforehand,
but we'll see this later on.
And so in case the alarm is being triggered
and what happens, maybe you want to add two capacity units,
or maybe you want to add 10% of your group.
And then add capacity units
in increments of at least two capacity units.
So this is a simple scaling policy.
So we can have a scaling policy that goes out
by adding instances,
or that goes in by removing instances here.
Or you can have a set to action as well.
And next we have step scaling.
So this is allowing you to set up multiple an alarm
and based on the alarm value to have different steps
to, for example, if the alarm is very, very high
in terms of the value, then add 10 capacity units.
But if it's high, but not too high, add one.
This is the idea behind step scaling,

# 154. Auto Scaling Groups - Lifecycle Hooks
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904508
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about Lifecycle Hooks in autoscaling groups.
So by default, when you launch an instance
it's in service right away in your autoscaling group
but you can use Lifecycle Hooks to actually
make sure you perform some work
before you actually go in service.
So when there is a scale out event
you go into a pending state
and then you go into the end service states
but you can actually run a Lifecycle Hook
so that you stay in pending until you complete some task.
For example, you may want to leave some time
for your instance to run some scripts.
So you're going to go
into the Lifecycle hook named Easy two Instance launching.
You go into the pending wait states
and then when you're done with these scripts
you notify back the autoscaling group that you're done.
The instance goes into the pending proceed state
and then the instance is in service.
So the idea here is that by using Hook
we allow the instance to do whatever it wants
and then proceed to in-service.
You can also perform some actions when
the instance is terminated.
So instead of terminating the instance right away
you may want to, for example
pause the logs or pause the instances for troubleshooting.
So upon initiating a termination
the instance goes into the terminating states
and then you can run a lifecycle hook
for the EC2 instance terminating.
So it will go into terminating weight
you can do whatever you want, and then when you're done
you notify the ASG that it can proceed with a termination
upon which the instance will be terminated.
So a use case
for the termination lifecycle hook is to do cleanup
or log extraction, or for example, the instance launching.
You can do special health checks to make sure
that the instance is ready to go in service.
So to get access to these Lifecycle Hooks
you can use EventBridge, SNS and SQS
but EventBridge is definitely the most used.
So the way it works is
that any lifecycle event will trigger an event
in EventBridge, and from there, for example
you can invoke Lambda function, whatever automation you want
so that you can deal with these lifecycle hooks.
So let's take an example.
The instance goes into terminating weight states
so it's being terminated
but we want to be able to collect the logs.
So this event will happen to be in EventBridge.
We can from there, invoke a systems manager run command
which is going to collect the logs and for example
send them to Amazon is free
for analysis or send them to CloudWatch logs.
And so that's it.
You know what Lifecycle hooks are now.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

and no control over the event shape or form.

but there is a better way, more complete way

And so here, for example,

that shows that the EC2 instance launch was successful.
So, there are a lot more events you can match

so you can know whether an instance is launching
or whether or not the launch was successful or unsuccessful.
Same for terminating
and whether or not it was successful or unsuccessful.
Then if you use the EC2 instance refresh feature

or whenever the refresh itself

So, what I like about using EventBridge events

# 156. Auto Scaling Groups - Termination Policies
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904522
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about Termination Policies
in your Auto Scanning Group.
So this allows you to decide which instances get terminated
in case of a scale-in event or an Instance Refresh
or an AZ Rebalancing,
that means when you have too many instances
in one Availability Zone
and they get terminated to rebalance it.
So there is the Default Termination Policy,
which is quite simple to explain.
You select the Availability Zone with the more instances
and then you terminate the instance
with the oldest Launch Template or Launch Configuration.
And then if they were launched
with the same Launch Template,
then the instance that gets terminated
is the one that is the closest to its billing hour.
So let's take an example.
We have the Auto Scaling Group
with two EC2 instances started with an old Launch Template
and then the new Launch Template allows us to keep
on scaling out and having now five EC2 instances.
Now, there is a scale-in event
because we don't need as much capacity.
So we first evaluate the AZ
with the most amount of instances,
so that's going to be AZ-A.
And then we look at the Launch Templates
and we choose the one with the oldest Launch Templates,
so the first one, and we terminate it.
If we had two with the same old Launch Templates,
we would choose the one with the closest next billing hour,
and that's it.
Now you can customize these Termination Policies
to either have the Default one,
which is the one I just explained,
or to have different ones.
For example, this one is called AllocationStrategy.
And so it will terminate instances to remain in line
with your Allocation Strategy.
So for example, if you're using Spot Instances
and you choose lowest-price,
it will choose to remain in line
with the lowest-price allocation for your Spot Instances.
Or if you're using On-Demand Instances
with a wide variety of instances,
then you would choose the one with the lower priority.
Also, you have OldestLaunchTemplate
to terminate instances that have the oldest Launch Template.
Or OldestLaunchConfiguration
for the oldest Launch Configuration.
ClosestToNextInstanceHour to terminate the instances
that are going to be closest to the next billing hour.
NewestInstance to actually terminate the newest instance,
which is very helpful
if you're testing a new Launch Template,
but then you're scaling back in
and it will automatically terminate
these new instances you've created.
OldestLaunchTemplate,
very helpful to terminate your old instances.
So this is very helpful and this is different
from Launch Configuration because, or Launch Templates,
because if you're upgrading the instance sites, for example,
you go from m5.large to m5.4xlarge,
then you're not changing the Launch Templates,
but you're changing the instance size.
In this case, you want to delete your oldest instances.
And you can choose one or more policies
and actually specify the evaluation order.
So you can say, you can combine OldestInstance
with ClosestToNextInstanceHour, and then AllocationStrategy.
Whatever you want.
And you could define your own Custom Termination Policy
if you wanted to, backed by a Lambda function.
So that's it for Termination Policies.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 157. Auto Scaling Groups - Warm Pools
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904524
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about warm pools.
And here is the problem, when you have an auto-scaling group
and it scales out, that means that when you add instances
into your auto-scaling group
you want to launch instances as fast as possible.
But sometimes your instances
they're doing some initialization,
they're doing some bootstrapping,
and that can take several minutes before your instances
are actually available to serve traffic.
So you could be also getting some data,
filling in some internal states for such as a cache
you run configuration scripts, etc. etc.
So historically, the solution was
to over-provision compute resources
in order to absorb the unexpected demand.
But then this is going to lead
to an increased cost because you're over-provisioned
or you try to fit as much as possible
into a golden image to try to reduce your boot time.
But none of these are perfect, and actually
you want to use the auto scanning group warm pools.
So what are these warm pools?
Well, the idea is that we have a pool
of pre-initialized instances, and by having this
we are going to reduce the scale-out latency.
So let me explain.
Say we have a auto-scaling group
with a desired capacity of 3 and a max capacity of 6.
Then the warm pool is going to be of size 3.
Three is by default the difference
between the max capacity and the desired capacity.
So 6 minus 3 equals 3.
That's basically the maximum number of instances
that can be put from the pool
into the auto-scaling group until we reach the max capacity.
And so these instances in the warm pool
they have been pre-initialized.
So all the setup you need has been done
and then there go into a state.
We'll see the state is either started, stopped,
or hibernated.
But the idea is that whenever you have a scale-out event
then the new instance is going to be going
from the pool into your auto-scaling group.
So the idea is that by doing this,
the instance that comes into the auto-scaling group
has done some pre-initialization work.
Now, let's go into the warm pool size setting.
So we have the minimum warm pool size.
This is the number of instances you always want
in the warm pool no matter what.
Then the max prepared capacity, either it is equal
to the max capacity of the auto-scaling group.
That means that to see how many instances you have
in your warm pool, you do the difference
of the actual desired capacity
of the ASG and the max capacity.
Or if you have, say for example, a max capacity
of 1,500 instances and a desired capacity of 1000
you may not want to have one 500 instances
in your warm pool.
So you may want to specify just a set number of instances
for example 100, so that it remains manageable,
but at small sizes the default is fine.
Now, more importantly, the warm pool instance state.
So we'll talk about this in a second, but it can be
either in the running state, stopped, or hibernated.
And the idea is that you may want to leverage the stopped
or hibernated state.
This is where you get the best cost savings
and that's where it makes the most sense.
So the idea is that you initialize your instance
and then when it's initialized, you either put it
in the stopped or the hibernated states
and then all of a sudden when you scale-out
it will be started and put
into the main auto-scaling group.
On top of it, any instance in the warm pool
does not contribute to your ASG metrics
until it is put into the ASG.
So this doesn't affect scaling policies.
So let's understand why it's also very cost effective
to have warm pools.
So as mentioned
we have definitely have latency improvements
because now the instances have been warmed
and they're ready to serve traffic
and then we put them into the ASG.
Let's take a look at the pricing
for one m5 large instance.
So if we decide to over-provision our ASG,
then we're going to pay for the running cost
of that instance.
For example, $70 plus the EBS charges
for the disk attached to your instance.
But if we decide to use a warm pool
and so the warm pool makes the EC2 instance
goes into the stopped states
then we're only going to pay for the EBS volume.
So the EBS volume, for example,
for 10 gigabytes EBS volume will cost us $1 for a month.
So that means that for each EC2 instance in the warm pool,
you're going to pay about $1 a month
which is very, very little compared
to the cost of actually running an instance.
So here for not that much money
we have the ability to keep a very large warm pool
of EC2 instances
in order to very quickly have these instances serve traffic.
So how do you choose between running
stopped and hibernated?
Well, I made this little diagram right here
and hopefully that helps you.
So the idea is that if you're in the running states
you're going to get your instances immediately
available to accept traffic and no start delay
because your instances are already running.
But I don't think this is very efficient
because while the instances are running in your warm pool
and therefore they will incur cost even when
they're not serving traffic.
So definitely not my first choice.
Next we have stopped.
So the scale-out delay is slower
because the instance needs to be started
before traffic can be served.
So that add some delay and the start delay is slower
because well, you have already initialized the instance
but you still need to, for example,
start your application again.
Now in terms of cost, you don't have any running cost.
You're only going to pay for the attached resources
such as your EBS volumes or elastic IPs
but I don't think you're going to use elastic IPs
with the ASG warm pools.
And so that makes it way more cost effective
as you saw from my previous analysis.
And the one I really liked right now is hibernated.
Well, hibernated makes the EC2 memory states
be put on disk before the instance
is quote unquote "stopped."
So the idea is that when you have a scale-out
the instance is pre-initialized
so it's going to be quite fast actually.
Then the startup is going to be faster as well
because the application is already started in memory
so it's going to be quite fast.
And then for the cost, well, you don't have any more cost
than for a stopped instance because you only pay
for the EBS volume attached to your EC2 instance.
But because you're using hibernation
the entire memory state is written to the disc
and so you may need to have a slightly
larger EBS volume to fit that memory state.
But that's why I love hibernation is because
everything is pre-initialized in memory.
And so to me, you're getting the best of both worlds
between stopped and running.
Now let's talk about the instance reuse policy.
So by default, your ASG, when it terminates an instance
it will terminate it from the ASG and then
there will be a new instance launched into the warm pool.
But you can set up an instance reuse policy to instead
return the instance back into the warm pool.
So the idea is that upon quote unquote "termination,"
a scale-in event actually the instance is not terminated
it is moved back into your warm pool, and then
your warm pool can do whatever it wants with the instance.
So you may want to use this or you may want to use
the default mechanism
which is that the instance actually gets terminated.
So when you're using warm pools
in order for everything to work correctly
you must use lifecycle hooks.
So let me explain why.
So when an instance gets started into a warm pool
it will go into the state named warm pending
and then you will have access
to the lifecycle hook named warmed pending wait.
And the idea is that the instance will stay
in that state until you have confirmed
that the initialization of the instance has completed.
So this is why it's very important to use lifecycle hooks.
So that's when the ASG knows, okay,
this warm instance is ready.
When it's ready, it's going to go into
the warmed pending proceed state, and then it will go
into whatever state you've chosen for your warm pool.
So it could be warmed stop, warmed running,
or warmed hibernated.
And so we've completed the initialization
of our instance in our warm pool.
Now, whenever we have a scale-out event, the instance
from the warm pool is going to be put into our ASG.
So we go into the pending state, then pending wait state,
this is exactly the same as a normal lifecycle hook.
Here we can do whatever we want, for example
more initializations, then we go into pending proceeds
and then the instance is in service.
So very similarly, if we terminate the instance
and we don't have an instance reuse policy,
then the lifecycle hooks are exactly the same
as a normal ASG.
So terminating, then terminating wait,
then terminating proceed, and finally terminated.
But in case we are using a instance reuse policy
then the instance is put back into the pool
and it goes again into the warmed pending state,
warm pending wait, warm pending proceed,
and then finally warm stopped or running or hibernated.
So to summarize, in case of a scale-out event
what's going to happen is that first the instance
will have a warmed pending wait state
in which we can do a lifecycle action to be completed
before the instance actually gets into the stopped state
or whatever state you've chosen for your warm pool.
And then when there's a scale-out event
then it will go into the pending wait state
because the instance is starting.
You can do again a life cycle action
before the instance is put in service
and then the instance will be put
in service and available to serve traffic.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 159. [SOA] Elastic Load Balancer - ALB Rules Deep Dive
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions

(Instructor) So a quick lecture
to understand rules as a whole.
So rules are set up on your application load balancer
and you can have many rules or one rule too,
and the last rule is called the default rule
and each rule will have a specific target. Okay?
Now, the rules are going to be processed in order. Okay?
The default rule is going to be the last one to be processed
and each rule supports different actions.
For example, it can forward to a specific target group,
it can redirect to a specific other URL,
or it can send a fixed response back.
Rules can have conditions in terms of which rule is
going to be hit first.
So, it could be having a rule on the host header. Okay?
This is part of the client request.
It could be an HTTP request method to see if the request is
a GET or a POST, or a PUT.
The path pattern, so where the request is sent to,
is it slash my app 1 or slash my app 2.
Source IP, so what, where's the request coming from.
And a specific HTTP header in general,
or the query string parameters as part of the request.
So this really allows you to create some complex routing to
different target groups based on certain conditions
on the originating request.
Another thing you should know is that for a single rule,
as part of your ALB, you could have
multiple target groups as a target.
And the idea is that you can specify weights for each
target group within a single rule.
So the idea behind this is that you want to be able to
evolve your backend services, okay,
from one target group to another, and to update them.
And so you want to have version one in one target group
and version two in another target group.
And you want to evaluate whether or not
version two make sense.
This is also called a blue green deployment.
So thanks to this weighting,
you can control how much traffic goes from your ALB to
a specific target group as part of a rule.
So let's have a look at an example.
So let's say that we have our users,
they talked to the ALB and the ALB has been wired to talk to
target group one historically. Okay.
Which is your blue group,
but now you're going to add a target group two,
which is a new version of your application.
And you will set up weights in your rule.
You have a weight of eight, for target group one
and a weight of two for target group two.
That means that now for a single rule,
the ALB will send 80% of the traffic to your first group and
20% of the traffic to the second group,
which would allow you to do some monitoring on your target
groups and to see whether or not they are receiving the
traffic correctly,
whether or not the metrics are good, and whether or not your
application version is behaving as expected. Okay?
So this is a cool new feature as well.
So that's it for this lecture.

# 160. Elastic Load Balancer - Extras
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904602
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about a few more concepts
for your load balancers.
The first one is the DualStack Networking.
So this allows clients to communicate
with your load balancer using either the IPv4 protocol
or the IPv6 protocol.
And this works for your application load balancer
and your network load balancer.
So let's consider a VPC that has an IPv6 sider in it,
so it's enabled for IPv6,
and we have public subnets that do have IPv6.
So we get an internet facing ELB
and this ELB is going to be accessible using three URLs.
The first one is your IPv4.
This is the blue one; we've seen it before.
The second one is for your IPv6
so your clients with IPv6 can access it.
And then the last one is DualStack.
And DualStack means if we give the same URL
to an IPv6 and an IPv4 client,
the DualStack will resolve to the proper IP,
so either the IPv6 or IPv4.
So bottom line is, if you don't know what versions
your clients are going to be using
in terms of IP protocol, you can just give them
the DualStack URL and automatically,
the correct protocol is going to be used.
Now, behind the scenes, your target groups
can be supporting IPv4 and IPv6,
but you cannot mix them together.
You need to have two separate target groups for that.
And then the ELB will ensure compatibility
between the client IP version
and the target IP version.
So that means that your IPv4 request can go
into IPv4 target groups and IPv6 requests will go
into your IPv6 targets.
But in case you do not have any IPv6 targets,
you only have IPv4, you can still enable DualStack.
And what's going to happen is the ELB is automatically going
to convert the request from IPv6 to IPv4 internally.
So that means that your EC2 instances,
if they're only issuing IPv4, they are still going
to work properly and the ELB is going
to be the thing doing the translation.
Finally, just like any networking for your load balancer,
just a reminder, you must enable an availability zone
in your load balancer before the traffic is being sent
to that availability zone in your backend instances.
Also, let's talk about PrivateLink Integration
for your network load balancer.
So in case we have a service consumer VPC
and a service provider VPC
and they have overlapping IP addresses,
then we cannot pair them together.
So let's say we have an application
in the service provider and an application
in the service consumer.
The way to manage communication between these two is
to expose the service with a network load balancer
in the service provider VPC
and then you would create a PrivateLink.
This will create a VPC interface
and point into the service consumer VPC.
And communication can be done this way, internally,
on the network of AWS.

# 162. Multi-AZ Architectures
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904650
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's quickly do a little check on
what is Multi AZ in AWS.
So there's some services where you want to use
multiple availability zones for high availability purposes,
for example, EFS, ELB, ASG, Beanstalk,
where you choose which AZs you want to be deployed in.
RDS and ElastiCache have a multi-AZ feature,
but this time it's not to distribute the service
across multiple AZ and serve it from multiple AZ.
It's instead to have a synchronous standby database
that is going to be very helpful
in case you have failovers.
For Aurora, the data is automatically stored
across multiple AZ by default, nothing to do,
but your Aurora instances themselves must be, by yourself,
spread out across multiple AZ to have the multi-AZ feature.
For OpenSearch, you have a managed cluster.
You can have it across multiple AZ
in a multi-master setting,
so that means that you can accept
queries into different AZs.
And if you use Jenkins, for example, self-deployed,
again, you have multi master,
but you need to make sure
you deploy across multiple AZ.
In some services in AWS, a multi-AZ is always there,
for example, if you use Amazon S3,
except the OneZone-Infrequent Access tier,
then you'll have multiple AZ.
DynamoDB is across multiple AZ, for example,
or really all of the AWS proprietary services,
managed services, are usually multiple AZ.
So if we look at a three-tier architecture
in a multiple AZ setting, so we have one public subnet,
one private subnet for our application tier,
and one private subnet for our data tier.
The ALB, the low balancer, is going to be spread
across multiple subnets in your VPC on multiple AZ.
So the requests are going to be
spread out across multiple AZ.
Then your target group also can extend
across multiple availability zones,
and your ALB will send traffic to your target group,
so either on the same AZ to save some network costs,
or if you've enabled cross-zone load balancing,
then it's possible for your request
to go across availability zones.
Finally, your RDS database, for example, is multi-AZ,
but this time we have one main instance
and then a standby instance,
which is going to be synchronously replicated.
And so, any application request in your database
are going to go into your main instance.
So that's it for multi-AZ.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 163. Blue-Green Architectures
# Section: Domain 3: Resilient Cloud Solutions
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-devops-engineer-professional-hands-on/learn/lecture/37904660
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk
about the different ways you can achieve blue-green on AWS.
So let's take an example of an ALB,
and you have a listener, and two target groups.
So you have the blue target group,
currently receiving requests,
and you can actually add a green target group
to the same listener and actually spread out
the request between the blue and the green target group.
So you can switch all the traffic at once,
if you wanted to by switching target groups,
swapping them, or if you wanted to assign weights
to the target group, you could as well, for example
put 90% on your blue, 10% on your green
and then if the green target group behaves properly,
slowly or all at once, switch all traffic.
The advantage of using this technique is
that the ALB is responsible for redirecting request
and so you can switch all the traffic at once
from the target group blue to the one that is green.
If you decide to use a different architecture,
where you have one ALB per target group, then
you must be able to switch from one ALB to the next ALB.
And for this, we need to use a DNS.
And so Route 53 is helpful and you can switch using the DNS
from one ALB to the next ALB.
But this is something that happens
over time because your clients actually cache the result
of your DNS query.
And so the DNS switch is not as immediate.
You don't have as much control over it.
You cannot do all at once at any point of time.
You have to slowly and gradually wait for your clients
to refresh their DNS record to use the new ALB.
So it's a little bit slower, but that works.
If we are using API gateway,
there are different strategies as well.
So we have a production stage connected to a
v1 Lambda function.
And so currently all the client request
into your API gateway go through that stage.
But we can deploy a canary stage, a green stage
which is going to be connected, for example
to the v2 version of your Lambda function.
And then what's going to happen is
that the clients internally will be redirected
to the canary stage to send a little bit of traffic to it.
And if we're happy with the canary stage,
then we can promote it as well.
So the benefit of this is that we are in full control
of the network traffic and we can switch all traffic
at once from prod to the canary whenever we want to.
The alternative is to use a Lambda alias.
So in that case, we only have one stage
in the API gateway and it's not changing,
but instead the Lambda alias is pointing
to the v1 version of your Lambda function.
But we can deploy a v2
and control how fast and how much we switch traffic
from v1 to v2 on the alias.
No changes required to your API gateway
and no changes required to your clients.
Okay, so that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it and I will see you in the next lecture.

you can create a CloudWatch dashboard of metrics

that are provided by every services in AWS,

out of an EC2 instance.
That is a classic use case

if you wanted to so instead of defining,
